## Editor's Preliminary Remark.

The manuscript of the <term>Theory of Collective Measurement<note>original: "Kollektivmaßlehre." This work by Gustav Fechner is considered a foundational text in the history of statistics, focusing on the mathematical analysis of variation within groups of objects or "collectives."</note> was found only partially completed among <term>Fechner's<note>Gustav Theodor Fechner (1801–1887) was a pioneering German physicist and philosopher who founded psychophysics, the scientific study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensations.</note> posthumous papers<note>original: "Nachlass." The collection of manuscripts, letters, and unfinished work left behind after a person's death.</note>. It was therefore necessary on one hand to organize the existing material, and on the other, to supplement what was missing. To carry out both tasks, a plan for the structure of the *Theory of Collective Measurement* was drafted, which can be seen from the grouping of chapters in the Table of Contents (p. IX). Based on this plan, the arrangement of the material was determined—which, incidentally, was already in a fixed order for the first four chapters—alongside the identification of gaps with clear certainty.

In filling these gaps, the guiding intention was to complete the work in the spirit of its author, so that it would represent a self-contained whole rather than a series of fragments. For this reason, the existing chapters were first supplemented wherever they had remained incomplete. Furthermore, since individual chapters were entirely missing, a replacement for them had to be provided, limited to the most necessary explanations. However, every addition, even if it consisted merely of the inclusion of citations, was placed in square brackets and thus made identifiable.

With this, the work has certainly by no means attained the degree of perfection that its author would have given it. In particular, the second part would have gained significantly through the detailed explanations that were part of Fechner's intention. It was, however, not feasible to continue the supplementary investigations—which would have had to rely on newly collected research material—any further

## Editor's Preliminary Remark.

...to carry out, so that the <term>printing<note>original: "Drucklegung." This refers to the mechanical process of setting type and printing the book, which was a significant undertaking for complex scientific texts in the 19th century.</note> of the work, which had already been long delayed, would not be postponed any further. Rather, I endeavored—after **FECHNER’S** manuscripts were delivered to me in the spring of 1895—to bring the editing of them to a swift conclusion.

I would also like to note that the calculations, which serve to a great extent partly to verify and partly to establish the theory, were thoroughly checked or performed anew. Therefore, the responsibility for any potential <term>oversights<note>original: "Versehen." The editor is explicitly taking credit for the mathematical rigor, protecting Fechner's reputation from any errors introduced during the posthumous compilation.</note> must rest with me alone.

Strasbourg in Alsace, January 1897.

Dr. G. F. Lipps.

# Preface.

---

The present work has been planned by me for many years; material for it has been collected and progress made in its elaboration, but this has been interrupted many times by other works, laid aside for a long time, and thus the completion of the work has been delayed until now. At my age, it would not be advisable to delay it any longer if the work is to appear at all; I also believe that, after repeatedly returning to it, it may finally venture to appear—not indeed as a perfect work, but as a foundation for a further development of the <term>theory<note>original: "Lehre." While it can mean "doctrine" or "teaching," in this scientific context, Fechner is referring to his specific theoretical framework for statistics.</note> treated here. The following introductory chapter speaks more specifically about the task of this theory; and so let only the following general remarks find space here.

With the new name under which the theory appears here, I do not present it as an entirely new doctrine; rather, the previous state of its development simply did not yet suggest the need to establish it under a special name of its own. Everywhere, science specializes through the course of its growing development and accordingly demands distinct designations for its various fields. Now, the most general, interesting, and meritorious aspects of our theory that have existed until now are likely to be found in **QUETELET’S** *Letters on the Theory of Probabilities* <note>original: "Lettres sur la théorie des probabilités" (1846).</note> and his *Social Physics* <note>original: "Physique sociale" (1869). Adolphe Quetelet was a Belgian astronomer and statistician who applied probability theory to social data, famously developing the concept of the "average man."</note> (1869); and if one wishes, one can see in him the father of the **Theory of Collective Measurement** <note>original: "Kollektivmaßlehre." This is Fechner's term for the statistical study of groups or "collectives" where individual measurements vary but follow a predictable distribution.</note> just as one sees in **E. H. WEBER** the father of **Psychophysics**; <note>Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795–1878) was a physician whose work on the "just-noticeable difference" in sensation became the basis for Fechner’s Law in psychophysics, the study of the relationship between physical stimuli and mental sensations.</note> yet one will be able to convince oneself from the course of this work how much cause...

<summary>In this preface, Gustav Fechner explains that his work on the "Theory of Collective Measurement" was delayed for years due to other projects and his advancing age. He frames the book as a foundation for future study, linking its origins to the statistical work of Quetelet and the psychophysics of E. H. Weber.</summary>
<keywords>Gustav Fechner, Theory of Collective Measurement, Kollektivmaßlehre, Adolphe Quetelet, E. H. Weber, psychophysics, history of statistics, social physics</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues Fechner’s original preface. The previous page ended while discussing the work of Adolphe Quetelet, the Belgian astronomer and statistician. Fechner is explaining that while his work builds on Quetelet’s "social physics," it also seeks to correct and expand it.</meta>

# Preface.

---

...yet it was my goal not only to significantly expand upon his work, but also to go beyond it by way of correction.

In this regard, I put forward—on one hand as the main fruit, and on the other as the main root of the entire following investigation—the mutually verifying mathematical foundation and empirical confirmation of a generalization of <term>Gauss’s Law<note>original: "Gauss’sches Gesetz." Today more commonly known as the "Normal Distribution" or the "Bell Curve," which describes how random variables cluster around an average.</note> of random deviations. Through this, the restriction of that law to symmetrical probability and the relative smallness of deviations on both sides of the arithmetic mean is lifted. Consequently, previously unknown legal relationships emerge, the most important of which can be found summarized in § 33. Indeed, this generalization provides the most universal regulator for all relationships discussed in <term>Collective Measurement Theory<note>original: "Kollektivmaßlehre." Fechner’s term for the statistical study of groups or "collectives," which paved the way for modern mathematical statistics.</note>, just as the simple Gauss’s Law serves as the regulator for all physical and astronomical determinations of accuracy. One might even ask whether, in principle, one should not also recur to this more general law in those fields as well; regarding this, one should not ignore the remarks in § 8.

Insofar as Collective Measurement Theory rests upon a connection between observation and calculation in mutual relation, it may count itself among the exact sciences. However, the disciplines that lay claim to such a designation allow for very different degrees of certainty in their results. At the top stand mechanics, astronomy, and physics. <term>Physiology<note>The study of how living bodies and their parts function.</note> lags far behind because of the difficulties presented by the complexity and variability of its objects; and further still, due to even greater difficulties in this regard, stands <term>Psychophysics<note>Fechner’s own discipline, which he founded to study the mathematical relationship between physical stimuli (like light or sound) and mental sensations.</note>. Collective Measurement Theory shares these types of difficulties without being subject to the same fundamental difficulties as psychophysics; it surpasses the latter in practical interest, while falling far behind it in philosophical interest. Yet Collective Measurement Theory is not entirely lacking such interest, insofar as the subordination of chance to more general laws—which is integral to it—comes into play here in a field and in a manner that have not previously been subject to consideration.

<summary>Fechner argues that his "Collective Measurement Theory" generalizes Gauss’s Law to account for asymmetrical data, positioning his work as an exact science that brings mathematical order to the "chaos" of random chance.</summary>

<keywords>Gauss’s Law, Normal Distribution, Collective Measurement Theory, arithmetic mean, Psychophysics, statistics, mathematical foundation</keywords>

# Preface.

Regarding the form and breadth of many of the explanations, it should be taken into account that the work is intended not so much for <term>professional mathematicians<note>original: "Fachmathematiker."</note>, to whom the fundamental points considered here are already familiar, as for those who are concerned with the study and application of the theory without already possessing such prior knowledge.

Next, for the advancement of our theory, I would like to address a request to professional calculators. In the well-known tables that usually represent the <term>Gaussian probability integral<note>original: "Gauss’sche Wahrscheinlichkeitsintegral." A mathematical formula used to calculate the likelihood of a value falling within a specific range under the "Bell Curve."</note> of random deviations from the mean (<term>errors of observation<note>original: "Beobachtungsfehler."</note>) expressed as

-> $\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_{o}^{t} e^{-tt} dt$ <-

the argument *t* is only carried out to two decimal places. This is sufficient for the limited use that physicists and astronomers make of it, when supplemented by <term>interpolation<note>A mathematical method of estimating unknown values that fall between known values.</note> using first and second differences. However, for the far more extensive use to be made of it in <term>Collective Measurement Theory<note>original: "Kollektivmaßlehre." Fechner's term for the statistical study of groups or "collectives."</note>, this is the equivalent of reducing the numerical argument for the many calculations performed via <term>logarithms<note>original: "Logarithmen." Mathematical tables used to simplify complex multiplication into addition, essential for calculation before the digital age.</note> to only two or three digits and leaving intermediate determinations solely to interpolation. It would therefore be desirable, in the interest of our theory—which, by the way, is shared by the psychophysical method of <term>right and wrong cases<note>original: "richtigen und falschen Fälle." A classic experimental procedure in early psychology used to measure sensory sensitivity.</note>—if tables were available in which *t* is carried out to at least four decimal places<sup>1</sup>). This would partly spare the need for interpolation and partly facilitate it; in any case, I personally felt the painful absence of such tables while performing this work. Naturally, the size of the tables would thereby...

# I. Introduction.

§ 1. By a <term>collective object</term> <note>original: "Kollektivgegenstand." This is a foundational term in Fechner's work, referring to what modern statistics would call a "population" or a "data set" of individual measurements that vary randomly but belong to the same category.</note> (C.O. for short), I mean an object that consists of an indefinite number of specimens, varying by chance, which are held together by a concept of species or genus.

Thus, "man" forms a collective object in a broader sense; man of a specific gender, a specific age, and a specific race forms one in a narrower sense, just as generally that which one might call the "extent" of a C.O. changes according to the scope of the genus or species concept under which it falls.

The specimens of a C.O. can differ in space or time and, accordingly, form a spatial or temporal C.O. Thus, the recruits of a country or the ears of grain in a cornfield <note>original: "Kornfeldes." In 19th-century German, "Korn" often referred generally to the local staple grain, such as rye or wheat, rather than strictly maize.</note> can be considered specimens of a spatial C.O. Similarly, the (mean) temperature of January 1st, tracked at a given location over a number of years, provides as many specimens of a temporal C.O. Instead of January 1st, one could use any other day of the year; instead of a specific day, a specific month; instead of temperature, the barometric pressure, and so on, and one would thereby obtain specimens of just as many temporal C.O.s.

Anthropology, zoology, and botany are fundamentally concerned with C.O.s, since in these fields it is not a matter of characterizing individual specimens, but rather only with what pertains to a totality of them, which is grouped together from one perspective or another as a genus or species of greater or lesser scope. Meteorology, according to the examples just cited, offers in its non-periodic weather phenomena—

The specimens of a <term>C.O.</term> <note>abbreviation for "Collective Object" (Kollektivgegenstand)</note> are, on the one hand, determined qualitatively, and on the other hand, quantitatively—that is, by measure and number—and it is only with the latter determination that the <term>Theory of Collective Measurement</term> <note>original: "Kollektivmaßlehre." This is Fechner’s term for what we would now call "statistics" or "frequency distribution analysis."</note> is concerned. A C.O. actually makes the same demands regarding its quantitative determination as a single object; except that, in a certain (admittedly only a certain) respect, the specimens of the C.O. represent the parts of the single object. If, for example, we were dealing with recruits of a given country, the questions arise: how tall are the recruits on average, how strongly do the individual measurements fluctuate around their mean, how large are the largest and smallest, and how do the measurements of the recruits behave according to these determinations in individual birth-years, or among different countries? Such questions and related ones, to be considered later, can be raised for every C.O.; and insofar as a physical object has various distinct parts and dimensions, these questions can be raised for each of these parts and dimensions individually, and these can be treated as distinct C.O.s. Examples include the skull, brain, hands, and feet of a human; or the height, weight, and volume of the whole person or specific parts of the person. But quantitative ratios will also come into question, just as the ratios of the average height, width, and length of the skull command a special interest when comparing people of different races.

§ 2. Above all these individual questions, however, rises a more general one—the most important one that can be dealt with in this theory, and which accordingly will be dealt with in the following: the question of the law of how the specimens of a C.O. are distributed according to measure and number. By the term <term>distribution</term> <note>original: "Verteilung"</note>, however, we are to understand the determination of how the number of specimens of a given C.O. changes according to their size. In every C.O. existing in a large number of specimens, the smallest and largest specimens—in short, the <term>extremes</term>—occur most rarely, while those of a certain middle size occur most frequently. ### Introduction.

...general law, applicable to all or at least most <term>C.O.s</term> <note>Abbreviation for "Collective Objects" (Kollektivgegenstände). These are groups of individual things—like the heights of a regiment of soldiers—that are treated as a single unit for study.</note>, regarding the dependency of quantity on the size of the specimens? In fact, such a law can be established, and a primary task of the following pages will be to determine it.

From the outset, one might certainly doubt whether, given the extraordinary diversity of C.O.s, lawful distribution patterns of any general validity can be found at all. However, since by definition a C.O. consists of specimens that vary according to chance, the general laws of probability — and every mathematician knows that such laws exist — certainly apply to them. In fact, the distribution patterns of C.O.s are generally governed by these laws, whereas the same laws of probability in physical and astronomical measurements are considered only secondary for determining the reliability of the averages obtained; thus, in those fields, they play a completely different and far less essential role than in the <term>Measurement Theory</term> <note>original: "Maßlehre." Fechner is contrasting the "science of measurement" used in physics with his new statistical approach for groups.</note> of C.O.s. However, insofar as chance operates under specific external and internal conditions—which differ for various C.O.s—it is possible, despite all randomness, to distinguish different C.O.s by characteristic constants derived from their distribution patterns. It is in these constants that their distinctiveness from one another lies; and it is these that we must seek out, while taking the general laws of probability into account. 

Now, in this regard, people have always focused on the <term>arithmetic mean</term> <note>The simple average, calculated by adding all values and dividing by the total number of items.</note> of the specimens and have diligently sought to determine it for various C.O.s; alongside this, they have perhaps considered the extremes <note>The highest and lowest values in a data set.</note>, and more rarely the <term>mean deviation</term> <note>A calculation showing how much the individual values typically differ from the average; a measure of "spread."</note> from the mean. But as important as these defining elements are and will always remain, they have hitherto been considered too one-sidedly, while others, no less important in principle, are overlooked.

Insofar as the treatment of C.O.s, based on the totality of the aforementioned relationships, is subject to different perspectives and entails different methods of determination than those used in physical and astronomical measurements, the...

# Introduction.

...Measurement theory of <term>C.O.s</term> <note>Abbreviation for "Collective Objects" (Kollektivgegenstände). These are groups of individual items—such as the heights of people or the sizes of leaves—that are studied as a single unit to find patterns.</note>, or let us say briefly, **Collective Measurement Theory**, must be established and treated as a distinct field of its own kind, and this will be the task of the following pages.

Since our concept of the C.O. includes the idea of a **random variation** of the individual specimens, one might desire a definition of "chance" and an explanation of its nature at the outset. However, an attempt to provide such a definition from a philosophical perspective would yield little benefit for the investigation that follows. It must suffice here to state the factual viewpoint—which is of a more negative than positive character—that forms the basis for what follows. By a **random variation** of the specimens, I mean one that is as independent of a deliberate *will* <note>In this context, "will" refers to human choice or intentional design, such as a craftsman deciding exactly how long to cut a piece of wood.</note> aiming at a specific size, as it is of a **natural lawfulness** <note>original: "Naturgesetzlichkeit." Here, Fechner means a rigid, predictable mechanical law that would make every specimen identical.</note> regulating the size proportions between them. While either of these factors may play a part in determining the objects, only those changes that are independent of them are considered "random." Therefore, no **law of chance** can determine how large this or that individual specimen is, although it can determine within which size limits a given number of them will fall with this or that degree of **probability**.

This does not deny that, from the most general point of view, there is no such thing as "chance," insofar as the size of every individual specimen can be seen as necessarily determined by existing laws of nature under existing conditions. But we speak of "chance" as long as we are unable to ascend to a derivation of individual determinations from such general laws, nor to infer them from the available **facts**. To the extent that this is the case, chance ceases, and the applicability of the laws to be presented here ceases or is disrupted by it.

**Vocabulary:** Measurement Theory, C.O., Collective Measurement Theory, random variation, chance, natural lawfulness, probability, law of chance, facts.

<summary>Fechner defines "Collective Measurement Theory" as a new field and clarifies that "chance" refers to variations that aren't caused by intentional choice or known mechanical laws. He argues that while individual sizes are unpredictable, the group as a whole follows predictable laws of probability.</summary>

## II. Preliminary Overview of the Most Essential Points to be Considered in the Investigation of a C.O., and the Related Designations.

§ 3. The following compilation will serve to provide a more definite overview of the extent and character of the investigations we will be dealing with hereafter, and to orient oneself in advance regarding most of the designations to be used in context; however, a more detailed discussion of these points is reserved for the following chapters.

Given the accidental order in which the specimens of a <term>C.O.</term> <note>Abbreviation for "Collective Object" (Kollektiv-Gegenstand).</note> usually present themselves, one would neither be able to gain an overview of their relationships in terms of measure and number, nor would a methodical processing of them be possible if one were to leave their measurements—generally designated as *a*—in the same accidental order in which they were obtained and recorded in a so-called <term>original list</term> <note>original: "Urliste"; the raw record of measurements taken in the field or laboratory before any sorting occurs.</note>; therefore, they must first and foremost be ordered according to their size and listed in a table so ordered, a so-called <term>distribution table</term> <note>original: "Verteilungstafel"; what modern statisticians call a frequency distribution table.</note>. Now, if one does not have a large number of specimens of an object, each *a*—or at least most *a*—will appear only once in the table, and the size distances between the successive *a* will change very irregularly; but with numerous objects—that is, those for which many specimens are available, which are mainly to be presupposed for the following—many or most *a* provided by the scale and the estimation will occur repeatedly to a greater or lesser extent. Then, one sets up the distribution table so that in a column of *a*, each *a* is listed only once

The total number of *a* values that enter into a distribution table naturally matches the sum Σ *z*, which one obtains by adding up all the *z* values in the table; I designate this sum as *m*.

The construction of such a table is, so to speak, the first *step* one must take when processing a large-numbered <term>C.O.</term> <note>Abbreviation for "Collective Object" (Kollektiv-Gegenstand).</note> starting from the original list.

A second *step* is this: that one determines the <term>arithmetic mean</term> <note>original: "arithmetischen Mittelwert"</note>—to be designated as *A*—of the individual measurements and the positive and negative deviations from it, whose number *z* naturally matches the number of the deviating *a* values.

For this purpose, however, many other values that can be derived with mathematical certainty from the distribution table can also serve as the starting point for the deviations instead of *A*; through every other choice in this regard, new relationships come to light, which will be discussed later. Generally, I call the values used as starting points for deviations to develop such relationships <term>principal values</term> <note>original: "Hauptwerte"</note> and designate them with *H*. Thus, *A* is only a special case, the consideration of which has hitherto been the sole focus in the treatment of C.O.s; however, this entails an arbitrary restriction of the <term>theory of collective measurement</term> <note>original: "Kollektivmaßlehre"</note>, as will easily emerge from later remarks. Generally, I call deviations—regardless of which principal value they are made dependent upon—<term>collective deviations</term> <note>original: "Kollektivabweichungen"</note>.

# Preliminary Overview of the Most Essential Points; Terminology.

...empirical ones, which consist of more or less close approximations of them.

All laws of probability concerning chance in general—and the distribution laws of the <term>C.O.</term> <note>Abbreviation for "Kollektiv-Gegenstand" or Collective Object: a large group of individual items (like heights of men or weights of seeds) treated as a single mathematical whole.</note> are of this kind—have this in common: their fulfillment can be expected with greater certainty the larger the number of cases to which they refer. They possess a so-called ideal validity only in the case of an infinite number of cases, which does not preclude the fact that, even with an empirically obtainable number of cases, the confirmation of the laws in question occurs with a high degree of approximation. Insofar as we are always dealing in reality with <term>C.O.s</term> consisting of a finite number of examples representing just as many cases, I designate the deviations from the ideal legal determinations—which occur due to the finitude of the number of examples—as **insignificant** <note>original: "unwesentliche"</note>. Since these deviations occur indifferently in one direction or the other, I consider them to be caused by unbalanced coincidences; meanwhile, I designate those determinations valid for the assumption of an infinite number of cases (in our instance, examples) as **significant** <note>original: "wesentliche"</note> or **normal**. The general characteristic of an **insignificant** determination is that it disappears the more one increases the number of cases or examples, while adhering to the conditions that define the concept of the <term>C.O.</term>, so that one can assume it would vanish entirely given an infinite number of cases. Consequently, only items occurring in large numbers are suitable for the investigation of the laws in our case.

However, even with a small *m* <note>The total number of samples in the collection.</note>, the insignificance of a determination is proven by the fact that upon repeating the determination with the same small *m* using ever-new examples of the same object, the magnitude and direction of the determination change indefinitely. In contrast, in the case of a **significant** determination, a definite result of magnitude and a definite direction emerge more firmly in the average of a majority of repetitions, the larger the number of repetitions and the *m* of each individual one are.

# Preliminary Overview of the Most Essential Points; Terminology.

...regarding a given main value *H*, if every deviation of a value *a* into the positive from *H* corresponds to an equally large negative deviation of another value *a* from *H*, such that the same frequency *z* <note>In Fechner's notation, *z* usually refers to the frequency or number of times a specific value occurs.</note> corresponds to values *a* that deviate equally on both sides of *H*. In a <term>C.O.</term> <note>Abbreviation for *Kollektiv-Gegenstand* (Collective Object), a large group of individual items—like heights of men or weights of seeds—treated as a single mathematical whole.</note> consisting of a finite number of examples, one cannot expect to find a completely symmetric distribution regarding any main value at all, due to unbalanced coincidences. Naturally, a symmetric distribution cannot exist for several main values simultaneously. However, it is an important subject of investigation whether a main value can be found toward which the distribution increasingly approaches symmetry as the number of examples *m* in the <term>C.O.</term> increases. This is done in such a way that one could assume a truly symmetric distribution is reached at an infinite *m*; in which case—since an infinite *m* is unattainable—one can nevertheless speak of a symmetric probability of deviations.

§ 5. However, from a perspective other than the previous one, one can distinguish an ideal distribution table from an empirical one, as well as the ideal and empirical results that depend upon them. In the measurement of examples, one cannot exceed certain limits of precision, which are determined by the divisions of the scale and the estimates made between them. One can, for example, distinguish millimeters, or tenths of millimeters, or hundredths of millimeters, but nothing beyond that. For someone who only distinguishes millimeters, all individual measurements that stay within the limits of a single millimeter merge indistinguishably; thus, they attribute the total number of examples *z*—which are actually distributed across an entire interval of 1 mm—to a single value *a*, which forms the midpoint of this interval. Generally speaking, if *i* represents the smallest recognizable difference in measurement, then the frequency *z* for each value *a* in the empirical table actually belongs to the entire interval of size *i* between $a - \frac{1}{2} i$ and $a + \frac{1}{2} i$. By contrast, in the empirical table, it appears as if—and when using the table it is mostly understood as if—the measurement *a* itself occurred *z* times. In an ideal...

<meta>This page continues Fechner’s distinction between empirical data sets and the "ideal" mathematical models they represent. ### Preliminary Overview of the Most Essential Points; Terminology.

...that is, if measurement and estimation reached the limit of accuracy, the interval *i* <note>In Fechner's system, *i* represents the interval of measurement or the smallest unit of precision used in a data set.</note> would be reduced to an infinitely small value^1). The distinct values *a* within the table would thereby increase in number, while their frequencies *z* would decrease accordingly; thus, the ideal table would deviate from the empirical one.

In cases where the empirical interval *i* is very small, the results of the empirical table—insofar as they concern the magnitude and proportions of the derivable main values and main deviation values—do not differ significantly from those of the ideal table. However, generally speaking, the difference remains something to be considered, and it will be addressed later in instances where it becomes significant. Empirical determinations and proportions in which this difference is not adequately accounted for—where it is instead assumed that the frequency *z* of every value *a* belongs entirely to that specific *a*—I call *raw* <note>original: "rohe"</note>. Those where the difference is taken into account as much as possible, I call *precise* <note>original: "scharfe"</note>.

§ 6. In every case, one must seek to ascend from the results of the empirical table to the ideal results of the ideal table—consequently moving from the unessential to the essential, and from the raw to the precise. This requires a corresponding processing of the distribution tables.

In this regard, a distinction must be made between *primary* and *reduced* tables. By *primary tables* <note>original: "primäre Tafeln"</note>, I mean those obtained directly by organizing measurements from the raw data list; these present the same experiential data as the list, simply in an ordered fashion. I call those *reduced tables* <note>original: "reduzierte Tafeln"</note> in which the frequencies *z* are distinguished for larger measurement intervals than in the primary tables. Specifically, the *z* values are grouped into equal intervals across the entire table, and the total frequency *z* of these larger intervals is assigned to the centers of those intervals as "reduced values of *a*." This offers the advantage of producing a more regular progression of the frequencies *z* in the table and—

This applies no less to the arithmetic mean *A* of the table, yet as such an approximation, the densest value deserves special attention and provides the basis for a more precise approximation through calculation in a manner to be considered later. Whether it be empirical or ideal, conceived in this or that approximation, I designate it generally with ***D***.

### Preliminary Overview of the Most Essential Points; Terminology.

However, it will be one of the most important results of the following investigation that a significant deviation between the arithmetic mean and the densest value is rather the general case, such that the magnitude and direction of this deviation are themselves characteristic of different collective objects <term>Kollektiv-Gegenstände; Fechner's term for groups of data points that belong together, such as heights of a population or measurements of a star</term>. Insofar as the deviations regarding both values maintain different ratios, the empirically densest value *D* must be recognized as an important principal value distinct from the arithmetic mean *A* of the same table—that is, a starting value for collective deviations.

To the two previous principal values *A* and *D*, however, a third must be added, distinct from the previous two, which I will designate as the **central value** or **value-middle** with *C*. This is the value of *a* that has just as many larger *a* above it as smaller ones below it, and in this respect, it divides the series of *a* right through the middle. It amounts to the same thing if one says it is the value for which the number of positive deviations is equal to the number of negative ones. It differs from the arithmetic mean by two definitions: first, while for *A* the sum of the deviations on both sides is equal <note>This means the total sum of positive and negative deviations is zero, balancing the scale.</note>, for *C* the *number* of deviations on both sides is equal; and second, while for *A* the sum of the squares of the deviations is a minimum (i.e., smaller than for any other starting value), for *C* the sum of the simple deviations (calculating the negative ones by their absolute values) is a minimum in the same sense¹. With the addition of this third principal value to the two previous ones, new characteristic relationships for collective objects now open up, which will be discussed later.

### § 8.
An animal is characterized, according to its internal structure, by the brain, heart, stomach, liver, etc., the size and position of these organs relative to one another, and the pathways leading to and from them. In the same way, a Collective Object <term>Kollektiv-Gegenstand; Fechner’s term for a group of individual values that belong together, such as the heights of people in a city</term> is characterized, according to its internal quantitative determination, by the arithmetic mean, central value, densest value, and other principal values that may be included; the size and position of these principal values relative to one another and the deviations from them. These values stand in a mathematical relationship to one another no less than those organs stand in an organic relationship. A Collective Object forms, so to speak, a **mathematical organism**, which is capable of a dissection <note>Fechner uses the word *Zergliederung*, which can mean analysis or an anatomical dissection, reinforcing his biological metaphor.</note> that will be explored in the following sections. It may be noted in advance that, under a certain assumption, the two principal values *D* <note>densest value or mode</note> and *C* <note>central value or median</note> would coincide with *A* <note>arithmetic mean</note>, and consequently all three would coincide with one another. This would happen under the assumption that the deviations on both sides of *A* possessed a **symmetrical probability**—that is, as *m* <note>the number of cases or measurements</note> grows, they approach a symmetrical distribution (in the sense mentioned above) such that with an infinite *m*, one could view such symmetry as having been achieved. But it will be shown that for Collective Objects, one must instead assume an **asymmetrical probability** of the deviations regarding *A*. According to this, as *m* grows, one does not approach a symmetrical distribution, but rather an essentially asymmetrical distribution that can be reduced to a certain law. This approach undoubtedly stems from the fact that the guiding principles of physical and astronomical measurement theory have been transferred to Collective Measurement Theory <term>Kollektivmaßlehre; Fechner’s pioneering branch of statistics dealing with varying natural phenomena rather than fixed physical constants</term> without taking into account <gloss>two essential differences</gloss> that exist between the two. This oversight makes that restricted approach as justified for the former discipline as it is prohibited for the latter. For the former, the <gloss>arithmetic mean *A*</gloss> of the observed values of a single object (whose measurement is to be determined) possesses <gloss>the dominant, and essentially only significant, meaning</gloss>, along with the deviations from *A*—that is, the observational errors. This is because, for reasons known to professional mathematicians and physicists, the <gloss>arithmetic mean</gloss> is the value for which the sum of the squares of the deviations (errors) is the smallest possible. At the same time, this mean is seen as the value that, with overwhelming probability, comes closest to the **true value** which we seek to determine. In the deviations from it, one finds a means to determine the size by which the true value might still be missed on one side or the other with a given probability.

Why, then, in that discipline <note>Referring to physics and astronomy</note> should one bother with other principal values, since neither they nor their deviations help fulfill the task of that science! Therefore, there is no mention of either a densest value or a central value in astronomical and physical measurement theory, despite the fact that the various observation values of one and the same object, taken as *a*, could just as easily give rise to the derivation of a *D* and *C* as the various...

For Collective Measurement Theory <term>Kollektivmaßlehre; the study of groups of varying objects, such as the heights of a population, rather than single fixed constants</term>, however, the viewpoint that allows the arithmetic mean and its deviations to be fundamentally preferred in physical and astronomical measurement theory has no significance at all. <gloss>All instances of a Collective Object, no matter how far they deviate from the arithmetic mean or any other principal value, are equally real and true,</gloss> and a preferential consideration of one over the other from a viewpoint that is equally invalid for all of them naturally makes no sense. Secondly, however, in physical and astronomical measurement theory, the three principal values do not differ significantly from one another—except through unresolved random chance—owing to the symmetrical probability of observation errors relative to the arithmetic mean of the observations (a symmetry that is admittedly postulated or presupposed rather than proven beyond doubt in cases of good observation). Thus, in the arithmetic mean of the observed values, which is preferred for the reasons stated, one simultaneously finds the most probable values of the other principal values. In contrast, for Collective Objects, as noted, an <gloss>asymmetric probability</gloss> of deviations relative to the arithmetic mean is to be regarded as the general case, according to which the various principal values also diverge significantly.

Furthermore, it may even appear questionable whether one is truly in the right with that postulate regarding observation errors—a question that does not essentially concern us here, but will be considered later in a special chapter¹). # Preliminary Overview of the Most Essential Points; Designations.

§ 9. In the analysis of a Collective Object <term>K.-G.; shorthand for Kollektiv-Gegenstand, referring to a group of varying individual items treated as a single whole</term>, I will generally understand the following values under the following designations, some of which have been used previously, as the *elements* or *determining components* of such an object.

1) The total number of specimens, generally designated as *m*, of the instances *a* within a distribution table under consideration.

2) The "principal values" <term>Hauptwerte</term> or starting points for measuring deviations, generally designated as *H*. As previously noted, the most important of these are the arithmetic mean *A*, the central value *C* <note>Known today as the median</note>, and the densest value *D* <note>Known today as the mode</note>. Since the central value is generally to be sought between *A* and *D*, as will be shown later, I will henceforth list these three principal values in the order *A*, *C*, *D*. In addition, there are several other principal values of secondary importance, which will be discussed in Chapter X.

The arithmetic mean determined from the values *a* of a "primary table" <note>Raw data in its original form</note> will be designated as *A₁*; that determined from a "reduced table" <note>Data that has been grouped or simplified into categories</note> will be designated as *A₂*. The same applies to *C*. For *D*, no such distinction is made, because—due to the irregularities of the available primary tables—it could only ever be derived from reduced tables, and would thus always be designated as *D₂*. On the other hand, a distinction must be made according to the method of derivation. When derived by what I call the "proportion method," in which I place the most confidence, I designate it as *Dₚ*; when derived by the less certain "interpolation method," I designate it as *Dᵢ*. The difference between these two procedures will be discussed further on.

All values that fall on the positive side of the principal value to which they relate shall be designated with a small stroke above; all those that fall on the negative side with a small stroke below. Meanwhile, for those that relate to both sides without distinction, I shall omit the strokes entirely. Accordingly, *a'* designates a value *a* that exceeds *H*, while *a⸝* designates one that is exceeded by *H*.

By Θ <note>The Greek letter Theta</note>, I generally mean deviations from any principal value *H*; thus, by Θ' = *a'* — *H* a positive deviation, and by Θ⸝ = *a⸝* — *H* a negative one...

Regarding the **arithmetic mean** $A$ in particular, the sums of the deviations on both sides, $\Sigma \Theta'$ and $\Sigma \Theta_{\prime}$, are necessarily equal; this is because it is inherent in the very concept of this mean <note>The arithmetic mean is the "balance point" of a data set, where the sum of distances to the right equals the sum of distances to the left.</note>. This entails that the one-sided **mean deviations** <term>mittlere Abweichungen</term>—defined as $\epsilon' = \Sigma \Theta' : m'$ and $\epsilon_{\prime} = \Sigma \Theta_{\prime} : m_{\prime}$ relative to $A$—are also generally unequal. ->$\epsilon = \frac{\Sigma \Theta' + \Sigma \Theta_{\prime}}{m} = \frac{\Sigma \Theta}{m}$<-

Instead, this is only the case if, when calculating the mean from $\epsilon'$ and $\epsilon_{\prime}$, one takes into account the **weights** <term>Gewichte</term> assigned to them by virtue of the $m'$ and $m_{\prime}$ from which they were obtained. One must therefore set:

->$\epsilon = \frac{m' \epsilon' + m_{\prime} \epsilon_{\prime}}{m' + m_{\prime}},$<-

which leads back to $\epsilon = \Sigma \Theta : m$ according to the following simple observation: Since the product of a mean of deviations and their count is equal to the sum of the deviations, then $m' \epsilon' = \Sigma \Theta'$ and $m_{\prime} \epsilon_{\prime} = \Sigma \Theta_{\prime}$. Thus, $m' \epsilon' + m_{\prime} \epsilon_{\prime} = \Sigma \Theta' + \Sigma \Theta_{\prime} = \Sigma \Theta$; on the other hand, $m' + m_{\prime} = m$.

### Preliminary overview of the most essential points; Terminology.

I content myself in the presentation of the elements generally with stating the common, i.e., uncorrected values $\Sigma\Theta$ and $\epsilon$, from which, by drawing on the always known $m$ <note>m represents the total number of observations or the sample size.</note>, the corrected values can easily be found, if it is necessary to do so. A similar remark will undoubtedly apply to the sums of deviations and mean deviations relative to principal values <note>Principal values refer to measures of central tendency, such as the mean or median.</note> other than $A$, even though direct investigation in this regard has so far only extended to the deviations from $A$ <note>A represents the arithmetic mean.</note>. However, there is all the less reason to prefer corrected values when citing and utilizing the elements obtained with a given finite $m$, because not only the sums of deviations and mean deviations relative to the various principal values, but also the deviations of the principal values themselves from one another, are under the influence of the same finite $m$; thus, their proportions would not be changed by the common correction. When investigating the laws of distribution <term>Verteilungsgesetze</term>, however, we are much more concerned with these proportions than with absolute values.

Where one does wish to use absolute values, however, regarding the correction of the one-sided values $\Sigma\Theta'$, $\Sigma\Theta_{,,}$, and $\epsilon'$ <note>These represent the sums of deviations and the mean deviation on just one side (positive or negative) of the central point.</note>, the note must be made that the correction is not to be done through $\sqrt{m' : (m' - 1)}$ and $\sqrt{m_{,,} : (m_{,,} - 1)}$ respectively, but rather, like that of $\Sigma\Theta$ and $\epsilon$, through $\sqrt{m : (m - 1)}$. This is because otherwise, by adding the corrected one-sided values $\Sigma\Theta'$ and $\Sigma\Theta_{,,}$, one would not recover the corrected total sum $\Sigma\Theta$. There is also the rational consideration that the sums of deviations on each side, as components of the total sum of deviations, must be jointly influenced by the size of their total $m$.

5) The **probable deviation $w$ and root mean square deviation $q$**. By probable deviation $w$ relative to a principal value, we mean that deviation which has just as many larger deviations (by absolute value) above it as smaller ones below it; thus, it has the same significance for the deviations $\Theta$ as the **central value $C$** <note>The central value *C* refers to the median; the "probable deviation" is essentially the median of the absolute deviations.</note> has for the raw values $a$. By **root mean square error $q$**, I mean in short the square root of the mean squared deviation; that is, the value obtained when one takes all deviations from a principal value $H$ specifically to the...

§ 10. When two values $\alpha, \beta$ are connected by round parentheses in the following manner, such as $(\alpha)(\beta)$, this expression is equivalent to $\alpha\beta$, i.e., the product of $\alpha$ and $\beta$. However, if they are connected by square brackets in the following manner: $\alpha[\beta]$, this does not mean that $\alpha$ is to be multiplied by $\beta$, but rather that $\alpha$ is a **function** of $\beta$. Thus, for example, $\Theta[A]$ designates a deviation from $A$, $\Theta[C]$ a deviation from $C$, and so on; $m[A]$ is the total number of deviations relative to $A$; $m[C]$ is the same relative to $C$, and so forth.

However, since the principal values $A$ <note>The arithmetic mean.</note> and $D$ <note>Likely the "Dense Value" (mode or median), representing the most frequent value in the set.</note> are used with such great frequency, the expressions and formulas relating to them would become inconvenient and cumbersome through such additions. Therefore, I generally prefer to use different simple designations for $\Theta, m, \epsilon$ depending on their dependence on $A$ or $D$. This will be done using the following designations placed under the respective principal values. Without a prime symbol, these refer indistinctly to the deviations on both sides; however, depending on whether they belong specifically to the positive or negative side, they are to be provided with a **prime** <term>Strichelchen</term> either above or below:

# Preliminary Overview of the Most Essential Points; Designations.

In deciding whether the expressions "higher," "lower," "upper," and "lower values" refer to the position in the table or the ratio of the values' magnitudes, a conflict arises. To avoid this somewhat tiresome formal conflict, it would be better in the future to have the distribution tables begin with the largest value $a$; however, since I followed the usual method of arrangement through the earlier, larger part of my investigations, I could no longer change it without rebuilding my tables and running the risk of confusing myself. The little marks above and below the values <note>original: "Strichelchen oben und unten"; these refer to the primes and subscripts such as $\mu'$ and $\mu_{\text{,}}$ introduced on the previous page.</note> refer in any case to the ratio of the magnitude of the values, not their positional relationship in the table.

Following this, we must discuss the meaning and manner of designation for the following expressions, which play an essential role in our investigations.

By **pre-count** <note>original: "Vorzahl"</note> and **pre-sum** <note>original: "Vorsumme"</note>, I mean respectively the number $\Sigma z$ <note>The sum of the frequencies of the values.</note> and the sum $\Sigma a$ <note>The sum of the actual measurement values.</note> of the $a$ which precede a given value $a$ of the table in magnitude; by **post-count** <note>original: "Nachzahl"</note> and **post-sum** <note>original: "Nachsumme"</note>, I mean those which follow a given value $a$ of the table in magnitude. Naturally, these counts and sums change according to the values $a$ in the table that they precede or follow, and to prevent verbosity, I am also introducing special designations here for the cases that must be primarily considered in applications. 

Generally, let $v, V, n, N$ denote the pre-count, pre-sum, post-count, and post-sum respectively regarding any initial $a$ and final $a$ under consideration in a given table distribution. Let $\mathfrak{v}, \mathfrak{V}, \mathfrak{n}, \mathfrak{N}$ denote the respective values regarding the $a$ to which the largest $z$ belongs—that is, the <term>empirically densest value</term> $D$ <note>The mode; the most frequently occurring value in the data set.</note>. Finally, let $v_i, \mathfrak{V}_i, n_i, \mathfrak{N}_i$ refer to an $a$ whose surrounding interval is to be interpolated for the precise determination of the elements in a manner to be specified later; incidentally, in most cases, this coincides with the previous value, the densest value, in which case the designation by the index can be omitted.

The former is not only by far the more frequent case and therefore to be considered to a greater extent than the second, but also the simpler case to handle. All definitions and designations in this chapter initially refer to this case; however, without including the second case, the entire investigation would lack the necessary generality.

The essential difference between the two methods of treatment is this: In the **arithmetic treatment**, the deviations of the individual *a* <note>The measurement values.</note> from their principal values are understood in the usual sense as arithmetic—that is, as positive and negative differences from their principal values—and the principal values themselves are determined directly from the *a* of the distribution table according to specified rules. In the **logarithmic treatment**, the deviations one operates with are understood as logarithmic—that is, as differences of the logarithms of the *a* from so-called logarithmic principal values. These are principal values derived from the log *a* according to the exact same rules as the arithmetic principal values are derived from the simple *a*. The transition from arithmetic to logarithmic treatment brings with it several new perspectives, definitions, and designations, which will only be discussed later when the occasion arises (see especially Chapter V (§ 36) and XXI).

To find $\log \exp[-t^2] = \log 1 : \exp[t^2]$, add $2 \log t$ to $0.637\ 78 - 1$ (that is, to the $\log$ of the *Mod.* <note>The "Modulus" is the conversion factor between natural and common logarithms, $\log_{10} e \approx 0.4343$.</note>), look up the resulting number in the logarithm tables and treat it as a negative value; you will then have the required logarithm$^2$), but in a form that deviates from the common one and is unsuitable for using logarithm tables to derive $\exp[-t^2]$ itself. Thus, if $\log \exp[-t^2]$ were found to be $-0.25$ or $-1.25$ or $-2.25$, one would have to set it as $0.75 - 1$; or $0.75 - 2$ or $0.75 - 3$, and so on.

## III. Preliminary Overview of the Research Material and General Remarks Thereon.

§ 12. A significant difficulty for an investigation such as this lies in the acquisition of the necessary material. Such material can only be sought in a plurality of <term>C.O.s</term> <note>original: "K.-G.", abbreviation for *Kollektiv-Gegenstände* or "Collective Objects." These are groups of similar items, like heights of people or weights of plants, used to study statistical variation.</note> from various fields. Each of these must be available in such a large number of individual examples that the randomness of distribution in terms of measurement and count can be considered balanced—or nearly so, as absolute balance is impossible—according to the <term>Law of Large Numbers</term> <note>A mathematical principle stating that as a sample size grows, its mean gets closer to the average of the whole population.</note>. Furthermore, for each of these, the other requirements to be asserted in the following chapter must be seen as nearly fulfilled. Finally, the information provided must contain all the data necessary for processing.

However, for many types of <term>C.O.s</term> that could not be bypassed if the investigation were to have the required generality, nothing at all was previously available. And while for others there is no lack of information—indeed, for some, such as <term>Recruit Measurements</term> <note>Data sets recording the heights or physical dimensions of military conscripts, a common source of 19th-century "social physics" data.</note>, there is an <note>original: "embarras de richesse"</note> embarrassment of riches—the existing versions do not satisfy all the demands that must be placed upon them for the purposes of this investigation. As for one's own measurements, only a few objects are at one's disposal; and since it is necessary to measure many specimens of each and record them in <term>Distribution Tables</term> <note>A chart showing how often different values occur in a group.</note>, time and patience easily find their limits in this equally patient and tedious business.

Nevertheless, I have succeeded, through what was at times a laborious and circuitous route, in bringing together the material listed below for our investigation, of which, admittedly, some...

# IV. Requirements; Abnormalities.

§ 13. If a <term>collective object</term> <note>Original: *Kollektiv-Gegenstand* (K.-G.). In this context, it refers to a set of individual specimens or data points that belong to a single category but vary randomly in their measurements, such as the heights of people or the weights of seeds.</note> is to allow for a successful investigation, it must fulfill certain conditions. These conditions arise partly from its very definition and partly from more general scientific perspectives.

According to the explanation provided in the introduction, a collective object should be something graspable under a specific concept, whose quantitative measurements fluctuate by chance across an indefinite number of specimens. Now, it is impossible to possess an infinite number of specimens; however, as previously discussed, one must strive to obtain as many as possible—so many that the ideal laws of chance (which strictly apply only to an infinite number) can still be confirmed with an approximation sufficient for the intended degree of accuracy. 

But even if this condition is sufficiently met, a collective object must also be "normal" or "flawless"—to use a brief expression—from other perspectives. This ensures it complies with the formal rules that can be established as the most general for collective objects that are not subject to such flaws.

Foremost among these requirements is that specimens are neither grouped together into a collective object, nor excluded from it, based on any criteria other than what is grounded in the core concept of the object. Thus, the object must not only be numerous from the previous perspective, but also complete, in the sense that all specimens presenting themselves within the limits of its definition are actually counted. One must not allow one part or another of the <term>measurement scale</term> <note>Original: *Maßskala*. This refers to the range of possible values or measurements within the data set.</note> to be omitted due to this or that secondary consideration, whereby the object, so to speak—

§ 14. It is certain that the boundary between healthy and pathologically altered skulls cannot be determined with absolute certainty, and a similar uncertainty regarding the delimitation of the subject matter recurs in many other cases. However, if this uncertainty remains within such narrow numerical limits that the "boundaries of uncertainty"—which one must tolerate due to unresolved random fluctuations—are not exceeded, then no significant disadvantage can arise for the whole. One may find satisfaction in the results themselves if the object, delimited to the best of one’s judgment, conforms to the normal laws of distribution—or if one can trim away enough specimens until that is the case.

However, a very important question arises here: it is, of course, logically self-evident that if healthy individuals (or parts of such, like skulls) are to be investigated regarding the distribution ratios of their specimens, then those recognized or assumed to be diseased must not be mixed in. It is no less self-evident that determining the ratios for healthy specimens is of greater interest than for a mixture of healthy and diseased ones. Yet, it seems to run contrary to the universality of the task of the <term>Doctrine of Collective Measurement</term> <note>Original: *Kollektivmaßlehre*. Fechner's term for the statistical study of groups and frequency distributions.</note> to prefer a <term>collective object</term> <note>Original abbreviation: *K.-G.* (*Kollektiv-Gegenstand*).</note> consisting only of healthy specimens over an object consisting of a mixture of healthy and diseased ones for the purpose of establishing the most general laws of distribution.

### Requirements; Abnormalities.

Indeed, even if pathologically altered skulls fall outside the concept of healthy ones, they still fall under the concept of skulls in general. What, then, justifies us, when seeking the most general laws for <term>collective objects</term> <note>Original: *K.-G.* (*Kollektiv-Gegenstände*). These are groups of individual things—like leaves on a tree or heights of soldiers—that can be analyzed as a single unit using statistics.</note>, in excluding diseased skulls? We could instead simply apply the broader concept that includes all skulls, rather than the narrower one of healthy ones. In fact, there are countless other cases where a similar choice between a narrower or broader definition exists. Strictly speaking, such a choice exists everywhere, since ultimately all collective objects can be united under the concept of an "existing being," which can then be narrowed in various directions. 

However, we would fare poorly if we attempted to validate our supposedly universal laws against very broad definitions of collective objects. They would fail to hold up, or would do so only imperfectly. In contrast, these laws remain consistent across the most diverse collective objects when the definitions are kept sufficiently narrow, thereby proving their general validity. The question now arises: what viewpoint is decisive for determining how much we should limit the scope of our definitions?

This seemingly difficult question is to be answered with consideration for the following factual circumstances.

If we mix objects that—when defined narrowly enough—each correspond to the distribution laws common to the most diverse objects, then the following condition must be fulfilled if the mixture is to still correspond to those same laws: The constants or essential elements by which the distribution ratios are determined—that is, at least the <term>arithmetic mean</term> <note>The mathematical average of a set of values.</note> and the <term>mean deviation</term> <note>A measure of how much the individual values in a set typically vary from the average.</note> from it, upon which other elements more or less depend—must not deviate further from one another for the constituent objects than can be explained by unresolved chance. By this standard, we can distinguish between "unanimous" and "disparate" objects: those that fulfill this condition and those that do not. Furthermore, we can distinguish between "unified" and "divided" objects: those composed of unanimous objects and those composed of disparate ones. Every expansion of the concept

It can also be readily conceded that if we were to significantly increase the sample size ***m*** of the student recruit measurements and then sort them into departments based on various criteria—for example, according to their origin from villages or cities, or from different birth years or different social classes—provided these departments still had a sufficient ***m*** to reliably discover subtle differences in the <term>essential elements|wesentlichen Elemente; the core statistical markers such as the mean, median, or distribution curve</term>, there would be no lack of such differences which run contrary to perfect unanimity; and nothing prevents us from making this a task for investigation.

But if these differences are only small, and the various divisions that one can make according to the most diverse points of view—and thus the differences between the elements themselves—vary with a character of randomness, then it can not only be reasonably assumed, but the fact itself teaches us, that the relevant differences of the elements merge indistinguishably into the unavoidable unbalanced chance occurrences and present no essential obstacle to the validation of the fundamental laws.

§ 16. All the less, however, should one see a contradiction to these laws in the deviations shown by the distribution patterns of an overly broad and therefore <term>discordant collective object|zwiespältiger Kollektiv-Gegenstand; a data set that contains two or more distinct groups with different characteristics, which "splits" the expected bell curve</term>. It is, in principle, sufficient to know the mixing ratios and the essential elements of the component objects within a discordant object in order to calculate the distribution patterns of the composite object according to the fundamental laws themselves; thus, even in this respect, they maintain their general validity.

### Requirements; Abnormalities.

Generally, it follows from the preceding that when determining and testing the most fundamental **laws of distribution**, we must be careful in two ways. First, we must not use the widely divergent distribution results of objects that are too broadly defined or improperly mixed to argue against the universal validity of laws established for sufficiently narrow, uniform objects. Second, when choosing between the results of a broader and a narrower definition, all other things being equal, we must prefer those of the narrower definition for establishing these fundamental laws. The following considerations are essentially subordinate to these previous points.

The origin of the individual specimens of a <term>collective object|K.-G. (Kollektiv-Gegenstand); a group of individual items considered as a single unit for statistical analysis, like "the height of recruits"</term> from different places or times, or both simultaneously, easily leads to not just qualitative, but also quantitative differences between them. This deserves special attention because, in order to obtain a sufficiently large ***m*** <note>m refers to the sample size or the number of specimens measured</note> for a successful investigation, one usually feels prompted or forced to assemble the collective object from specimens belonging to different locations or times; indeed, they cannot belong to exactly the same space and time.

In this regard, a conflict arises. Grouping specimens from very distant or very broad regions and time periods risks uniting disparate objects and thereby missing the fundamental distribution patterns. Conversely, grouping specimens from too narrow spatial and temporal boundaries gives <term>unbalanced chance occurrences|unausgeglichene Zufälligkeiten; random statistical noise or outliers that have not yet been smoothed out by a large sample size</term> too much influence to derive essential determinations with any degree of certainty. The boundaries to be maintained in this respect cannot be drawn <term>in advance|a priori; reasoning from theory rather than from observation</term>. Ultimately, success itself must decide whether the assumed temporal or spatial breadth of the object leads to a satisfactory fulfillment of the fundamental laws of distribution. If not, the narrowing must be pushed further. If this leads to values of ***m*** that are too small to obtain results of sufficient certainty, the investigation must [continue] until a larger number of...

§ 17. Regarding the question of whether an object is composed of disparate <note>meaning: essentially different or distinct in kind</note> components, the following relationships within the distribution tables—some of which have already been mentioned—deserve special attention.

The foundation of our fundamental laws is that the *z* <note>frequency of occurrence</note> rises continuously with the *a* <note>the measured value</note> up to a certain size of *a*, but as *a* continues to grow, the frequency descends just as continuously. This results in a maximum of *z* in the middle part of the distribution table (at the so-called most frequent value <note>original: "dichtesten Werte"; in modern statistics, this is known as the "mode"</note>) and two minima at the beginning and end of the table respectively (at the extreme values of *a*). If one takes the *a* as the abscissae <note>the horizontal or x-axis</note> and the *z* as the ordinates <note>the vertical or y-axis</note>, one can represent the legal distribution graphically in the familiar way. This produces a curve which, when the intervals *i* are small, rises smoothly to a peak and descends again from there. However, in what I call "primary" tables—that is, those derived directly from the original lists of measurements—one will generally find an irregular rising and falling of *z* throughout the entire table as *a* continuously grows. This results in a bumpy quality to the distribution curve; the primary distribution tables in Chapter VII provide sufficient examples of this. In any case, the most general and indeed never-failing cause of such irregularities lies in unbalanced random chance. The "bumps" in the curve caused by this disappear through a sufficiently far-reaching reduction of the table—that is, according to the explanation given earlier (§ 6), by combining the *z* values for equal intervals of *a* across the whole table, as demonstrated in Chapter VIII and supported by examples of reduced tables. However, the cause may also partly lie in the fact that <term>Collective Objects|K.-G. (Kollektiv-Gegenstände); groups of individual items considered as a single unit for statistical analysis</term> of disparate character in their principal values have been mixed together.

Indeed, it can already be seen from a general perspective that if we, for example, wanted to mix the measurements of an equal number of men and women, whose arithmetic mean and most frequent value differ greatly from one another, this would essentially...

# Requirements; Abnormalities.

...that is, apart from uncompensated random factors <note>original: "Zufälligkeiten"; referring to noise or outliers in the data</note>, an occasion for the emergence of two **maximum-*z*** <note>original: "Maximal-z"; the point of highest frequency in a data set</note>, and thus two most frequent values <note>original: "dichtesten Werte"; in modern statistics, this is called the "mode"</note>, would arise. Indeed, by mixing even more disparate objects, distribution tables with significantly more **maximum-*z*** could emerge. In any case, only distribution tables with a single **maximum-*z** in the main body of the table are suitable for testing the fundamental laws of distribution, whereas small irregularities toward the ends of the table are of no significant consequence. Therefore, if distribution tables are present that do not meet this condition, they are only useful for testing the laws after a **reduction** <term>Reduction: The process of grouping data into larger categories (intervals) to smooth out random fluctuations.</term> that brings them into compliance through sufficient leveling of random factors. After this, the relevant laws can still be very well confirmed on the reduced table, provided that the plurality of **maximum-*z*** in the main body of the table really only depended on uncompensated random factors.

However, it should not be ignored that since the intervals of a distribution table are increased by its reduction, the plurality of **maximum-*z***—which may depend on the disparate <note>essentially different or incompatible</note> nature of the table's components—can disappear along with the uncompensated random factors. This happens if these peaks fall near each other at values of *a* <note>the measured value</note> that jointly enter into the interval increased by the reduction, and thus become indistinguishable. Indeed, one only needs to go as far as one likes with the reduction (and the accompanying increase of the intervals) to surely achieve this result. Thus, while we should maintain the rule of reducing a table to just one **maximum-*z** (with the *z* values descending from there in both directions) before testing its distribution, any possible deviation from the fundamental laws might still depend on a disparate nature of the table's components that was blurred by the reduction. Consequently, in this regard as well, only the investigation of the distribution itself can be decisive.

# Requirements; Abnormalities.

...are subject—despite the intentions that prevailed during their creation—to the <term>laws of collective measurement</term> <note>These are the statistical laws governing how measurements are distributed around a mean in a large group.</note> regarding the determination of sizes, which still leave free room for chance. However, if secondary considerations or auxiliary purposes significantly restrict the freedom of chance by favoring or excluding certain dimensions, these laws can be substantially undermined, as illustrated by the following examples.

Visiting cards, as well as the so-called business cards of merchants and manufacturers, are seen to vary in the most diverse ways in both length and width. I initially thought I had an excellent subject for testing our laws here, as they can be obtained in great numbers—whether from daily correspondence or from the sample books of their makers, in which specimen copies are pasted (many of which I have used for measurements from various manufacturers). They also offer the advantage that one has more control over the accuracy of measurement and estimation than with many other objects. But although they by no means completely escape our laws—whether measured by length or by width—they offer only a very imperfect confirmation of them, the reason for which can be found in the following circumstances.

Despite all the variation in their dimensions, the freedom of chance is restricted by the fact that manufacturers generally prefer those dimensions that allow the cardboard sheets, from which the cards are cut, to be utilized as fully as possible—that is, to be consumed as completely as possible. Additionally, they tend to maintain certain particularly popular ratios between width and length, especially 2:3 or 3:5 (approximations of the **golden ratio** <note>original: "goldene Schnitt"; a mathematical ratio of approximately 1.618, often considered aesthetically pleasing</note>). Indeed, during the measurements of such cards that I performed in the sample books of several manufacturers, I became convinced that for each of them, certain dimensions occur more frequently than could be regarded as accidental. Regarding natural objects, on the other hand, one of the requirements dictated by the concept itself is that the individual specimens do not exist in a state of natural dependency upon one another that steps outside the laws of chance. This point is particularly relevant for meteorological <term>collective objects</term> <note>German: "Kollektiv-Gegenstand" (K.-G.). A technical term in this work referring to a group of individual cases that can be treated as a single statistical population.</note>. Thermometer and barometer readings, as well as other meteorological values, show a lawful rising and falling at every location—though disturbed in detail by chance occurrences—that clearly manifests in average values, both throughout the hours of a day and no less through the days or months of a year. These so-called periodic meteorological values do not fall under the concept of a collective object; rather, only the non-periodic values do, insofar as they can be viewed as changing by chance. We shall have to go into this somewhat more specifically here, as there will be frequent occasion to return to them. To proceed from the specific concepts of an example by <term>Quetelet<gloss>Adolphe Quetelet (1796–1874), a Belgian astronomer and statistician who was a pioneer in applying social statistics to human behavior.</gloss></term> (see Quetelet’s *Letters*, last vertical column of the table on p. 78), let us assume that the temperature of all January days—calculated as the mean between the minimum and maximum temperature of each day at a specific location (Brussels)—has been observed for 10 years. This is far too small to study the laws of distribution. In contrast, we will obtain an *m* = 310 for the entire month of January as a collective object if we follow Quetelet’s procedure. In his example, he combines the 31 daily temperatures of January for the 10 years as individual instances of "January daily temperature." This yields 310 instances. From these, we calculate the arithmetic mean by dividing by 310, take the 310 deviations $\Delta$ from that mean, and, if we wish, determine other primary values and their deviations from them.

Now, it is certainly clear from the outset that—aside from random fluctuations—the temperature in January naturally increases from the 1st to the 31st day. By doing this, we create a complication: we are mixing random variation with a natural, law-governed progression of daily values. It is similar with all so-called irregular periodic changes.

In this regard, it seems useful to me to make the remark that there is a very simple means of convincing oneself both of the requirements of pure chance for such cases and of the lack of satisfaction <note>The failure of natural data to meet the requirements of pure randomness.</note> by these cases.
