Furthermore, if instead of the previous designation of successive lottery numbers, we mark every instance of a number exceeding the previous one with a $+$ and every instance of it falling below the previous one with a $-$, we find by following a large number of entries (setting aside unbalanced coincidences) that the number of alternations is twice as large as the number of sequences. However, if we do the same with a corresponding designation of successive meteorological daily values, the number of alternations falls far short of double the number of sequences. This is a second proof that the rising and falling of meteorological values from day to day does not obey the pure laws of chance. This investigation, which I am only sketching out for now in order to return to it in a later chapter, is completed and refined by also taking into account the probable and mean deviations from the laws of chance—deviations which depend on the finiteness of the sample size <italic>m</italic> <note>In statistics, "m" or "n" usually represents the number of observations or data points in a set.</note>—to account for unbalanced coincidences, since those laws strictly apply only to an infinite <italic>m</italic>. Indeed, formulas can be established for this purpose.

From a thorough investigation, it has now become clear to me<sup>1</sup>) that while the meteorological values of successive days within the same month show the aforementioned signs of dependence to an eminent degree, even the monthly deviations of successive years are not entirely free of them. However, they show this so weakly and with so little certainty that one need not fear any significant disruption of the laws of chance when using them. This subject undoubtedly deserves an even more thorough and extensive investigation by professional meteorologists using these criteria, in the interest of meteorology itself, than I—

To illustrate this, let us imagine an urn with an infinite number of white and black balls, marked with numbers that correspond to the magnitudes of deviation from a given main value. Specifically, let the frequency of each kind of ball match the frequency of the corresponding deviation values as they exist for pure laws of chance. Thus, in the case of symmetrical probability, ***Gauss's Law*** <note>Original: *Gauss'sche Gesetz*; now commonly known as the Normal Distribution or Bell Curve, which describes how data clusters around an average.</note> regarding deviations from the arithmetic mean would be represented in this way; in the case of asymmetrical probability, our more general law, to be discussed later, would be represented. In this model, white balls represent positive deviations and black balls represent negative ones. 

If many draws are now made by chance from this urn, the proportions of the drawn balls will correctly represent the law in question—aside from the remaining, unbalanced coincidences that result from the number of draws always being finite. But the same will still be the case if two, three, or more balls, which are close to each other in value, are glued together—whether according to a specific rule or not—so that they can only be drawn out together. In this scenario, a larger number of draws, a larger sample size *m*, would be required to achieve an equally good fulfillment of the laws in question compared to the case with loose balls.

Accordingly, I did not shy away from the effort of extracting the data for the *Geneva* rainfall amounts from all the volumes of the *Geneva* journal in which they appear. This is because they exhibit an enormous asymmetry, which causes the main values to fall far apart, while simultaneously offering very large average deviations in relation to those main values. As a result, they elude the applicability of standard arithmetic methods of treatment (see *Chapters XXI*, as well as *XXVI* and *XXVII*). And it is undoubtedly of particular interest that such diverse things as painting dimensions and rainfall amounts collectively submit to such specific and peculiar laws of distribution as we shall have to establish.

It was stated above that QUETELET established the temperature of every day of each month as the mean between the maximum and minimum temperature of each day (for Brussels) and continued this for 10 years. The deviation between these two temperatures, for which the daily temperature serves as the mean, is what QUETELET calls the "diurnal variation." In this regard, one must clearly keep in mind that this deviation of the two daily extremes from each other can be large or small even with the same mean temperature between them—that is, the same daily temperature—and consequently, the <term>successional dependence<gloss>Successionsabhängigkeit: The statistical tendency for one measurement (like temperature) to be influenced by the measurement immediately preceding it in time.</gloss></term> shown by daily temperatures does not necessarily need to extend to the diurnal variations. Indeed, the same daily temperature, for example 10°, can result from a mean of 9.5° and 10.5°, from 8° and 12°, or from 5° and 15°, which yields variations of 1°, 4°, and 10° respectively; indeed, if the temperature remained entirely constant on a given day, it could be as high or low as you like, and the variation would still be zero. Just as QUETELET followed the temperature of the days of each month through 10 years—which can be treated as specimens of a <term>collective object<gloss>K.-G. or Kollektiv-Gegenstand: Fechner's term for a group of varying individual items that can be analyzed as a single unit using probability laws.</gloss></term>—so too he followed the corresponding diurnal variations, in which one can see specimens of another collective object. While QUETELET did not specify the diurnal variations for every day of every month—which would have required tables of enormous size without allowing for a clear summary—he did provide tables on pp. 410 and 411 indicating how often over 10 years the diurnal variation amounted to between 0° and 1°, between 1° and 2°, between 2° and 3°, and so on; in short, <term>reduced interval tables<gloss>reduzierte Intervalltafeln: Frequency tables that group raw data into specific ranges or "bins" to show the distribution of values.</gloss></term> in the sense of our later (VIII.) chapter.

# Requirements; Abnormalities.

If, as remarked above, the <term>diurnal variations<gloss>original: "variations diurnes"</gloss></term> appear essentially independent of the magnitude of the daily temperatures occurring between them, and therefore do not necessarily need to share the <term>successional dependence<gloss>Successionsabhängigkeit: the tendency for one day's weather to be similar to the day before, which complicates simple probability math.</gloss></term> of those temperatures, then another factor also seems to contradict such a dependence. Specifically, the tables of monthly diurnal variations—with a sample size ($m$) that fluctuates between 282 (February) and 309 to 310 (January and August)—show a progression so regular and a correspondence with the laws of <term>asymmetric distribution<gloss>A statistical pattern where data does not cluster symmetrically around a central point, often leaning more toward one side.</gloss></term> so good that one would hardly expect it if successional dependence were present. Nevertheless, the table of July temperatures provided by *Quetelet* on page 78, when compared with the associated table of diurnal variations on page 411, shows that the progression of the values ($x$) in both tables is similar and equally regular. Thus, even without assuming the aforementioned independence, one could—based on the principle just discussed—view this table as useful in the sense that we shall employ it.

## § 22. Further general remarks on this subject:

In general, I shall designate points where <term>collective objects<gloss>original: "K.-G." (Kollektiv-Gegenstände): groups of similar individual items that can be measured as a whole.</gloss></term>—even with a sufficiently large sample size ($m$), and thus disregarding unresolved chance occurrences—evade the proof of our laws as **improprieties** or **abnormalities**; however, objects that are free from these shall be called **unobjectionable**. As we can see, these **abnormalities** are of various types and can impair the validity of the laws in very different respects and to varying degrees. It can be considered a general task of <term>Collective Measure Theory<gloss>Kollektivmaßlehre</gloss></term> to determine the influence of these abnormalities. This can be done partly theoretically, with regard to the distribution laws identified in error-free objects, and partly empirically. The latter can be achieved in two ways. # Requirements; Abnormalities.

...exactly correspond to flawless distribution laws, then apply one abnormality or another to them and derive the effect on the values of the elements and their ratios from that result.

Here lies a field of investigation for others, as I have by no means sufficiently settled this matter, given the already extensive task of determining the ratios of <term>Collective Objects<gloss>original: "K.-G." (Kollektiv-Gegenstände): Fechner’s term for groups of individual items or measurements that can be treated as a single statistical unit.</gloss></term> under the assumption of flawlessness.

In every respect, perfectly flawless objects with a large *m* <note>The variable *m* typically represents the total number of individual cases or the sample size.</note> are hardly obtainable given the diversity of possible errors. Therefore, regarding the objects which serve empirically to establish or prove the fundamental laws of collective objects—aside from the deviations from ideal, lawful distribution ratios due to the finiteness of *m* and the size of *i* <note>The variable *i* refers to the "interval" or class width used when grouping data into a frequency table.</note>—deviations due to a lack of fulfillment of the requirements, or simply due to "faultiness," must be permitted, provided they remain within sufficiently narrow limits so as not to raise doubts against the validity of the established fundamental laws themselves. Of course, a certain amount of subjective discretion always remains in this regard. Values and ratios that are removed from deviations caused by the finiteness of *m*, the size of *i*, and the failure to meet requirements, I shall hereafter call—in addition to the term "fundamental" already used—**normal** or **ideal**, insofar as they only occur in reality as approximations.

Moreover, one can see from the above where the difficulty lies for <term>Collective Measurement Theory<gloss>Kollektivmaßlehre: The name Fechner gave to his statistical system, which he viewed as an "exact" science of measuring mass phenomena.</gloss></term> in bringing its applications to completely certain results, despite the fact that it can be counted among the "exact" doctrines based on the viewpoints given in the preface. These difficulties involve different points than those existing for physiology and <term>psychophysics<gloss>The scientific study of the relation between stimulus and sensation, a field Fechner pioneered.</gloss></term> in this regard; but they lead to a similar outcome. Nevertheless, it remains a merit of all these doctrines, as exact sciences, to push certainty in individual cases as far as possible on the one hand, and to lead to general laws on the other.

# V. Gauss’s Law of Random Deviations (Errors of Observation) and its Generalizations.

§ 24. ### Gauss’s Law and its Generalizations.

...law must be introduced first. While it has long been known and familiar to professional astronomers and physicists—who use it to calculate the <term>probable error<gloss>a statistical measure of the range within which a measurement is likely to be accurate</gloss></term> when determining a <term>mean of observations<gloss>original: "Beobachtungsmittel"; the average of multiple scientific measurements</gloss></term>—I must also address a broader audience and different ways of applying the law. Therefore, instead of starting with the unpopular <term>integral expression<gloss>a complex mathematical formula involving calculus</gloss></term> of the law, I will begin with the easily understandable tabular expression into which the law can be translated, and indeed must be translated everywhere for practical use. Later (Chapter XVII), we will return to the law by starting from its integral expression; for now, the following will suffice.

What is stated here about the law are only its essential characteristics in the sense discussed in § 4; however, insofar as the law holds at all, one may expect to come closer to these characteristics the more the number of values—and thus the deviations to which it refers—multiplies. Let us now discuss this law specifically in its application to <term>collective deviations<gloss>deviations found in groups of natural objects, such as the varied heights in a population, rather than just errors in human measurement</gloss></term>. § 25. This is done under the assumption of a symmetrical probability of deviations relative to the arithmetic mean *A* and a large—strictly speaking, infinite—number *m* <note>the total number of individuals or observations in the set</note> upon which the derivation of *A* is based. One must keep in mind that this determination can be empirically distorted by unresolved coincidences the smaller the number *m* underlying the derivation of *A* (and thus the *m* of these deviations themselves) is. $^1)$ In short, Gauss's Law is a distribution—

# Gauss’s Law and its Generalizations.

...law of deviations and the values *a* that deviate from it, under the assumptions stated above.

Suppose one has a multi-numbered <term>Collective Object<gloss>Fechner’s term for a large dataset or population of similar items, like the heights of men in a city</gloss></term> (K.-G.) before them which satisfies the requirements given in the previous chapter. From the individual specimens—which, as noted, are to be designated as *a*—one has calculated the <term>arithmetic mean<gloss>the average value, found by adding all values together and dividing by the total number of items</gloss></term> *A* = $\Sigma$ *a* : *m* <note>The sum ($\Sigma$) of all values *a* divided by the number of items *m*</note>. From this, one has taken the positive and negative deviations $\pm$ *$\Theta$* of every single value *a* from the mean *A*. From the sum of these deviations *$\Theta$*, regardless of their sign (that is, using their absolute values), one has calculated the mean *$\varepsilon$* = $\Sigma$ *$\Theta$* : *m*. According to the explanations provided earlier, this value is the so-called simple <term>mean deviation<gloss>a measure of how much the individual values typically differ from the average</gloss></term> relative to *A*, which shall be considered here simply as the "mean deviation."

§ 26. To explain the application of this law by looking at its prediction for a specific case: we wish to find the number of deviations that fall between the mean *A* (where the deviation *$\Theta$* = 0) and a specific deviation limit of *$\Theta$* = 0.25 *$\varepsilon$*. Or, what is essentially the same thing, the number of values where the ratio *$\Theta$* : *$\varepsilon$* ranges from 0 to 0.25. According to a table into which <term>Gauss's Law<gloss>G. G.; the "Normal Distribution" or bell curve</gloss></term> can be translated, this number is found to be 15.81 percent of the total number *m*, or 0.1581 *m*. This assumes that the number is tracked on both sides of the mean *A* up to the same limit and then added together. For any deviation limit other than *$\Theta$* : *$\varepsilon$* = 0.25, the same table gives a different relative number of deviations; but let us first illustrate the previous determination with a concrete example.

Let us assume we have 10,000 <term>recruits<gloss>young men drafted for military service, a common source of data for 19th-century statisticians</gloss></term>. We have determined their mean height *A* and their mean deviation *$\varepsilon$*, finding the former to be 71.7 inches and the latter to be 2.0 inches (values which are close to the measurements of student recruits in Leipzig). Under the assumption that Gauss's Law applies here, 1,581 recruits would fall between *A* + 0.25 *$\varepsilon$* on one side and *A* − 0.25 *$\varepsilon$* on the other—that is, between 71.2 and 72.2 inches <note>Since 0.25 times the mean deviation of 2.0 equals 0.5 inches</note>. § 28. To judge the validity and applicability of Gauss's Law to empirical data <note>"Empirical data" refers to information gained through observation or experiment rather than theory alone.</note>, we must return to the fact that it is based on the assumption of a symmetrical probability of the deviations $\Theta$ from the average $A$ on both sides. This is based on the condition that, assuming a large—strictly speaking, an infinite—number of cases $m$, for every deviation $\Theta$ on the positive side, an equally large deviation $\Theta$ on the negative side is to be expected. The ratio numbers $\Phi$ and $\varphi$ are to be viewed as expressions for the probability of occurrences up to given limits of their deviation from $A$, or within given intervals of this deviation.

As has already been noted, this does not exclude the possibility that, despite the fundamental validity of the law, more or less significant empirical deviations from its requirements occur under the conditions it assumes. This happens because the condition of an infinite number of cases $m$ cannot be fulfilled in practice. Therefore, deviations from the law's requirements can only be used as an argument against it if increasing the number of cases $m$ does not help bring these deviations closer to disappearing. In short, they only count if they cannot be blamed on unresolved "accidents" caused by the finiteness of $m$. There is no lack of evidence regarding this, which will be discussed in its proper place. But first, let us follow the consequences of the law assuming its fundamental validity.

<summary>This page explains that while Gauss's Law assumes a perfect, symmetrical distribution in an infinite sample, real-world data will always show minor deviations because our sample sizes are finite. It highlights that the probability of finding extreme deviations drops off rapidly as one moves away from the average.</summary>

# Gauss’s Law and its Generalizations.

In the preceding section, it was indicated how the ratio number $\Phi$ <note>$\Phi$ (Phi) represents the proportion or percentage of cases falling within a certain range.</note> and the absolute number $m \Phi$ <note>$m$ represents the total number of observations; $m \Phi$ is the actual count of cases.</note> for both sides combined depend on the value $\pm \Theta : \varepsilon$, up to which one tracks them in both directions. If this is done for only one side, then according to the assumed symmetrical probability, the absolute number up to the given limits on each side must be taken as half as large as if it had been tracked for both sides up to the same limit of deviation. However, since the total number of both sides combined also reduces to ½ $m$ for each side given a large—strictly speaking, an infinite—$m$ according to that same symmetrical probability, the ratio numbers for each side (respectively $\Phi'$ and $\Phi_{,,}$) calculated according to Gauss's Law remain equal to the total ratio number $\Phi$. In contrast, the one-sided absolute numbers ½ $m \Phi'$ and ½ $m \Phi_{,,}$ are to be assumed, according to Gauss's Law, as half as large as the two-sided number $m \Phi$ up to the same limit $\pm \Theta$.

Empirically, of course, the equality of the absolute numbers on both sides up to the same limit does not hold because of unresolved random occurrences; but Gauss's Law abstracts from these random occurrences and presupposes the case where the difference $m' - m_{,,} = u$ vanishes compared to $m$. It would therefore also be incorrect to take $\varepsilon$ <term>$\varepsilon$ (epsilon); the mean deviation, a measure of how spread out the data is</term> as $\Sigma \Theta' : m'$ for the calculation of $\Phi'$, and as $\Sigma \Theta_{,,} : m_{,,}$ for that of $\Phi_{,,}$. Instead, for both $\Phi'$ and $\Phi_{,,}$, just as for $\Phi$, the value $\varepsilon = \Sigma \Theta : m$ calculated from the totality must serve. Otherwise, contradicting the assumption of symmetrical probability that underlies Gauss's Law, one would obtain different numbers of deviations on both sides up to the same limits of deviation. Furthermore, QUETELET <note>Adolphe Quetelet (1796–1874) was a Belgian astronomer and statistician who applied the normal distribution to human characteristics, such as height.</note>, in his comparison tables between calculations according to Gauss's Law and observation, understood it no differently. It is different, of course, where an asymmetrical probability of deviations (regarding $\Delta$) exists, as is actually the case with collective deviations <note>The term "collective deviations" refers to data sets that do not fit a perfect bell curve, requiring more complex mathematical models.</note>; there, Gauss's Law is generally only applicable with a modification to be discussed later. Above all, however, it is necessary to start from the purely conceived Gauss's Law itself, and so we follow its consequences even further.

# Gauss’s Law and its Generalizations.

The number of deviations on both sides is equal and essentially coincides with the arithmetic mean *A*—with respect to which the sum of the deviations on both sides is equal—that is, the two can only deviate from one another due to unresolved random occurrences. For if, according to symmetrical probability <note>original: *W.*, short for *Wahrscheinlichkeit* (probability)</note>, for every positive $\Theta$ on one side an equally large $\Theta$ is to be expected on the other, then with an equal sum, an equal number of deviations on both sides must also be expected. However, the requirement that, by virtue of symmetrical probability, the difference $u = \pm (m' - m_{,})$ between the number of positive and negative deviations vanishes more and more as *m* grows, refers not to the absolute size of *u*, but to its ratio to the total number *m* (i.e., $u : m$). This is because *u* itself, according to known laws of chance, grows in proportion to $\sqrt{m}$ as *m* increases; but this value vanishes compared to *m* all the more the larger *m* is, and vanishes entirely when *m* is infinite. Moreover, despite the absolute growth of *u* in proportion to $\sqrt{m}$, the direction of the difference remains inherently undetermined.

That, assuming the validity of Gauss’s Law <note>original: *G. G.*, standing for *Gauss’sches Gesetz*</note>, the densest value *D* <term>The "densest value" refers to the mode, or the value that appears most frequently in a data set.</term> also essentially coincides with *A*, follows from an inspection of the $\phi$-table. This is because the number of deviations (and consequently the deviating values *a*) on both sides for equal intervals is greater the closer the intervals come to *A*. It is therefore greatest in the intervals adjacent to *A* itself and encompassing it, no matter how small one makes them.

# Gauss’s Law and its Generalizations.

§ 30. Hereafter, I come to the reasons which provide the occasion to go beyond the simple <term>Gauss’s Law (G. L.)</term>, as it has been explained thus far, when dealing with "collective deviations."

Gauss himself did not establish the law for collective deviations—meaning the variations of individual specimen sizes *a* from their arithmetic mean—but, as is well known and noted, for "errors of observation," meaning the deviations of individual measured values of a single object from their arithmetic mean. In itself, it is anything but self-evident that the law should be transferable from the latter to the former. Indeed, from the outset, it is something quite different to face deviations obtained because of a lack of precision in measuring instruments or the senses and accidental external disturbances during the repeated measurement of a *single* object, as opposed to deviations which the many specimens of a <term>collective object (C. O.)</term> <note>The author uses "K.-G." for *Kollektiv-Gegenstand*, referring to a group of natural objects, like a population of plants or people.</note> present from their arithmetic mean for reasons rooted in the nature of the objects themselves and the external circumstances influencing them. It could therefore not be predicted at all *a priori* <note>from theoretical deduction rather than observation</note> that nature, in these deviations from the mean, follows the law of errors of observation; rather, it first required a direct test of the law on collective objects themselves.

At the same time, according to both <term>QUETELET’S</term> and my own experience, it has been shown that depending on the type of C.O., the deviation between *U'* and *U* or the deviation between *m'* and *m,,* follows a specific direction; thus, while its size exceeds the value that could be expected due to unbalanced chance, its direction is simultaneously characteristic of one or another kind of C.O.

Now, I designate it as **asymmetry** in general whenever a deviation exists between *U'* and *U* or *m'* and *m,,*; but since such a thing will rarely be absent due to unbalanced chance, one must distinguish **essential asymmetry**—as that which cannot be made dependent on unbalanced chance—from **unessential or accidental asymmetry**—as that which can be made dependent on it.

### Special laws of essentially asymmetric distribution for <term>Collective Objects</term> (C.O.) where their relative fluctuation is not too strong.

1) **Starting Law.** To arrive at a distribution that can be captured under a simple rule and that corresponds to experience, the deviations must be calculated from the **densest value** *D* <note>The "mode," or the most frequent value in a set</note>, rather than from the arithmetic mean *A*. In cases of essential asymmetry, *D* also deviates essentially from *A*. This rule leads back to the standard rule of Gauss’s Law in cases where the essential asymmetry vanishes and *D* essentially coincides with *A*.

2) **Two-sided Gauss’s Law.** Briefly stated, the distribution of deviations relative to *D* follows the same rule on each individual side as is followed jointly for both sides in a symmetric probability distribution relative to *A*. The only difference is that instead of the standard values for $m$, $\Theta$, and the mean error $\varepsilon = \Sigma \Theta : m$ <note>$\Sigma$ denotes the sum of the individual errors $\Theta$, and $m$ the number of cases</note> relative to *A*, we use specific values for each side. On the positive side, we have $m'$, $\Theta'$, and $\varepsilon' = \Sigma \Theta' : m'$, and on the negative side, we have $m_{\prime}$, $\Theta_{\prime}$, and $\varepsilon_{\prime} = \Sigma \Theta_{\prime} : m_{\prime}$ relative to *D*; with this...

In this regard, the same tables—the $\epsilon$-table and $t$-table <note>Statistical reference tables used for calculating the probability of certain deviations</note>—remain useful for distribution calculations on each side individually, just as they would be applied together for both sides in a calculation according to Gauss’s Law <note>original: "G. G." for *Gauss'sches Gesetz*</note> in the case of symmetric probability <note>original: "W." for *Wahrscheinlichkeit*</note> relative to the arithmetic mean $A$. Let us now, in the sense of the convention established in § 10, replace the general designations $m', m'', \Sigma\partial', \Sigma\partial'', \epsilon', \epsilon''$, which apply to any principal values, with $m', m'', \Sigma\partial', \Sigma\partial'', e', e''$ insofar as they relate to the densest value $D$. Consequently, the positive and negative relative deviation counts $\Phi'$ and $\Phi''$, as well as the absolute numbers $\Phi' m'$ and $\Phi'' m''$, and likewise $\varphi'$ and $\varphi''$, $\varphi' m'$ and $\varphi'' m''$ on each side, also transform into functions of these designations.

3) **Law of Proportion.** The deviation counts <note>The number of individual observations or cases</note> on both sides, $m', m''$, relative to the densest value <note>The mode</note>, behave like the simple mean deviations $e', e''$—that is, like $\Sigma\partial' : m'$ and $\Sigma\partial'' : m''$ relative to $D$; therefore:

->$m' : m'' = e' : e'' = \frac{\Sigma\partial'}{m'} : \frac{\Sigma\partial''}{m''},$<-

from which the following are corollaries <note>original: "Korollare"</note>.

a) The squares of the deviation counts on both sides, i.e., $m'^2, m''^2$, behave like the sums of deviations on both sides $\Sigma\partial', \Sigma\partial''$, thus:

->$m'^2 : m''^2 = \Sigma\partial' : \Sigma\partial''.$<-

b) The densest value $D$ can itself be determined as the value whose deviation counts and mean deviations satisfy the law of proportion. Indeed, generally speaking, I consider this to be not the most convenient, but the most accurate method of determination, and I will state later (Chapter XI) how it is to be carried out. For the sake of brevity, it may be called the proportional method, and the $D$ determined in this way, when it is necessary to refer explicitly to this method of determination, shall be designated as $D_p$. This $D_p$ can then be compared with the empirically determined $D$—that is, the value where the maximum number $z$ falls in a distribution table. From the fact that it deviates from it only within the limits of allowable uncertainty, one can find one of the proofs for the validity of our asymmetric lawfulness.

Fechner proposes using this mathematical relationship as the most accurate way to calculate the mode, calling this the "proportional densest value" (Dp).</summary>

4) **The Distance Laws.** The distances between the three principal values <note>The arithmetic mean, median, and mode</note> are determined as follows. Let $m''$ be the total number of observations, $\Sigma \delta''$ the total sum, and $e'' = \Sigma \delta'' : m''$ the mean of the deviations on the same side as $C$ or $A$ relative to $D$ (depending on whether one is seeking the distance of $C$ or $A$ from $D$). That is, those deviations which go toward the same side of $D$ on which $C$ or $A$ lies, whether this be the positive or negative side. Meanwhile, the index with two lower dashes <note>referring to the subscript $_{,,}$</note> shall have the corresponding meaning for the values on the opposite side. Thus, according to § 131, we find:

->$C - D = t'' e'' \sqrt{\pi},$<* <note>$\pi$ refers to the mathematical constant Pi, approximately 3.14159</note>

where $t''$ represents the value of $t$ that corresponds to

->$\Phi = \frac{m'' - m_{,,}}{2 m''},$<-

or simply $\Phi''$, in the table of $t$ values. Furthermore:

->$A - D = \frac{\Sigma \delta'' - \Sigma \delta_{,,}}{m}$<-

a value which, according to the law of proportion, agrees with $2 \Phi'' e''$, as shown in § 131, according to which one can also set:

->$A - D = 2 \Phi'' e'' = \frac{(m'' - m_{,,}) e''}{m''}.$<-

From this, $A - C$ is found as the difference of the two previous distances:

->$A - C = (A - D) - (C - D) = (2 \Phi'' - t'' \sqrt{\pi}) e'',$<-

where $\Phi''$ and $t''$ are determined in the manner specified.

5) **The $\pi$-Laws.** For the case that usually occurs, where the distance of $C$ from $D$ has a small (strictly speaking, infinitely small) ratio to the mean deviation $e'$ or $e$ on the side where $C$ lies relative to $D$ (simply $e''$), one notably has:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| $\frac{C - D}{A - D}$, or simply $p = \frac{\pi}{4} = 0.785 40$ | $(\log = 0.895 09 - 1)$ |
| $\frac{A - C}{A - D} = \frac{4 - \pi}{4} = 0.214 60$ | $(\log = 0.331 63 - 1)$ |
| $\frac{C - D}{A - C} = \frac{\pi}{4 - \pi} = 3.659 79$ | $(\log = 0.563 46 \quad )$ |

§ 34. It has been explicitly mentioned that the previous laws can be considered sufficient for cases where the proportional fluctuation of the <term>Collective Objects</term> <note>Original: "K.-G." or *Kollektiv-Gegenstände*. This refers to groups of individual items or observations that form a single distribution</note> is not too strong (in the sense of § 9, page 19). However, in cases of strong proportional fluctuation, a further generalization of the <term>Gaussian Law</term> <note>Original: "G. G." or *Gauss'sches Gesetz*. This is the famous "Normal Distribution" or bell curve</note> is required. Now, we must specify what gives rise to this and how this generalization should be understood.

The Gaussian Law, by its very nature, can only be an approximation law, even with an infinite number of observations ($m$), and was declared as such by <term>Gauss</term> himself$^{2)}$; for it sets no limit to the size of the deviations from the average ($A$) in either direction, but rather only allows the probability of those deviations to decrease further and further as their size increases.

# Gaussian Law and its Generalizations.

It is obvious, however, that if the deviations from the <term>Arithmetic Mean</term> (*A*) in the negative direction were to become larger than *A* itself, the resulting values *a* would become less than zero, which is impossible <note>In many biological or physical measurements, such as height or weight, a value cannot be negative. This reveals a flaw in applying a standard bell curve—which extends to infinity in both directions—to such data</note>. Thus, the <term>Gaussian Law</term> <note>original: "G. G." or *Gauss'sches Gesetz*. Also known as the Normal Distribution or the "bell curve"</note> cannot claim unlimited validity from the outset, even if it remains valid with the greatest approximation for cases where the deviations from the arithmetic mean—at least the vast majority of them—remain close to it and are, on average, very small. However, what applies in this regard to negative deviations from *A* according to the pure Gaussian Law applies no less to the negative deviations regarding *D* <note>The "mode" or densest value</note> and the previous generalization (and thus modification) of the Gaussian Law. There are <term>Collective Objects</term> <note>original: "K.-G." or *Kollektiv-Gegenstände*. This refers to groups of individual items or observations that form a single distribution</note> in which the relative fluctuation around *D* is so great that the previous principle of generalization is no longer sufficient.

According to this, a generalization of the Gaussian Law for application to Collective Objects must be distinguished in two directions or in a double sense: 1) insofar as collective deviations do not show the symmetrical <term>probability</term> <note>original: "W." or *Wahrscheinlichkeit*</note> attributed to errors of observation regarding the arithmetic mean, where the case of asymmetry can be seen as the more general one, encompassing symmetry only as a special case; 2) insofar as collective deviations—though not in all, but in the majority of Collective Objects—do not show the low relative fluctuation around the <term>principal values</term> <note>The central tendencies like the mean or mode</note> that is typical of errors of observation.

Since those Collective Objects that can be handled with a generalization of the Gaussian Law in the first direction are not only far more numerous but also much easier to treat than those requiring the even broader generalization in the second direction—and since the presentation of the second principle is made easier by first addressing the first—this priority has been given here. § 35. So far, we have only kept in mind <term>arithmetic deviations</term> <note>Differences calculated by subtraction, e.g., $a - H$</note> relative to any <term>main values</term> <note>A general term for central measures like the mean, median, or mode</note>—that is, those that can be understood as positive and negative differences from them; and usually such things, as will continue to happen here, are understood simply as deviations. I denote them generally, as stated, with $\Theta$. But one can also speak of **ratio deviations** relative to given main values—that is, ratios in which a given main value $H$ is exceeded or fallen short of, which we will generally denote with $\psi$. Thus, if $\Theta = a - H$ is an arithmetic deviation, then $\psi = a : H$ is a ratio deviation; and while we distinguish between $\Theta'$ and $\Theta,$ as positive and negative arithmetic deviations (depending on whether $a > H$ or $a < H$), we distinguish from the same point of view $\psi'$ and $\psi,$ as **upper and lower ratio deviations**.

While strong arithmetic deviations from a main value lead downward into the negative—below the magnitude of the main value itself—and thus become impossible <note>For example, if the average height is 170cm, a negative deviation of 200cm would result in a height of -30cm, which is physically impossible</note>, this does not apply to strong lower ratio deviations. Rather, however far they may go down, they only lead to increasingly smaller fractional values of the main value, which remain just as positive as the main value itself to which they refer; for negative ratio deviations do not exist at all. There are only positive ones: those that exceed 1, and those that (as proper fractions) do not reach 1. Accordingly, one might consider that the <term>distribution law</term>—in order to remain just as applicable to relatively strongly fluctuating <term>collective objects</term> <note>original: "K.-G." or *Kollektiv-Gegenstände*; groups of items forming a distribution</note> in the downward direction as to weakly fluctuating ones—might fundamentally be relatable to ratio deviations instead of arithmetic deviations.

Thus, an exact proportionality of the average magnitude of deviations with the average size of the objects is not to be expected from the outset. 2) That as long as the arithmetic deviations are relatively small compared to their main value—meaning that only a relatively slight fluctuation around it occurs, as is presupposed in the Gaussian Law—the ratios of the arithmetic deviations noticeably coincide with those of the corresponding logarithmic ones. This is not only mathematically provable but also empirically demonstrable using logarithm tables, by comparing the differences between logarithms with the differences between their corresponding numbers.

Thus, even in the case of relatively weak fluctuation, we could advantageously make use of the logarithmic principle as the most generally sufficient approach. However, in cases of weak fluctuation, this advantage is too small to reward the increased effort that logarithmic processing entails; whereas in cases of relatively strong fluctuation, it emerges decisively—for which empirical evidence will follow. # Gaussian Law and its Generalizations.

Without empirical evidence, the previous view could only appear as a hypothesis built into the air. The application of logarithmic treatment to empirical data, however, is this:

One reduces the given individual measurements $a$ of the <term>Collective-Object</term> <note>Original: K.-G. (*Kollektiv-Gegenstand*). In early statistics, this refers to a large set of individual cases belonging to the same category, like heights of a population.</note> to their logarithms $\alpha = \log a$. One then searches—in the same way as when finding the <term>densest value</term> <note>The "mode," or the most frequently occurring value in a data set.</note> $D$ from the raw values $a$, which will be discussed more specifically later—for the densest value of these $\alpha$. This value shall be called $\mathfrak{D}$ and, as will be explained more precisely later, is not to be confused with $\log D$. From this value $\mathfrak{D}$, one takes the logarithmic deviations $\lambda = \alpha - \mathfrak{D} = \log a - \mathfrak{D}$, which will be partly positive and partly negative. From these $\lambda$, one then seeks the simple arithmetic means (or so-called "mean logarithmic deviations") $e'$ and $e_{\text{,}}$ specifically for each side—that is, for $\lambda'$ (positive) and $\lambda_{\text{,}}$ (negative) respectively:

-> $e' = \frac{\Sigma \lambda'}{m'}$, $e_{\text{,}} = \frac{\Sigma \lambda_{\text{,}}}{m_{\text{,}}}$, <-

where $m'$ and $m_{\text{,}}$ signify the number of positive and negative deviations (not of $a$ from $D$ as before, but of $\alpha$ from $\mathfrak{D}$). One then determines the distribution of the logarithmic deviations $\lambda'$ and $\lambda_{\text{,}}$ on each side specifically in relation to $e', e_{\text{,}}, m',$ and $m_{\text{,}}$ according to the <term>two-sided Gaussian Law</term> <note>Original: *zwiespältigem G. G.* This refers to an asymmetrical distribution where the curve might be steeper on one side than the other.</note>, just as was indicated above (§ 33, point 2), except that $e', e_{\text{,}}, m',$ and $m_{\text{,}}$ are determined here logarithmically rather than arithmetically.

From these determinations valid for logarithmic deviations, one can then—by translating them back into numbers using logarithmic tables—derive determinations for the ratio deviations and their principal values. We will not go into this for now, however, as the necessary elaborations are reserved for a later chapter that deals more closely with the logarithmic treatment of Collective-Objects (Chapter XXI).

Besides the logarithmic densest value $\mathfrak{D}$, one can also determine the <term>logarithmic mean</term> <note>The "geometric mean" when converted back from logarithms.</note> $\mathfrak{G}$ as $\Sigma \alpha : m$ (the arithmetic mean of the logarithms of $a$) and the <term>logarithmic central value</term> <note>The "median."</note> $\mathfrak{C}$, which is the value of $a$ that has an equal number of measurements above and below it.

# Gauss’s Law and its Generalizations.

One can further transition from the logarithmic values to the numerical values that correspond to them according to the logarithm tables, and establish special designations for them; this is not a trivial task, as these values have their own noteworthy significance. Thus, the numerical value belonging to $\mathfrak{D}$ <note>The logarithmic mode or "densest value" described on the previous page.</note> can be designated as $\mathfrak{F}$, the **densest ratio value**. It signifies that, at the same ratio-distance from it on either side, more values of *a* (and thus more units of *a*) are clustered than at the same ratio-distance from any other *a*.

The numerical value belonging to the logarithmic <term>central value</term> <note>The "median," or the middle value in a ranked list.</note> $\mathfrak{C}$ coincides with the arithmetically determined *C*; for if a value of *a* (that is, *C*) has an equal number of *a*-values above and below it, then the logarithm of *C* (that is, $\mathfrak{C}$) also has an equal number of logarithms of *a* (that is, an equal number of *a*-values) above and below it.

The value to be designated as *G*, which corresponds to $\mathfrak{G}$ as a numerical value, represents the **geometric mean** of the *a*-values.

§ 37. We must therefore distinguish the following three general laws or principles, each of which can be regarded as a generalization and, at the same time, a refinement of the preceding one. Their essential differences shall be briefly summarized here:

1) The pure, simple, original **Gauss**ian law or principle, based on the assumption of symmetrical probability of the arithmetic deviations $\Theta'$, $\Theta$ on both sides of the arithmetic mean. Here, the starting point is taken from the arithmetic mean *A*; the deviations on both sides are determined as arithmetic; the mean deviation $\varepsilon = \Sigma \Theta : m$ is calculated directly for both sides together as the quotient of the sum of the absolute values of the deviations divided by their total number (or, according to a well-known formula, from the sum of the squares of the deviations as $\varepsilon = q \sqrt{2 : \pi}$), and the distribution is determined according to the *t*-table. To explicitly distinguish the relationship of these deviations to *A*, I replace the general designations *m*, $\Theta$, $\varepsilon$ with $\mu$, $\Delta$, $\eta$.

2) The arithmetic generalization of the **G. L.** <note>Gaussian Law</note>, for the assumption of asymmetrical probability of the deviations $\Theta'$, $\Theta$ from the

From the logarithmic values, one can then arrive at the ratio values as the numbers belonging to them according to the logarithm tables.

## VI. Characterization of Collective Objects by Their Determining Components or So-called Elements.

§ 38. Let us now go into somewhat more detail regarding the general remarks made earlier (Chap. II) concerning the characterization of collective objects <term>collective objects: (Kollektivgegenstände) Fechner’s term for a group of individual specimens that belong together as a species or type, which can be studied statistically.</term>.

Should a collective object be completely determined according to measure and number, it would be necessary to count not only all present specimens, but also past and future ones, and to take measurements of each in every respect that allows for quantitative determination, such as size in the three primary dimensions, weight, density, and duration. This is generally impossible. The quantity of specimens of a given object is usually indeterminately large, and of this indeterminately large quantity, usually only a very limited number is available for measurement. Furthermore, it is clear that if, for example, the brain weight of Europeans and Africans <note>original: "Negers." The text reflects 19th-century anthropological categories and terminology.</note> is to be compared, this cannot be done simply by contrasting the weights of a thousand European brains with the weights of a thousand African brains. If one is satisfied now, as is often the case, with stating the <term>arithmetic mean</term> of a collective object, one certainly has an important and essential value for determination and comparison with other objects; but two collective objects may coincide entirely or nearly so in this regard and yet deviate greatly in other relationships. ### Characterization of <term>Collective Objects</term> <note>original: "K.-G." (Kollektiv-Gegenstände); groups of varying individual items treated as a single entity, such as the heights of all men in a city.</note> by their Elements.

...properties can be characterized. It should therefore be regarded as a fundamental result of experience that the most diverse collective objects that have been investigated do, in fact, allow for the determination of a "most probable value," and that the latter coincides closely enough with that value for which the ratio of the mutual mean deviations (*e'* : *e''*) is equal to the ratio of the mutual number of deviations (*m'* : *m''*). In the **Theory of Collective Measurement**, the **densest value** <note>The mode; the most frequent value in a dataset.</note> is thus fundamentally different from the **arithmetic mean** and instead stands in a fundamentally required agreement with the value defined by the proportion *e'* : *e''* = *m'* : *m''*. This latter value (which, according to the rule established in Chapter II, is to be designated as *Dₚ*, while *Dᵢ* names the empirically densest value calculated through interpolation from the table) therefore claims the same attention here as the arithmetic mean does in the **Theory of Errors**. It also possesses entirely corresponding significance; for based on the principle that the most probable value of a collective object should fulfill the proportion *e'* : *e''* = *m'* : *m''*, or that *Dₚ* should equal *Dᵢ*, one finds the **extended Gaussian Law**—already established proactively in the previous chapter—as the law of distribution. This is found in a similar way to how the simple Gaussian Law results as the law of errors based on the principle that the most probable value should be the arithmetic mean, or that *A* should equal *Dᵢ*.

[Only to this extent can *A* <note>The arithmetic mean.</note> maintain its dominance here: in collective objects endowed with weak **asymmetry**, it falls so close to *Dₚ* that it suffices to apply the simple Gaussian Law as an approximation in place of the two-sided one.]

**§ 43.** In choosing between the various principal values, the degree of ease and certainty with which they can be obtained must not be ignored. If one only requires a rough determination, that of the **densest value** is decidedly the simplest and easiest, since in a distribution table one merely needs to look for the value *a* to which the largest frequency *z* belongs; next in this regard follows the determination of the **central value** <note>The median; the middle value in a ranked list.</note>, for which one only needs to count the *a* or $\varTheta$ from both sides according to...

### Characterization of <term>Collective Objects</term> <note>original: "K.-G." (Kollektiv-Gegenstände); Fechner's term for datasets or groups of varying individual items treated as a single entity, such as the heights of all men in a city.</note> by their Elements.

...requires moving from the center until equality of *m'* and *m* is achieved; the most cumbersome calculation is that of the *A* <note>The Arithmetic Mean.</note>, since the addition of all individual values *a* in a large <term>distribution table</term> <note>original: "Verteilungstafel"; a table showing how often different values occur in a dataset.</note> or—what amounts to the same thing—the formation and addition of the products *z a* to obtain the sum $\Sigma a$ (which must be divided by *m*), is a long and laborious operation when *m* <note>The total number of cases.</note> is large.

But the relationship is different—indeed, exactly the reverse—if one wishes to move toward precise determinations that approach the ideal values as closely as possible. From a rough determination of the <term>densest value</term> <note>The mode; the most frequent value in a dataset.</note> based on the maximum frequency *z* falling upon it, one can only expect a very uncertain approximation of the ideal value. The sharpest possible determination, however—based on the ratio *m'* : *m*, = *c'* : *c*—can indeed be reduced to a specific and not difficult calculation; yet, in execution, it lacks rigor, requiring <term>reduction</term> and <term>interpolation</term> <note>Mathematical techniques used to estimate values between known data points or to simplify complex data to fit a model.</note>, which ultimately leave a small margin of error for the calculated result. Even the precise determination of *C* <note>Likely referring to the median or central value.</note>, though much simpler than that of *D* <note>The mode.</note>, cannot manage without such aids, whereas the determination of *A* does not require them. The tediousness of forming the products *z a* can be avoided by a procedure to be specified later (Chapter IX).

§ 44. Following the previous discussion on the properties and performance of the various <term>principal values</term> <note>original: "Hauptwerte"; central tendencies like the mean, median, and mode.</note>, something remains to be said regarding the perspectives from which the extremes and <term>deviation functions</term> <note>Functions that describe how much individual data points differ from the central average.</note> come into consideration.

Two collective objects can agree entirely or nearly so in their principal values, and yet the <term>range of fluctuation</term> <note>original: "Schwankungsweite"; the spread or variety within the data.</note> and the mean fluctuation value of the individual specimens around their principal values can be very different—representing distinguishing characteristics that are by no means trivial. Thus, the <term>mean temperature</term> of an island in the middle of the ocean and a location in the middle of a continent can be the same; however, the deviations of individual temperatures from the mean temperature are kept within narrower limits in the former and are, on average, smaller than in the latter. It is by this that we distinguish between a <term>maritime climate</term> and a <term>continental climate</term>.

Generally speaking—although this may suffer exceptions and an exact proportionality does not take place—the mean fluctuation grows with the size of the objects. Thus, it can be of interest to eliminate this influence as far as possible by dividing the mean fluctuation by the size of the fluctuating object, thereby taking into account the **relative** mean fluctuation in addition to the **absolute** mean fluctuation.

Even more important than these absolute differences, however, are the relative ones:

->$\frac{\mu' - \mu,}{m}$ and $\frac{U' - U,}{U' + U,}.$<-

Regarding the use to be made of this later, the following should be noted for now.

Of course, there can be no question of a difference between the sum of the positive and negative deviations from $A$—that is, $\Sigma \Delta'$ and $\Sigma \Delta,$—since $A$ is specifically determined in such a way that both sums are equal; however, this does not automatically imply that both counts of deviations, $\mu'$ and $\mu,$, are also equal to each other, and one will find them to be so only by chance. What one finds generally, or with only accidental exceptions—certainly on average in the case of <term>collective deviations</term> regarding $A$—is that $\mu' - \mu,$ increases with the size of $m$ <note>The total number of observations in the sample.</note>.

Specifically, under the assumption of equal <term>probability</term><note>original: "W." (Wahrscheinlichkeit)</note> of positive and negative deviations, probability theory—after reducing the case to an urn with an equal number of black and white balls—teaches that $\mu' - \mu,$ increases in its absolute value, on average, in proportion to $\sqrt{m}$. However, the more $m$ increases, the smaller the ratio of $\sqrt{m} : m$ becomes, so that with an infinite $m$, $\frac{\mu' - \mu,}{m} = \frac{u}{m} = \text{zero and } \frac{\mu'}{\mu,} \text{ becomes one.}$

A consequence of this is that in the investigation following later—as to whether the positive and negative deviations regarding $A$ actually have an equal <term>probability</term>—one must not simply stick to the absolute difference $u$, which generally is not absent even with equal probability, but rather to its ratio to $m$. This ratio must not exceed a certain magnitude if the assumption of equal probability is not to become very improbable, about which more will be said later.

# Characterization of <term>Collective Objects</term><note>Fechner’s term for statistical populations or groups of varying items, like measurements of plants or human heights.</note> by Their Elements.

So far, we have taken the inequality between the number of deviations on both sides of $A$ <note>The arithmetic mean.</note>—that is, $\mu'$ and $\mu$,—as a characteristic and, in a certain respect, as a measure of asymmetry. Naturally, one could not speak of asymmetry based on an inequality in the *sum* of deviations ($\Sigma \Delta'$, $\Sigma \Delta,$) relative to $A$, because it is inherent in the concept of $A$ that $\Sigma \Delta' = \Sigma \Delta,$. In other words, $A$ must be determined precisely so that this equality occurs. On the other hand, a characteristic or measure of asymmetry could also not be based on an inequality in the *number* of deviations relative to $C$ <note>The "central value" or median.</note>, because it is inherent in the concept of $C$ that the number of deviations on either side of it is equal.

However, nothing would inherently prevent us from determining asymmetry relative to the <term>most dense value</term><note>The mode, or the value that occurs most frequently in a data set.</note> $D$, based on the inequality of the deviation counts $m'$ and $m,$, in cases where both main values <note>The mean and the mode.</note> diverge sufficiently from one another. This would have the advantage that, relative to $D$, one obtains a stronger divergence between the deviation counts $m'$ and $m,$ (grounded in the laws of asymmetry) than the divergence between $\mu'$ and $\mu,$ relative to $A$. Furthermore, one could then relate $m'$ and $m,$ to the <term>two-sided Law of Error</term><note>original: "zweiseitige G. G." (Gauss’sches Gesetz). This refers to the Gaussian or Normal distribution law.</note>, whereas when asymmetry exists relative to $A$, neither the simple nor the two-sided Law of Error is valid regarding the count of deviations from $A$. 

It should be noted that if, relative to $A$, the count $\mu'$ exceeds $\mu,$, then conversely, $m,$ will exceed $m'$ relative to $D$. But since $A$ (and consequently $\mu'$ and $\mu,$) is much easier to determine than $D$ (and consequently $m'$ and $m,$), and since one can always infer from a greater or lesser asymmetry regarding $A$ a greater or lesser inequality regarding $D$ in the opposite direction (which in every case exceeds the asymmetry at $A$), it generally appears more practical to stick first to the results of determining asymmetry via $\mu' - \mu,$ relative to $A$. This is because the inequality of $m'$ and $m,$ relative to $D$ can already be inferred from it; however, if a precise determination is required, this must still be investigated specifically according to both theory and empirical evidence.

### § 48.

[If one wishes to investigate a Collective Object, the individual specimens must first be measured in the random, spatial, or temporal order in which they appear, and these measurements—designated as *a*—must be recorded in a <term>Primary List</term><note>Original: "Urliste." This is a raw, unorganized list of data points as they are first collected.</note>. Care must be taken to ensure that the requirements specified in Chapter IV are met, particularly that a sufficient number of measurements are collected while excluding abnormalities.]

[As already noted (§ 3), such a primary list is not yet suitable for mathematical processing. However, it is valuable in another respect, as it allows one to determine whether the specimens of the Collective Object vary independently of each other or exist in a relationship of dependency. Regarding this, rules were given in § 20, which will be further expanded in Chapter XXIII. For the sake of mathematical treatment, however, the measurements must be ordered by size, thereby creating a **distribution table** from the primary list. To distinguish it from the "reduced table," the creation and treatment of which will be taught in the next chapter, it is called a **primary distribution table**. In this table, the measurements *a* form a column progressing from smaller to larger values, containing each *a* only once, while an accompanying column lists the corresponding counts *z*, which indicate how often each individual *a* occurs.]

[This primary table now forms the starting point for the entire investigation. However, it is usually still characterized by significant irregulari—]

§ 51. [A comparative look at these tables shows a significant difference between the first three tables and the last one, both regarding the progression of the *z* <note>original: *z*; refers to the frequencies or number of occurrences</note> and the sequencing of the *a* <note>original: *a*; refers to the specific measured values or categories</note>. Specifically, the former possess a central **main body** <note>German: *Hauptbestand*</note> whose *z* values generally increase toward the middle of the table, and whose *a* values—aside from individual interruptions toward the ends—form an **equidistant series** <note>A series where the gaps between measurements are equal, such as every 0.5 cm</note>. Thus, in Table I, the equidistant *a* values extend in an uninterrupted sequence from 378 to 428 and from 430 to 435, while simultaneously the *z* values, albeit with constantly recurring fluctuations, first increase and then decrease again. In Table II, the series of equidistant *a* values goes from 488 to 550 and continues, after an interruption caused by the missing value *a* = 551, from 552 to 555, while the *z* values again show a similar progression. Finally, Table III is characterized by an undisturbed equidistance of the *a* values between the limits of 64.75 and 78.50, with a corresponding behavior of the *z* values.

Attached to this main body in each of the three tables at the beginning and the end is a relatively small number of *a* values whose distances vary irregularly, and whose *z* values are predominantly equal to 1: these represent **end sections** with scattered *a* values. In the fourth table, by contrast, the *a* values progress throughout in irregular intervals, and it can only be noted that the smaller intervals are found more frequently in the middle than at the ends; at the same time, the vast majority of the *z* values are equal to 1. One can thus distinguish between tables that possess a main body of equidistant *a* values alongside end sections with scattered *a* values, and those whose *a* values are irregularly scattered throughout the entire table. Tables I through III are to be considered representatives of the first type; Table IV represents the second type. Both types are essentially different from each other; for it will be shown that tables of the second type require a much more extensive <term>reduction</term> <note>German: *Reduktion*; in statistics, this refers to grouping raw data into larger classes or intervals to make the pattern visible</note> than those of the first, if their analysis is to be successful.]

[In defining the main body of a table, however, it must be taken into account that it does not [end] with sharp certainty]

separates itself from the end sections. One could certainly counter any uncertainty by establishing the rule that the **main body** <note>German: *Hauptbestand*; refers to the central, most significant portion of a data set</note> should extend exactly as far as the **equidistance** <note>The state of having equal intervals between measurements</note> of the *a* <note>original: *a*; the specific measurement values, such as the length of a rye stalk</note> reaches. However, it is clear from the start that no essential definition would be achieved this way. For in many cases, it may happen that even toward the middle of the table, the equidistance is disturbed by a missing *a*; even more frequently, moving from the center toward the beginning or end, a series of equidistant *a* values will follow a missing *a* value, as is actually the case for Tables I and II due to the absence of *a* = 429 and *a* = 551, respectively. In such cases, if the above rule were strictly followed, the main body would either be excessively restricted or called into question entirely. On the other hand, it is also possible for the *a* values to proceed without any gaps, yet the progression of the *z* <note>original: *z*; the frequency or number of times a value occurs</note> values makes it desirable to exclude them from the main body. 

The determination of the main body must therefore be left to a certain degree of discretion, as a rule can only be established to the extent that the equidistance of the *a* values is not subject to significant disturbances and that, regarding the *z* values, an increase toward the middle remains generally recognizable—at least on the whole. Thus, one can set the boundaries of the main body for Table I at 378 and 435, for Table II at 488 and 555, and for Table III at 64.75 and 78.50, with the caveat, however, that these boundaries could certainly be shifted.]

[Moreover, the equidistance of the *a* values can, at least formally, be established even in the case of missing values if the missing *a* values—assigned a *z* value of 0—are included in the table. This shall be referred to as **inserting empty *a* values**. For example, the main body of Tables I and II becomes consistently equidistant in this way if 429 is inserted into Table I and 551 is inserted into Table II with a *z* value of 0.]

[Furthermore, regarding the progression of the *z* values in the main body of Tables I–III, it has already been noted that the increase toward the middle is subject to constant fluctuations. Now, to be sure, an uninterrupted growth and subsequent decline is not possible at all, simply because of the ever-present, unbalanced **random variations** <note>German: *Zufälligkeiten*; refers to the noise or chance fluctuations inherent in biological data</note>...

# Primary Tables.

...to be expected. However, if the cause lay in this alone, the unmistakably emerging **periodicity** <note>The quality of occurring at regular intervals</note> in the fluctuations of the *z* <note>original: *z*; representing the frequency or count of a specific measurement</note> would remain inexplicable. There must, therefore, be another underlying cause. This becomes clear from the following remarks.

[Within the **main body** <note>German: *Hauptbestand*; the central, most significant portion of a data set</note> of Table I, a total of 18 relative maxima and 17 intervening minima occur; 8 maxima fall on those values of *a* <note>original: *a*; the specific measurement values, such as length</note> that represent whole or half centimeters, while not a single minimum belongs to such an *a*. Of the 17 maxima in the main body of Table II, 10 fall on values of this kind, whereas none of the 16 minima do. This demonstrates sufficiently that during the measurement of the **skulls** <term>Schädel: human skulls, often measured in 19th-century anthropology to study physical variations</term> using a **tape measure** <note>original: *Bandmaß*</note>—where the millimeters were evidently obtained by estimation—whole and half centimeters were preferred. Otherwise, according to the laws of probability, the maxima and minima would have to be distributed evenly across the subdivisions of the centimeter. Thus, the source of the periodically recurring irregularities in the progression of *z* is found in this non-uniform estimation—that is, in the preference for the whole and half divisions of the scale used. This is further confirmed by Table III. Of the 19 maxima in its main body, 9 fall on whole inches and 7 on half inches; of the 18 minima, only 2 are associated with whole-inch values, while the rest belong to 1/4- or 3/4-inch values.]

[One must therefore be careful when processing the **distribution tables** <note>original: *Verteilungstafeln*</note> to avoid errors caused by non-uniform estimation and consider their elimination through an appropriate **reduction** <note>A statistical method to simplify or correct data by grouping or adjusting values</note>. This leads to the necessity of dividing the tables into main sections, corresponding to the period of the non-uniform estimation. For example, in Tables I and II, these sections must progress every 5 mm, and in Table III by half-inches or, better yet, by whole inches. Generally, one should begin these main sections at the start of the table's main body. It may then be found advantageous to define the boundaries of the main body so that it contains exactly a full number of main sections. In Table I, for instance, three values would then have to be trimmed from the main body as defined above, and perhaps the values 380 and 434 [should be set] as the boundaries...]

<summary>The author identifies a systematic "rounding error" in measurement data, noting that researchers tend to favor whole or half centimeters and inches when estimating measurements. To correct this human bias, the author suggests organizing data into larger blocks (such as 5mm intervals) to smooth out the resulting statistical fluctuations.</summary>

§ 52. [Finally, the following points, which are valid for every distribution table in its entire scope, should be mentioned. Every measurement is subject to limits of precision, so that the **a** <note>original: *a*; the specific measurement values or dimensions</note> can never be strung together continuously, but must instead run separated by an interval, the size of which depends on the degree of precision of the measurement. This interval shall be called the **primary interval** <term>primäres Intervall: the smallest unit of measurement possible given the tools used; for example, if a ruler only shows millimeters, the primary interval is 1 millimeter</term> and be denoted by **i**. It is constant for the entire extent of the table, as it is determined only by the scale used, and not by the size of the objects being measured.]

[One must look to the existence of this interval for the reason why an equidistant main body <note>German: *äquidistanter Hauptbestand*; a set of data points spaced at equal distances</note> is possible in the distribution tables at all. For the interval of the main body is nothing other than that primary **i**, which cannot be fallen below; rather, it emerges all the more clearly the larger the number of measured specimens of the class <note>original: *K.-G.*, likely *Klassengattung* or *Körper-Gattung*, referring to the type of specimen being studied</note>—the **m** of the table—becomes. The primary **i** is, of course, also directly visible from the **a**-values for tables without a main body. For Table IV, for example, it is equal to the tenth part of $\epsilon$, i.e., = 0.05 cm.]

[The essential significance of the presence of a primary interval, however, lies in the fact that it puts the relationship of the **z** <note>original: *z*; the frequency or number of times a specific measurement occurs</note> to the **a**, next to which they are written in the tables, into the proper light. Namely, one recognizes that the **a** are merely to be understood as representatives of the primary intervals, representing their centers; therefore, the **z** are also to be understood as belonging not to the **a** itself, but to the primary intervals designated by the **a**. Within these intervals, the values are thought to be uniformly distributed, as there is no basis for any other kind of systematic distribution. Insofar as the primary interval encompasses or circles the **a**, it shall be called the **surrounding interval** <note>German: *Umkreisintervall*</note> of **a**. Its boundaries on both sides are $a - \frac{1}{2}i$ and $a + \frac{1}{2}i$; these boundaries join one another directly throughout the entire table, so that the first boundary of any given interval coincides with the second boundary of the preceding one.]

# Primary Tables.

[The **a** and **z** values <note>original: *a*- und *z*-Werte; *a* represents the measurement value and *z* represents the frequency or number of occurrences</note> are thus linked to one another by means of the associated surrounding interval. Should this connection be dissolved and the **a** be considered and understood on its own, it shall be designated as a **naked a** <note>original: *nacktes a*; this refers to the raw measurement value stripped of its statistical context or the range of error/precision represented by the interval</note>.]

[The just-explained association of the **z** with the **a** now also permits an accurate geometric representation of the distribution tables. Specifically, the **a** values are to be plotted on an abscissa <term>Abscissenlinie: the horizontal x-axis of a graph</term> and, by marking the values $a - \frac{1}{2}i$ and $a + \frac{1}{2}i$, their surrounding intervals <term>Umkreisintervalle: the range of space around a measurement that accounts for the precision of the instrument</term> are to be added; then, rectangles are to be erected upon these intervals, the areas of which must represent the **z** values assigned to the **a** in the table; here, of course, an arbitrary scale can be used as a basis for both the measurement of the **a** and the construction of the rectangles, since the goal is merely to obtain a picture of the proportions of the table values.]

## VIII. Reduced Distribution Tables.

§ 53. Partly to make the distribution tables more compact and thus occupy less space, partly to smooth out irregularities in the progression of their values and neutralize any inconsistencies in estimation, and partly to facilitate the calculation of the defining parameters <term>Bestimmungsstücke: the specific mathematical values, such as means or deviations, that define a set of data</term> or so-called "elements" of the collective object <note>original: *K.-G.*, abbreviation for *Kollektivgegenstand*; a term used by the author to refer to a statistical population or a group of phenomena treated as a single unit</note>, one must transition from primary distribution tables to reduced ones and allow the latter to stand in for the former. Even though, in certain respects, a primary table can never be entirely replaced by a reduced one, the reduced table does, in fact, retain advantages over the primary one in the aforementioned regards. Therefore, it becomes necessary to concern ourselves with how they are constructed, their internal relationships, and the methods by which they are utilized.

Let us first consider the reduction of those primary tables which, like Tables I through III, allow us to distinguish a main body <term>Hauptbestand: the central, most densely populated portion of the dataset</term> with equidistant values of *a* from the end sections with scattered values of *a*. To produce a reduced table from a primary one of this kind, one divides its main body—as was already anticipated in § 50—into sections that contain an equal number of equidistant (made equidistant, if necessary, by inserting empty values of *a*) so-called "naked values" <note>original: *nackte a*; raw measurements stripped of their surrounding statistical range or interval</note> in their *a*-column. One then sums the frequencies <note>The author uses *x* here to denote the frequency or number of occurrences</note> for each of these sections individually. According to this method, the reduced interval <term>i: the width of the newly formed group or "bin"</term> is the size of the entire interval in which the set of primary values, including their surrounding intervals <term>Umkreisintervalle: the range of space around a measurement that accounts for the precision of the instrument</term>, is grouped together. The reduced frequency *x* is the sum of the frequencies that fall upon the primary values contained within that reduced interval.

<summary>This section explains the transition from primary (raw) data tables to reduced (grouped) tables, a process intended to save space, smooth out data irregularities, and simplify the calculation of statistical parameters.</summary>

### Reduced Tables.

...as a reduced *a*, to which the reduced *z* is assigned; it is the mean of all the naked *a* values <term>naked a: the raw, individual measurement values recorded in the data set</term> or, what amounts to the same thing, the mean of the extreme naked *a* values included within the interval.

For clarification, let us look at the reduction of a specific section of the main body of primary Table I, as follows:

| naked *a* | 380 | 381 | 382 | 383 | 384 |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| primary *z* | 2 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 3 |

By summing the primary *z* <term>z: the frequency or count of how many times a specific value occurs</term>, we obtain the number 11 as the reduced *z*. Meanwhile, the reduced *a* is the mean of the five primary naked *a* values in the section in question. Because these values are equidistant <note>original: *Äquidistanz*; meaning they are spaced at regular, equal intervals</note>, this is the same as the mean of the outermost *a* values, 380 and 384; thus, it is 382, to which the reduced *z* = 11 is assigned. 

The boundaries of the reduced *i* <term>i: the interval or width of the grouping bin</term>, however, are not simply the outermost naked *a* values (380 and 384), and therefore the reduced interval is not 384 - 380 = 4. This is because the surrounding intervals of the boundary *a* values are also included in the reduced interval. This expands the entire interval by a primary 1/2 *i* on both sides. Since the primary *i* = 1, the boundaries of the reduced interval are 380 - 1/2 = 379.5 on one side, and 384 + 1/2 = 384.5 on the other. The size of the entire reduced interval is the difference between these two = 5.

Thus, while one obtains the reduced *a* itself as the mean of the outermost primary naked *a* values included in the section to be reduced, one cannot determine the size of the reduced interval simply as the distance between these two boundary *a* values. It can only be found by extending that distance on each side by half a primary *i*—and therefore, in total, by one whole primary *i*. This must be carefully noted, as it has not been correctly observed in all cases, as will be noted later.

If *n* equidistant naked *a* values (and thus *n* intervals of *i*) are combined in each main section of the primary table, then the *i* of the reduced table is also *n* times the *i* of the primary table. In the main sections of Tables I and II, there are 5 naked *a* values each, and in Table III, there are 4 naked *a* values...

§ 54. Just as with the primary tables, one should not assume in the reduced tables that the reduced *a* <term>a: the representative value or mean of a group</term> itself occurs as many times as its assigned reduced *z* <term>z: the frequency or count of occurrences</term> indicates. Instead, one must assume that within the interval represented by the reduced *a*, there are *z* values of *a* distributed between the boundaries of that reduced interval. And since even the *a* values in the primary tables essentially represent a whole interval over which their *z* is distributed—only a smaller one than the reduced *a*—there is essentially only a relative difference between primary and reduced *a* values. 

Instead of the reduced *a*, however, the reduced tables can also list the interval itself that it represents. In the reduced tables available so far, both methods occur, leading me to distinguish between **a-tables** and **interval-tables**. Merely for the sake of a shorter presentation, I mostly prefer the format of the *a*-table; however, there is no substantive difference between *a*-tables and interval-tables. One can easily convert from one form to the other, provided that the reduced *a* in the *a*-table is the mean <note>The arithmetic average</note> between the boundaries of the reduced intervals. Meanwhile, the boundaries of the intervals—just as in the primary tables—are *a* – 1/2 *i* and *a* + 1/2 *i*, except that here the reduced *a* and *i* take the place of the primary ones. This is illustrated in the following example, where the reduction is continued through one more section according to the stated principle, resulting in the following corresponding *a*-column and interval-column:

| red. *a* | red. Intervals |
| :---: | :---: |
| 382 | 379.5—384.5 |
| 387 | 384.5—389.5 |

If we now continue the reduction in our example through Table I according to the same principles, we obtain the following corresponding reduced *a*-table and interval-table:
