However, one does not find the interval boundaries correctly stated according to the previous rule everywhere else. Instead, while neglecting the surrounding intervals <note>The mathematical range around a central point</note>, the boundary-*a* values of the reduced sections themselves are given as interval boundaries. But here we immediately encounter the disadvantage of this method of designation: the intervals do not connect to one another, but rather leave gaps of one unit of measurement between them. In reality, measurements also fall into these gaps, which the table fails to account for. However, one can remedy this grievance—as can also be done with the Belgian measurement tables—by taking the mean <note>The process of "Mittelziehung" or averaging the boundaries</note> of the boundaries of successive intervals to make these boundaries coincide.

§ 55. § 57. Let us now return to <term>distribution tables</term> <note>original: "Verteilungstafeln"; tables showing how often different values occur in a dataset</note> like I, II, and III, in which a main body of data with <term>equidistant</term> <note>evenly spaced</note> values in the $a$-column can be distinguished from end sections with scattered values. We must still specify how to handle the latter. This can be done in two ways. Either **$\alpha$)** one makes the $a$ values of the end sections just as equidistant as those in the main sections by inserting empty $a$ values, and then reduces them according to the previous principles, as they no longer fundamentally differ from the main sections; or **$\beta$)** one does not continue the reduction through the end sections, but instead settles for <term>bulk figures</term> <note>original: "Bauschangaben"; summarized or "lumped" data often used for the extreme high or low ends of a scale</note> regarding them. The latter method, as far as I can see, has been the only common one until now; however, the former is preferable for reasons to be stated and will be the only one I follow in the future.

### Reduced Tables.

Thus, one commonly observes in the case of <term>recruit measurements</term> <note>Historical height or weight data collected from military conscripts, a common source for early 19th-century statistics.</note> that according to Method $\beta$, the <term>reduced main body</term> <note>original: "reduzierten Hauptbestande"; the central, most frequent part of the data set</note> is preceded by a bulk figure representing the number of measurements that are smaller than the lower limit of that main body. Similarly, the table concludes with a bulk figure for the number of measurements larger than the upper limit of the main body, without further specifying these measurements. However, one should not limit oneself to this approach; while it still allows for the determination of the <term>central value</term> <note>The median; the middle point of the data.</note>, it makes it impossible to calculate the <term>arithmetic mean</term> <note>The average; the sum of all values divided by the number of values.</note>, not to mention other disadvantages. Rather, if one wishes to forgo performing the reduction for the end sections entirely, one should provide not only the sum of the number of measurements but also the sum of the values themselves contained within those end sections; it is also useful to include the <term>primary extremes</term> <note>The absolute lowest and highest values in the raw data.</note>.

If we therefore designate the "pre-count" as *v* and the "pre-sum" as *V* (the number ($\Sigma x$) and sum ($\Sigma ax$) of the primary values *a* that are smaller than the first boundary of the reduced main body), and similarly designate the "post-count" as *n* and "post-sum" as *N* (the number and sum of the primary values *a* that are larger than the second boundary), and let *E* and *E'* represent the smallest and largest value *a* of the entire primary table, then the reduced main body should be supplemented by stating *v*, *V*, *n*, *N*, *E*, and *E'*. This makes the table much more useful, though one admittedly loses the advantage of brevity offered by the pure Method $\beta$.

Method $\alpha$, however, is not only more methodical—in that it allows the reduction of the entire primary table to be carried out according to the same principle without the somewhat arbitrary boundary between the main body and the end sections—but, strictly speaking, only tables reduced in this way are truly useful for the <term>distribution calculations</term> <note>original: "Verteilungsrechnungen"; mathematical analysis of how data is spread out.</note> that must be performed.

If I now apply this principle to carry out the reduction with an interval *i* = 5 mm throughout Tables I and II, I must take care to make the values of the entire table <term>equidistant</term> <note>evenly spaced</note> by inserting empty values *a* where necessary. Furthermore, I must ensure that the first valid primary value *a* receives as many...

# Reduced Tables.

If the values increase until they reach a maximum and then decrease just as uninterruptedly through a subsequent descent—thereby providing a smooth <term>distribution curve</term> <note>original: *Verteilungskurve*; a graph showing how often different measurements occur, ideally forming a bell shape.</note> in the sense of § 17—then all reduced tables show, at first glance, the most striking advantage of regularity compared to the primary tables from which they were derived. And only after the progression of values has become regular through reduction—at least around the center—can one speak of an underlying lawfulness, determine that law, or test a presumed law against the data.

That Table I shows two adjacent, identical <term>maximum-z</term> <note>The highest frequency or "count" in the data set.</note> values is merely accidental and does not stand in the way of a regular progression, as would be the case if they were separated by intervening *a* values with a smaller *z*. Table II has, as is usual, only one maximum-z. Looking closer, Table I shows only one insignificant exception to the regular progression toward one end, insofar as the values *z* = 17 and 19 would have to swap their sizes to follow each other correctly; and such small irregularities are rarely absent toward the ends, though they matter little when utilizing the tables. This is even more true if such irregularities occur in the region of the "densest *a*," that is, the measurement that has the largest *z*. If, for the sake of brevity, we understand the <term>core of the table</term> <note>original: *Kern der Tafel*; the central "heart" of the data distribution where most observations cluster.</note> to mean the densest *a* along with its two higher and two lower neighboring *a*-values, we will primarily require regularity from this core to find our <term>normal laws of distribution</term> <note>Mathematical patterns, such as the Gaussian distribution, used to describe how data points naturally spread out.</note> confirmed with a satisfactory approximation. While the core of Table I—which extends over six *a*-values due to the double maximum-z—satisfies the condition of regularity, this is not the case for Table II toward the top (toward the smaller measurements); likewise, toward the bottom, the number 43 follows incorrectly against the limit-value of 39 in the core.

From this, it can be concluded from the outset that Table II for <term>horizontal circumference</term> <note>original: *Horizontalumfang*</note> will conform less well to the normal mode of distribution and be less suitable for proving the normal laws than Table I for <term>vertical circumference</term> <note>original: *Vertikalumfang*</note>.

§ 60. There is a certain conflict between the advantages and disadvantages of increasing or decreasing the <term>reduction interval (*i*)</term>. From certain points of view, it is most advantageous to keep the interval *i* as small as possible because, according to the discussion already held earlier (§ 5), the <term>ideal laws of distribution</term><note>These "laws of distribution" refer to what we now call a Normal Distribution or a Bell Curve.</note> strictly speaking presuppose this case. # Reduced Tables.

If a given <term>measurement (*a*)</term><note>Representing the specific value or category being measured.</note> for a recorded <term>frequency (*z*)</term><note>The count or number of times a particular measurement occurs.</note> actually belongs to an entire interval—which, in both primary and reduced tables, grows with the size of the <term>interval (*i*)</term>—this must be taken into account when determining the statistical elements. To do this, as will be explained later (Chapter IX), one must use <term>interpolation</term><note>A mathematical method of estimating values between known data points.</note> for the interval in question. One should try to keep the intervals small enough so that simple interpolation is sufficient. The <term>Theory of Collective Measurement (*Kollektivmaßlehre*)</term><note>The author’s term for his systematic study of statistical distributions in groups.</note> would become practically impossible to carry out if one had to use complex interpolation with "second differences" for every determination of elements and every comparison between calculation and observation. Although I will provide the procedure for this later, I have generally made no use of it; I found that by limiting myself to the sizes of *i* used here, I could gain no advantage that would justify the difficulty of the work or the complexity of the presentation.

In contrast, smoothing out the random occurrences that disturb the regular flow of the frequency *z* in the primary table—and which stand in the way of comparing the data with the mathematically required patterns—can only be achieved through reduction and, consequently, the enlargement of the interval *i*. In this regard, an interval *i* that is not too large does much less harm than excessive irregularity. Therefore, it is best to choose an *i* that is large enough—but no larger than necessary—to ensure a regular progression occurs at least within the core of the reduced table. Irregularities in the progression of the extremely small frequencies (*z*) have no significant disruptive influence on the determination of the elements or the mathematical relationships. 

However, in cases like our first three example tables, where irregularities caused by unbalanced randomness are joined by those caused by <term>uneven estimation</term><note>A common bias where observers round numbers to preferred digits, like 0 or 5, creating "lumps" in the data.</note>, a special condition applies: one must not choose an *i* smaller than the period of the uneven estimation. Consequently, the number of <term>equidistant</term> measurements *a* to be grouped together must not be less than this period. Furthermore, when increasing *i*, one should only do so in whole multiples of that period, because only under this condition can one expect to compensate for errors caused by uneven estimation. As is the case with Tables I, II, and III, one is also not bound to exactly double the initially chosen *i* <note>The letter 'i' represents the interval size, or the width of the "bins" used to group measurements.</note> in order to achieve a regular core. Doubling only offers the formal advantage that the higher level of reduction can be derived simply from the previous lower level. However, if a regular core can be obtained through a weaker <term>reduction</term><note>The process of simplifying data by grouping individual measurements into larger categories to smooth out the distribution.</note> than by doubling the previous *i*, one should not resort to this doubling; in that case, however, one must return to the primary table to derive the reduction in question.

§ 62. To now observe how these results are reflected in other <term>collective objects</term><note>Original: "K.-G." or "Kollektiv-Gegenstände." This term refers to any group of individual things—like people's heights or skull widths—that can be analyzed as a single statistical set.</note> under different conditions, we turn from Table I, which applies to skull measurements with a sample size of *m* = 450¹), to Table III, which concerns the measurements of student recruits with a sample size of *m* = 2047.

In Table I, the behavior of <term>uneven estimation</term><note>Refers to the tendency for human observers to round measurements or favor certain numbers, creating "lumpy" data.</note> forced us to reduce the primary interval of *i* = 1 mm by five times in the first stage. In Table III, for the same reason, we are required to reduce the primary interval of *i* = 0.25 inches four-fold (that is, to 1 inch). For the reasons stated above in § 55, the procedure using "divided *z*" <note>A mathematical adjustment for how data points are assigned to specific categories.</note> must be applied here. § 64. Meanwhile, in addition to the choice between reduction levels, we must also consider the choice between **reduction positions**, as previously noted.

The variation in reduction positions is based on the fact that the reduced table turns out differently depending on where one begins the process of "combining" the primary bare $a$ <note>Fechner uses "bare $a$" to refer to the raw, individual measurement values before they are grouped into intervals.</note> values. Let us first consider this in relation to the main contents of the primary Table I. In the example in § 53, the grouping of $a$ began with the first $a = 380$ of the first main division, and we thereby obtained a reduced $a$ of 382 with a reduced frequency $z = 11$. If we proceed consistently, the reduction of the second main division—containing the five bare $a$ values 385, 386, etc.—will give a reduced $a = 387$ with a reduced $z = 25$. However, nothing prevents us from shifting the start of the grouping of every five bare $a$ values by a single $a$. This creates different divisions to be reduced. For instance, looking at the first two:

| bare $a$ <note>Raw measurement values.</note> | 381 | 382 | 383 | 384 | 385 | 386 | 387 | 388 | 389 | 390 |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| primary $z$ <note>Original frequency count for each value.</note> | 1 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 8 | 2 | 6 | 4 | 5 | 7 |

from which follows:

---

1) [The correspondence between the values of $A_2$ for $i = 8$ and $i = 16$, as well as $C_2$ for $i = 4$ and $i = 8$, is due to the specific nature of Table IV. Specifically, the equality of the two $A_2$ values follows from the fact that, at reduction level $i = 8$, the sum of the first, third, fifth (etc.) frequencies happens to equal the sum of the second, fourth (etc.) $z$, while the equal frequencies $z$ at level $i = 4$ (for $a = 82$ and 86) result in the equality of the two $C_2$ values.]

As one can see, this results in a different reduced table for the main data set than the previous one; while the former began primarily with $a = 380$ and was reduced with $382$, this one begins primarily with $381$ and is reduced with $383$. Furthermore, instead of starting with a primary $a = 380$ or $381$, one could also start with $382, 383,$ or $384$. Only when one begins at $385$ would one fall back into the first method of reduction, because that method, starting with $380$, already includes the one starting with $385$ as its continuation.

In total, there are as many possible **reduction positions** <note>Fechner’s term for the various ways a grid of intervals can be shifted over the raw data.</note> as there are primary $a$ or $i$ values <note>In this context, $i$ refers to the interval size.</note> grouped together within the $i$ of the **reduction level** <note>The "reduction level" is the chosen bin size (e.g., grouping by 5s or 10s).</note>. Since the $i = 1$ mm of the primary Table I is increased to $i = 5$ mm in the first reduction level, five reduction positions are possible here; if reduced to $10$ mm, ten positions would be possible, and so on. And if we treat the primary end-sections—by filling them in with "empty" $a$ values—as being in uniform connection with the main sections (in the sense of method $\alpha$), then the corresponding number of reduction positions extends to these as well.

Now, to exhaust all possible reduction positions of a given reduction level, we must not only fill the gaps between the primary $a$ values with empty $a$ values, but also work backward from the first valid $a$ value with enough empty $a$ values so that the first valid $a$ is still included among those being grouped together. That is, for five possible positions, we must work backward with four, three, two, or one empty $a$ value respectively, depending on the position. Thus, in Table I, where $368$ is the first valid $a$ with $z = 1$, we would have to set the following for the first position:

| *a* | 364 | 365 | 366 | 367 | 368 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| *z* | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

Note that the *A*₁ of the primary table equals 408.5, and that the *A*₂ values for all five positions deviate only slightly from this and consequently from each other; on average, however, they agree entirely with *A*₁. Likewise, the other principal values show only little variation depending on the different positions; the deviation numbers, the sums of deviations, and the resulting <term>mean deviations</term> <note>the average amount that individual data points differ from the mean</note> appear somewhat more divergent.

Yet one can already notice that, as little as the values *A*, *C*, and *D* of the same position differ, they nevertheless appear in the same order across all reduction positions. Specifically, *D* is greater than *A*, and *C* falls between both values, as is required by the <term>laws of asymmetry</term> <note>rules describing the relationship between mean, median, and mode in non-normal distributions</note>. The asymmetry also clearly emerges from the fact that *m*ᵣ > *m'* is true everywhere; indeed, the requirement applicable to cases of asymmetry is also fulfilled, namely that *p* = (*D* — *C*) : (*D* — *A*) is very approximately equal to 1/4 $\pi$ <note>pi</note> = 0.785.

§ 65. While we thus obtain the possibility of five different reduced tables for Table I by increasing the primary *i* fivefold, for Table III we obtain the possibility of four <term>reduction positions</term> <note>different ways to align the starting point of grouped data intervals</note> due to a fourfold increase.

§ 67. The question now arises as to which of the various reduction positions one should adhere to when deriving the elements or testing the established laws. Regarding this, it is likely that completely general, fixed rules cannot be given; however, the following can be stated in general terms.

First, it can be shown from the appearance of our tables themselves that with values of *m* <term>the total number of observations</term> as large as those underlying our tables, the changes in the elements depending on the reduction position are only insignificant. They are generally of the same order as the uncertainty that is permissible in the determination of elements anyway. Consequently, in this regard, it seems fairly indifferent which reduction position one chooses, and one only has to observe the rule of determining all elements to be investigated from the same reduction position. 

Occasionally, however, it happens that among different reduction positions, one or another shows a disadvantage compared to the rest regarding the regular progression of *z* <term>the frequencies or counts of observations</term>. For example, among our five tables in Section I (§ 64), the last one with $E_r = 370$ <note>Referring to a specific starting point or shift in the data</note> shows a deviation from regularity, insofar as it yields a sequence of reduced *z* values of 55, 50, 73, whereas the *z* values should rise continuously until the maximum of 73. All the other four tables, by contrast, show nothing of the sort and are therefore preferable to that one. This draws attention to the fact that if one happens to have encountered a core <note>a central grouping of data</note> with an irregular progression, one can check whether another position might yield better results. 

In general, when comparing different reduction positions, the one to be chosen is that which shows the least deviation from the general laws of distribution. Incidentally, one could avoid the need for any choice by taking all possible reduction positions into account and calculating the mean from the results

...draws, except that this is laborious to carry out and would entail little rewarding complexity.

If we now take a comparative look at the value of primary and derived reduced tables, it becomes clear that for the complete treatment of a Collective Object <note>The author uses the abbreviation "K.-G." for *Kollektiv-Gegenstand*, a term referring to a large group of individual items or measurements treated as a single statistical set.</note>, both tend to complement rather than replace each other. It is only to be regretted that the large amount of space that primary tables generally occupy usually necessitates dispensing with sharing them and being content with reduced ones. In any case, the primary table provides the direct empirical basis for the entire treatment of a given Collective Object. Since the reduction can be carried out in various ways—depending on the size of *i* <term>the interval or class width</term>, the position of those intervals, and according to whole or halved *x* <term>the specific value or measurement being tracked</term>—anyone presented with the primary table remains free to choose which method they wish to use. They also retain the possibility to modify or check a choice already made. Furthermore, the arithmetic mean cannot be obtained as reliably from any reduced table as it can from the primary one, even if the difference may be negligible for sets with a high number of items.

On the other hand, when tracking the lawful progression of values within a Collective Object, a general reduction of the table is indispensable. Similarly, when determining elements that are particularly affected by local irregularities, a local reduction is necessary. Ultimately, the reduction of the table has the advantage of bringing to light a regularity that is not visible in the primary table.

### Determination of $\Sigma a, \Sigma a_{\prime \prime}, \Sigma a', m_{\prime \prime}, m'$ etc.

$S_{\prime}$ and $S'$ are explained as follows: The first $S_{\prime}$ is equal to the first $z$, the second $S_{\prime}$ is equal to the first $+$ second $z$, the third is equal to the first $+$ second $+$ third $z$, and so on, so that the last is equal to the sum of all $z$ and thus $= m$ <note>The author is describing the calculation of "running totals" or cumulative frequencies</note>. Accordingly, each $S_{\prime}$ belonging to a given $a$ is obtained by summing the $S_{\prime}$ belonging to the preceding $a$ with the $z$ of the $a$ in question.

In the column of $S'$, the same procedure is applied, but with summation from the bottom in the opposite direction.

§ 69. Now, apart from the total sum $\Sigma a$ and the total number $m$, a distinction must be made between a rough and an exact <term>original: "scharfe" (sharp); referring to a high-precision calculation</term> determination of the values in question, in the sense already indicated earlier; a rough one, insofar as one calculates as if the number $z$ (the frequency) assigned to each midpoint $a$ in a primary or reduced table belonged entirely to that specific point; an exact one, insofar as consideration is given to the fact that the frequency is actually thought of as being distributed within the surrounding interval <term>the specific range of values, such as 10–12, that a single midpoint like 11 represents</term> of each $a$. According to this, the value of the elements in the interval where the determination takes effect—shortly, the entry interval <term>the specific interval within which a statistical value like the median or mean actually falls</term>—is to be determined by means of interpolation, as shown below. Until now, this has not been addressed; in the following, it will be addressed, and the advantage of it will be proven.

The interval to be interpolated for an exact determination, the so-called entry interval, I will generally denote according to its position and size with $I$. In our example table, its size is $= 2$, consistent with the interval width $i$ used throughout the table, while its position may change depending on the nature of the task. Generally, let its first limit, resulting from the column of intervals, be denoted by $g_1$, and its second by $g_2$; thus, if $10-12$ is the entry interval, $g_1 = 10, g_2 = 12$.

Let it further be generally:
$z_o$ is the frequency $z$ which falls into the entry interval $I$,

$z_o \cdot a_o$ is the corresponding measurement product <note>The result of multiplying a value by its frequency, $z \times a$</note> which falls within $I$,
$v$ is the so-called prefix-number <note>original: "Vorzahl"</note>, i.e., the sum of the $z$, and $\mathfrak{V}$ the sum of the

### Determination of $\Sigma a, \Sigma a_\prime, \Sigma a', m, m'$ etc.

[When] a table is very long, the values for *a* in the *a*-column and the resulting measure-products *za* <term>original: "Maßprodukte"; the product of a value *a* multiplied by its frequency *z*</term> to be calculated from them are very numerous. This is particularly true for primary tables, making this process of calculation and summation extraordinarily cumbersome and prone to calculation errors. One need only try it with any of our primary tables; and even with reduced tables, the same difficulty persists, albeit to a lesser degree. Therefore, it is highly desirable to have a method available—applicable to both primary and reduced tables of every level and position—to find $\Sigma a$ (and consequently $A$) with the exact same value, but in a far more convenient way than the previous procedure. I shall call the previous procedure the *za* method, while calling the method to be explained below the *S* method. It only requires—which is not essential for the *za* method—that the tables to which the *S* method is applied are equidistant <term>spaced at equal intervals</term> or made equidistant by inserting empty *a* values. Consequently, one can restrict the use of the inconvenient *za* method to those cases where equidistance cannot be established.

One can now use either $S_\prime$ or $S'$ as desired to determine the sum $\Sigma a$. In the first case, the determination is made according to the following formula:

->*$\Sigma a = mE' - Z_\prime i ;$* (1)<-

In the second case, according to the formula:

->*$\Sigma a = mE_\prime + Z' i .$* (2)<-

In these formulas, the letters have the following meanings: *m* refers to the total number of values *a* whose sum is to be taken, i.e., $\Sigma z$. $E'$ represents the largest *a* or upper extreme (which, admittedly, stands at the bottom of the table). $E_\prime$ represents the smallest *a* or lower extreme among these *a* values. If the values to be summed constitute only a portion of an entire distribution table, these values <note>referring to $E'$ and $E_\prime$</note> should refer only to that section, not the entire table. Furthermore, let $Z_\prime i$ be the total sum of the $S_\prime$ values belonging to the *a* values being summed, minus the $S_\prime$ that belongs to $E'$; or, to put it another way, the total sum of the $S_\prime$ exclusive of the extreme $S_\prime$. Furthermore, $Z'$ is the...

If we were to take the $\Sigma a$ <note>the sum of all measured values</note> for the entire example table, then $m = \Sigma z$ <note>the total number of observations</note> for that table is 80; $E' = 17$ <note>the highest value</note>; $E_\prime = 3$ <note>the lowest value</note>; $Z_\prime = 304 - 80 = 224$; $Z' = 416 - 80 = 336$; $i = 2$. In exactly the same way, the sum $\Sigma a$ can be found for any segment of the example table, provided that the values for $m, E', E_\prime, S_\prime,$ and $S'$ are modified accordingly. For instance, if the summation were only to be performed for the four $a$ values in the $a$-column from 5 to 11, one would have: $m = \Sigma z = 47$, $E' = 11$, $E_\prime = 5$, $i = 2$. | $S_\prime$ | $S'$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| 2 | 47 |
| 7 | 45 |

| **Sum: 73** | **162** |

consequently ->$Z_\prime = 73 - 47 = 26; Z' = 162 - 47 = 115,$<-
which gives: ->$\Sigma a = 465.$<-

With very long series, one may find it inconvenient to have to ascend to very large values of $S$ as the calculation progresses; this can easily be remedied, however, by dividing the entire series into two or more sections and finding their $\Sigma a$ separately using the previous method, finally combining them. Yet, the combined use of the $S_\prime$ and $S'$ columns in the following manner is even more practical.

One should select a value for $a$ somewhere—most practically around the middle of the table—which shall be called $c$. Then, continue the $S_\prime$ column up to this $c$ (excluding it), and likewise continue the $S'$ column (excluding $c$). Sum the $S_\prime$ and $S'$ values obtained in this way separately; let the first sum be called $Z_\prime$ as before, and the second $Z'$, and then one has:

### Determination of $\Sigma a, \Sigma a_{\prime}, \Sigma a', m, m'$ etc.

->$\Sigma a = mc + (Z' - Z_{\prime})i$,<- (3)

from which:

->$A = c + \frac{Z' - Z_{\prime}}{m} i$,<- (4)

where $m$ is the total number of all $a$ values <note>the total count of observations</note> to be summed.

§ 71. I found the <term>S-procedure</term> cited in an American treatise on <term>recruit measurements</term> <note>the physical dimensions, such as height, of military recruits; a common source of data for early statisticians</note> (by Elliott)$^1$) without any indication of how the author arrived at it, and without proof of its general validity. Now, this proof can certainly be provided, but although it is elementary$^2$), it is rather circumstantial and tedious to follow; I therefore pass over it, since the procedure passes every empirical test. However, to ensure its correct application, I add the following remarks.

1. Naturally, the correctness of the determination of $\Sigma a$ and, consequently, of $A$ <note>the arithmetic mean</note> depends on the correctness of the $S$-columns. If one $S$ in the sequence is wrong, all subsequent ones will also be wrong because every earlier $S$ is incorporated into all later ones; when ascending to high values of $S$, a mistake can easily occur. However, one has a simple and never-to-be-neglected means of control: when using a single $S$-column, the final $S$ value, which is not included in $Z$, must agree with $m$ <note>the total number of cases</note>. In the combined procedure of $S_{\prime}$ and $S'$, however, the final values of $S_{\prime}$ and $S'$ (those not included in $Z$) must, when added to the $z$-value of $c$, give the total number $m$.

2. The $S$-procedure is equally applicable to tables with and without inserted empty $a$ values <note>placeholders for measurements where no observations occurred</note>, and the formation of the $S$-column—

### Determination of $\Sigma a, \Sigma a_{\prime}, \Sigma a', m_{\prime}, m'$ etc.

In both cases, this is done according to the same rule; however, it will nonetheless be useful to specifically explain the application of the rule for the case of "empty" values of *a* where the frequency *z* = 0, in order to prevent any potential misunderstandings and resulting errors in advance. According to the stated rule, each cumulative value *S* belonging to a given value *a* in the *a*-column <note>the column representing the measurement or category</note> is obtained by adding the frequency *z* of that *a* to the *S* of the preceding *a*. If this *a* is an empty one with a frequency of *z* = 0, then its *S* is naturally just a repetition of the previous *S*. If several empty *a* values follow one another, the *S* of the preceding valid *a* is repeated as many times as there are empty entries. Our two example tables (in § 68 and § 70) provide no occasion to illustrate this, because like most <term>reduced tables</term> <note>tables where data has been grouped into larger categories to save space</note>, they do not contain empty *a* values. However, <term>primary tables</term> <note>raw data tables showing every individual measurement increment</note> offer much more opportunity for this, especially in their final sections. To provide a brief illustration, we will arbitrarily construct a small table here with some empty *a* values. We will place the repeated *S* values belonging to these empty *a* entries in parentheses to make them easier to distinguish from the others. However, they must not be excluded from the summation when forming the total sum of *S* (and thus *Z*); rather, they must be counted just like any other entry:

---

| *a* <note>value</note> | *z* <note>freq.</note> | *S,* <note>sum up</note> | *S'* <note>sum down</note> |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 3 | 2 | 2 | 50 |
| 5 | 0 | (2) | (48) |
| 7 | 0 | (2) | (48) |
| 9 | 10 | 12 | 48 |
| 11 | 30 | 42 | 38 |
| 13 | 5 | 47 | 8 |
| 15 | 0 | (47) | (3) |
| 17 | 3 | 50 | 3 |
| **Sum** | 50 | 204 | 246 |

Therefore, this check must not be neglected, but one must also realize that even if the final total matches, it does not guarantee against an incorrect application of the empty *a* values within the sequence.

Aside from direct summation of the relevant $za$ values, these sums can be obtained in the specified manner using the **S-procedure** <note>the method of using cumulative sums discussed previously</note>.

For a **precise determination** <note>a "sharp" calculation that accounts for fractions of an interval rather than rounding to the nearest category</note>, one must conceive of the sum $\Sigma a_1$ as being composed of two parts: the **preliminary sum** $\mathfrak{V}$, which extends from the beginning of the table to the start of the **interval of entry** $I$, and the **entry sum** $Y$. This entry sum extends from that point to $H$ (in our case, to $A$) and is obtained through simple **interpolation** <note>estimating an unknown value between two known points</note>, by assuming that the entry sum $Y$ relates to the total sum of the interval $I$ (that is, to $z_o a_o$) just as the **entry measure** $x$ <note>the distance from the start of the category to the target point</note> relates to the total interval $I$; therefore:

-> $Y : z_o a_o = x : I$, <- (5)

hence:

-> $Y = \frac{x}{I} z_o a_o$; <- (6)

and accordingly:

-> $\Sigma a_1 = \mathfrak{V} + \frac{x}{I} z_o a_o$. <- (7)

In our example table, $\mathfrak{V} = 138, z_o a_o = 330, x = 1.4, I = 2$; consequently:

-> $\Sigma a_1 = 369; \Sigma a' = \Sigma a - \Sigma a_1 = 912 - 369 = 543$, <-

which deviates significantly from the rough determinations.

Should any other **principal value** $H$ occur instead of $A$, the previous formulas would remain the same, except that $x$ would be taken as $H - g_1$ <note>where $g_1$ is the lower limit of the interval</note> instead of $A - g_1$. -> $\Sigma a_1 = 138 + \frac{1.467}{2} \cdot 330 = 380 + 0.055$ <-
-> $\Sigma a' = 912 - \Sigma a_1 \qquad = 532 - 0.055$, <-

<term>Summation</term>: The process of adding a sequence of numbers.
<term>S-procedure</term>: A method for managing cumulative frequency.
<term>Preliminary sum (Vorsumme)</term>: The sum of all values in categories prior to the one currently being analyzed.
<term>Entry sum (Eingriffssumme)</term>: The portion of a category's total that falls below a specific calculated threshold.
<term>Interval of entry (Eingriffsintervall)</term>: The specific category or "bin" in a data table that contains the calculated mean or median.
<term>Interpolation</term>: A mathematical method of estimating values between two known points.
<term>Entry measure (Eingriffsmaß)</term>: The exact distance one must move into a specific interval to reach the target value.
<term>Principal value (Hauptwert)</term>: A central statistical value, such as an average or median.
<term>Decimal</term>: A digit representing a fraction of a whole number in a base-10 system.

If one wished to obtain an even more precise determination of the **entry sum** *Y* <note>the partial sum of values within a specific interval</note> by replacing simple interpolation with a more refined method using **second differences** <note>a mathematical technique using the rate of change of the differences to improve accuracy</note>, this would not be permissible. This is because the products *ax* <note>value times frequency</note>, which serve as the basis for the **first differences** here, represent the sum of values *a* falling within an interval *i* only under the assumption that these values are distributed evenly across the entire interval. This conceptual approach already establishes the relationship between the entry sum *Y* and the **entry measure** *x* <note>the distance from the start of the interval to the target value</note>. Specifically, it prevents the entry sum from being influenced by the product values *ax* that precede or follow the interpolated interval, which is an influence that the use of second or higher-order differences would necessarily assume.

Therefore, if one wishes to determine the entry sum *Y* with the greatest possible precision from the same perspective that governs the summation of all values *a* falling within a whole interval, one must consider the values of *a* involved in forming the entry sum (the count of which is the **entry number** *y* <term>Eingriffszahl: the frequency or number of observations within the partial interval</term>, which will be found in the following paragraph to be $\varkappa_{\circ} x : I$) as being concentrated at the midpoint of the partial interval designated as the entry measure *x*—that is, at $g_{1} + \frac{1}{2}x$ <note>$g_1$ represents the lower limit of the interval</note>. Thus, one sets:

-> $Y = \frac{x}{I} \varkappa_{\circ} \left( g_{1} + \frac{x}{2} \right)$ (8) <-

instead of setting it equal to $\varkappa_{\circ} a_{\circ} x : I$, as was done above. The sum of $a_{,,}$ <note>a secondary sum variant</note> is then found to be:

-> $\Sigma' a_{,,} = \mathfrak{V} + \frac{x}{I} \varkappa_{\circ} \left( g_{1} + \frac{x}{2} \right),$ (9) <-

where the index added to the summation symbol <note>the prime symbol in $\Sigma'$</note> serves to distinguish it from formula (7). In the case of a proportional determination of *Y*, the value $\Sigma a$ is consequently calculated as being too large by the amount:

-> $\frac{x (I - x)}{2 I} \cdot \varkappa_{\circ}$ <-

so that the more precise method of determination (8) generally offers a significant advantage...

## § 73. Determination of the deviation counts m₁, m'.

According to a rough determination, m₁ is easily found by summing the values *z* <note>In this context, *z* typically refers to the frequency or number of observations within a specific data group</note> which belong to the values *a* that are smaller than *H*; if we take $A = 11.4$ <note>Referring to the Arithmetic Mean calculated in earlier sections</note> for *H* in our example table, this gives $\mu_1 = 48$ and $\mu' = m - \mu_1 = 80 - 48 = 32$.

If a precise determination <note>original: *scharfe Bestimmung*</note> is required, then m₁ is composed of the **pre-count** *v* <note>original: *Vorzahl*; the sum of frequencies in all intervals preceding the one containing the threshold</note>, which extends to the beginning of the interval *I*, and the **entry count** *y* <note>original: *Eingriffszahl*; the portion of the frequency within the specific interval where the threshold falls</note>, which extends from that start point to *H*. This latter value is obtained, knowing that $x = H - g_1$, through interpolation by setting up the proportion:
-> y : z₀ = x : I, <- (12)
therefore:
-> y = \frac{x}{I} z₀ <- (13)
and consequently:
-> m₁ = v + \frac{x}{I} z₀. <- (14)

If we take the value $A = 11.4$ for *H* and accordingly use the above values $v = 18; x = 1.4; z_0 = 30; I = 2$, we obtain $\mu_1 = 39$ and $\mu' = 80 - 39 = 41$. This is a determination that again deviates significantly from the rough one—indeed, it even causes the majority <note>original: *Übergewicht*, literally "overweight" or "preponderance"</note> to fall on the opposite side.

If m' is to be determined directly rather than by subtracting m₁ from *m*—which can be useful for verification <note>original: *Kontrolle*</note>—then the general precise formula is:
-> m' = n + \frac{I - x}{I} z₀, <- (15)
which, when setting $H = A$ and by virtue of $n = 32$, leads back to:
-> \mu' = 32 + \frac{2 - 1.4}{2} \cdot 30 = 41 <-
as expected.

[This determination of the entry count <term>entry count (Eingriffszahl): the calculated portion of the frequency within a specific interval where the threshold falls</term> *y* through simple interpolation is considered exact as long as the distribution of the values *a* within the individual intervals can be assumed to be uniform. This is because the grouping of the counts of *a* by interval into *z*-values—which serve as the basis for interpolation as first differences—is not dependent on specific assumptions about the distribution of *a* within the relevant intervals, unlike the corresponding grouping of the sums of *a* into *za*-values. in which third differences are included. In particular, the use of formula (16) results in the application of formulas (10) and (11).]

# Determination of Σa, Σa₁, Σa', m₁, m' etc.

## § 74. Determination of the mutual sums of deviations ΣΘ', ΣΘ₁, relative to a given main value H.

We obtain the positive sum of deviations relative to any starting value *H* directly if we sum the individually determined differences Θ' = a' — H; the negative sum of deviations, which from here on is always to be taken as an absolute value <note>Taking the "absolute value" means treating negative differences as positive numbers so they can be summed effectively</note>, is obtained if we sum the individually determined differences Θ₁ = H — a₁; however, the individual determination of the many differences is laborious and easily subject to calculation errors. Both are avoided by determining them according to the following formula:

->ΣΘ' = Σa' — m' H  <-
->                  |  (18)<-
->ΣΘ₁ = m₁ H — Σa₁ /<-

In fact, the sum of the positive Θ, i.e., ΣΘ', is gained by subtracting the value *H* from each of the *m'* values of *a'* (that is, the values of *a* which are greater than *H*), thus subtracting *H* from Σa' a total of *m'* times¹); which gives the first of the above equations. On the other hand, the sum of the negative Θ is obtained as an absolute value when the sum of the *m₁* values of *a₁* (that is, the values of *a* which are smaller than *H*) is subtracted from *m₁* times *H*, which gives the second of the above equations.

These formulas apply to both crude <term>crude determination (rohe Bestimmung): a basic calculation using raw grouped data without refined interpolation</term> and precise determination <term>precise determination (scharfe Bestimmung): a calculation that uses higher-order interpolation to account for data distribution within intervals</term>, with the only difference being that for crude determination *m₁* and *m'*, Σa₁ and Σa' are determined crudely, and for precise determination, they are determined precisely. If we now again take *A* <note>The variable *A* here refers to the arithmetic mean used in the author's ongoing example</note> as the main value for our example table, in which case μ is substituted for *m* and Δ for Θ, then for both crude and precise determination we can use the values already determined earlier, according to which, crudely, μ₁ = 48; μ' = 32; Σa₁ = 468; Σa' = 444; this gives:

->      / ΣΔ₁ = 48 · 11.4 — 468 = 79.2<-
->crude {<-
->      \ ΣΔ' = 444 — 32 · 11.4 = 79.2<-

Regarding the <term>mean deviation: the average amount by which individual data points differ from the mean</term>, one obtains first ΣΔ by doubling ΣΔ₁, and hereafter:

->η = ΣΔ / m and η_c = η √(m / (m - 1)) (22)<-

It would be incorrect to attempt to determine η as the mean of η₁ = ΣΔ₁ : μ₁ and η' = ΣΔ' : μ'—that is, = 1/2 (η₁ + η')—as Elliott <note>Likely Ezekiel Brown Elliott (1823–1888), an American statistician known for his work on the physical characteristics of Union soldiers</note> did in his treatise on <term>American recruit measurements: statistical data concerning the height and health of soldiers</term>. For not only does this run contrary to the sense of the original <term>Gauss's Rule: a fundamental principle in error theory developed by Carl Friedrich Gauss</term>, but one also neglects the different weights that belong to η₁ or η' depending on their derivation from μ₁ and μ' values; according to which the correct mean:

->η = (μ₁ η₁ + μ' η') / m = (ΣΔ₁ + ΣΔ') / m = ΣΔ / m (23)<-

is.

# X. Summary and Relationship of the Main Properties of the Three Primary Values $A, C, D$, and also $R, T, F$.

§ 76. In addition to the three primary values that I generally prefer—the arithmetic mean $A$, the central value $C$ <note>original: "Zentralwert"; known today as the median</note>, and the densest value $D$ <note>original: "dichtester Wert"; known today as the mode</note>—the following three secondary values will also be considered, which I list as the partition value $R$, the heaviest value $T$, and the deviation-weight value $F$.

Arranged clearly according to their main differences, they are as follows.

**Partition value** $R$ <term>Partition value: a specific point in a dataset that divides the total sum of all values into two equal halves</term>, the value $a$ regarding which $\Sigma a' = \Sigma a'' = \frac{1}{2} \Sigma a$; thus, the sum of the larger values is equal to the sum of the smaller values, and therefore each of the two is equal to half the total sum of all $a$ values.

**Arithmetic mean** $A$, the value $a$ regarding which $\Sigma \Theta' = \Sigma \Theta''$; that is, the sum of the positive deviations is equal to the sum of the negative deviations; and regarding which $\Sigma \Theta^2$ <note>The sum of the squared deviations from the mean</note> is a minimum.

**Central value** $C$ <note>The median</note>, the value $a$ regarding which $m' = m''$; that is, the count of positive deviations is equal to the count of negative deviations, and $\Sigma \Theta$ <note>The sum of the absolute deviations</note> is a minimum.

**Densest value** $D$ <note>The mode</note>, the value $a$ regarding which the counts of deviations on both sides $m_1 : m'$ relate as their respective mean errors $e_1 : e'$, and the frequency $z$ <term>Maßzahl: in this context, the number of times a specific value occurs in the dataset</term> is at a maximum.

**Heaviest $a$-value** $T$, the value $a$ whose product with its frequency ($z \cdot a$) is at a maximum.

**Deviation-weight value** $F$, the value $a$ regarding which $z \Theta$ <note>The frequency of a value multiplied by its distance (deviation) from the center</note> is at a maximum.

**Main Properties of the Main Values.**

I will not, however, treat these values in the previous order, but according to the sequence *A*, *C*, *D*, *R*, *T*, *F*.

Aside from *A*, the previous values—like the values in the preceding chapter—are capable of both a coarse and a precise <note>original: "scharfen"; here meaning mathematically exact or refined</note> determination, whereas for *A*, no such distinction can be made. The same small distribution table will serve here as it did there to illustrate the derivation, and the notations used therein are to be understood in the sense specified in § 9 and 10. Regarding *A*, here too $m_{,,}, m'$ <note>These represent the count of values below and above the center</note> transition into $\mu_{,,}, \mu'$, and $\Theta, \Theta'$ <note>General deviations</note> transition into $\Delta_{,,}, \Delta'$ <note>Specific deviations from the arithmetic mean</note>.

### § 77. Arithmetic Mean A.

The arithmetic mean of a series of values *a* unites the following three properties within itself:

1) The property by which it is defined: that it is the quotient of the sum of the *a* values divided by their number *m*, thus:

->$$A = \frac{\Sigma a}{m}$$ (1)<-

or, insofar as $\Sigma a$ is obtained by the summation of the products *za* <note>The value multiplied by its frequency</note>, then $= \Sigma az : m$;

2) that the sum of the positive deviations $\Delta'$ from it is equal to the sum of the negative deviations $\Delta_{,,}$ according to their absolute value, thus:

->$\Sigma \Delta' = \Sigma \Delta_{,,}$, or $\Sigma \Delta' - \Sigma \Delta_{,,} = 0$; (2)<-

3) that the sum of the squares of the deviations from it is smaller than from any other value; in short:

->$\Sigma \Delta^2 = \Sigma \Delta'^2 + \Sigma \Delta_{,,}^2 = \text{Minimum}$. (3)<-

The preceding properties of *A* are so interconnected that once one is given, the others are simultaneously provided, and the mean can be derived from any of them with an identical result, though the derivation according to the first property remains the most practical. Furthermore, these properties are independent of any specific law of distribution for the values *a* and apply beyond collective measurement theory <note>original: "Kollektivmaßlehre"; Fechner’s term for the study of distributions in large datasets</note> not only for an ideal series assumed to be infinite, but also for every finite series of *a* in any arbitrary distribution.

<sig>Fechner, Collective Measurement Theory.</sig>

# Main Properties of the Primary Values.

The connection of the second and third propositions <note>original: "Satz"; in this mathematical context, it refers to a theorem or formal statement of property</note> with the first, which is given by the definition, is found as follows.

**Second Proposition.** Every positive deviation from $A$ is $a' - A$, and every negative deviation, according to its absolute value, is $A - a_{ \prime}$. Developed hereafter:

-> $\Sigma \Delta' = (a' - A) + (a'' - A) + \dots$ } (4) <-
-> $\Sigma \Delta_{ \prime} = (A - a_{ \prime}) + (A - a_{ \prime\prime}) + \dots$ } <-

consequently, if $\mu'$ is the number of positive deviations and $\mu_{ \prime}$ is the number of negative deviations,

-> $\Sigma \Delta' = \Sigma a' - \mu' A$ <-
-> $\Sigma \Delta_{ \prime} = \mu_{ \prime} A - \Sigma a_{ \prime}$ <-
-> $\Sigma \Delta' - \Sigma \Delta_{ \prime} = \Sigma a' + \Sigma a_{ \prime} - (\mu' + \mu_{ \prime}) A$ (5) <-

or, because the sum of all parts equals the whole ($\Sigma a' + \Sigma a_{ \prime} = \Sigma a$) and the total number of observations is the sum of both groups ($\mu' + \mu_{ \prime} = m$),

-> $\Sigma \Delta' - \Sigma \Delta_{ \prime} = \Sigma a - m A,$ (6) <-

and because $A$ is defined as the sum divided by the count ($A = \Sigma a : m$)

-> $\Sigma \Delta' - \Sigma \Delta_{ \prime} = \Sigma a - \Sigma a = 0.$ (7) <-

**Third Proposition.** Let the value for which the sum of the squared deviations ($\Sigma \Delta^{2}$) is a minimum <note>This is the foundational principle of "Least Squares," a method used to find the best-fitting value in a dataset.</note> be set initially as an unknown $= x$; thus we have:

-> $\Sigma \Delta^{2} = (a' - x)^{2} + (a'' - x)^{2} + \dots + (a_{ \prime} - x)^{2} + (a_{ \prime\prime} - x)^{2} + \dots$ (8) <-

To be sure, insofar as we take the negative deviations as positive according to their absolute value, every negative deviation should be set as $x - a_{ \prime}$ etc. instead of $a_{ \prime} - x$ etc.; however, $(a_{ \prime} - x)^{2}$ is equal to $(x - a_{ \prime})^{2}$, which allows the previous value of $\Sigma \Delta^{2}$ to be developed in the manner indicated. Now we obtain the minimum value of $\Sigma \Delta^{2}$ by setting the differential <note>A calculus technique used to find the lowest or highest point of a function</note> of its expression with respect to $x$ equal to zero; this gives:

-> $2 [(a' - x) + (a'' - x) + \dots + (a_{ \prime} - x) + (a_{ \prime\prime} - x) + \dots] dx = 0$ (9) <-

consequently, by summing all $a$ and all $- x$ terms:

-> $\Sigma a - m x = 0,$ | (10) <-
-> $x = \frac{\Sigma a}{m} = A.$ | <-

# Main Properties of the Primary Values.

<sig>11*</sig>

§ 78. Even if the arithmetic mean value cannot claim an equally predominant interest for <term>collective measure theory</term> <note>The study of how large groups of variable data—like heights of people or weights of seeds—are distributed; today we call this statistics.</note> as it does for physical and astronomical measure theory, the combination of its three main properties still grants it an inherent mathematical interest. This interest grows even further because the mean establishes a relationship between both fields of study. Compared to the **densest value** *D* <note>Known today as the **mode**, or the most frequently occurring value in a dataset.</note>, the mean has the advantage of greater ease and simplicity in its precise determination. While it is surpassed in this regard by the **central value** *C* <note>Known today as the **median**, the middle value when all data is ranked from smallest to largest.</note>, the fact that the magnitude of deviations <note>The distance of each individual data point from the average.</note> is factored into the mean’s calculation—rather than just the count of items—gives it a weightier significance than *C*. 

The following can also be noted: If one takes an arbitrary series of values *a* in the random order they appear in the original list and divides them into a given number of fractions (subgroups) of equal size, and determines the arithmetic mean *A* for each subgroup individually, the arithmetic mean of these subgroup means will match the general mean of the entire series. However, if one proceeds similarly with the determination of *C*, neither the central value nor the mean of the various individual *C* values will generally match the *C* obtained from the totality of the values. If one does the same with *D*, while the *D* of the whole is preserved, the mean of the individual *D* values does not match the *D* of the total set.

Finally, the following practical advantage is linked to the determination of *A*. If one has determined the *A* of a <term>collective object</term> <note>original: "K.-G." (Kollektivgegenstand); an individual entity made of many varying parts, like "the height of the German soldier."</note> from a distribution table with a sample size *m* that is not too small, one can find not only the total magnitude "Gr." <note>original: "Gr." (Größe)</note> of the object for that table by multiplying *A* by *m*, but also predict the total magnitude of the object for any larger or smaller sample size *m* by multiplying that first determined *A* by the new *m*. This calculation is subject to a probable error that increases the smaller the sample size *m* is, and the further the new *m* deviates from the original. Conversely, one can probabilistically estimate the number of specimens *m* required to reach a given total magnitude Gr.

§ 79. It may happen that one wishes to derive a common mean from the $A$ <note>The arithmetic mean.</note> of different <term>collective groups</term> <note>Abbreviated in the original as K.-G. (*Kollektiv-Gegenstand*); these are groups of data points belonging to the same category, like heights of a specific population.</note> or from the specifically determined $A$ of different sections of the same collective group. If these $A$ values are obtained from different sample sizes ($m$), one must distinguish whether the definitive mean should be calculated with or without regard to the difference in those sizes. Let $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3 \dots$ be specific means, drawn respectively from $m_1$, $m_2$, $m_3 \dots$ measurements. Without regard to the difference in the sample sizes ($m$), the mean of the relevant $A$ values will be:

-> $\frac{A_1 + A_2 + A_3 + \dots}{N}$, (11) <-

where $N$ is the number of $A$ values; however, taking into account the difference in the sample sizes ($m$), it will be:

-> $\frac{m_1 A_1 + m_2 A_2 + m_3 A_3 + \dots}{m_1 + m_2 + m_3 + \dots}$ (12) <-

and this matches the mean obtained by dividing the total sum of all individual measurements ($a$) by the total sum of all sample counts ($m$).

The former mean shall be called the *singular*, and the latter the *summary* mean. Depending on the nature of the task, one or the other method of calculating the mean may be preferable. Suppose the mean body height of Chinese, Black, Malay, American, and Europeans of the Caucasian race <note>The author uses 19th-century racial classifications typical of early anthropological statistics.</note> is to be determined; but for the Europeans, 1,000 measurements are available, while for each of the other races, only 10–20 measurements are provided. In this case, the second type—the summary calculation—would be inadmissible; for, as is easily understood, the average body height of these different races would—due to the disproportionately heavy weight given to the Europeans by their large $m$—coincide almost entirely with that of the Europeans—

### § 80. Central Value *C*.

In contrast to the three main properties of the arithmetic mean *A*, the **central value** *C* <note>Known in modern statistics as the median.</note> combines the following three main properties:

1. The property given by its definition: having just as many larger values *a'* above it as smaller values *a,* <note>The author uses a comma as a subscript to denote values below the central point.</note> below it.
2. The property of having an equal number of positive and negative deviations dependent on it, so that $m' = m, = \frac{1}{2} m$ <note>Meaning that exactly half the total number of observations lie on either side of the median.</note>.
3. The property that the sum of the positive and negative deviations from it, according to their absolute values <note>Ignoring whether the difference is positive or negative.</note>, is smaller than from any other value; consequently, with respect to it, $\Sigma \Theta$ <note>The sum of absolute deviations.</note> is a <term>minimum</term> <note>This is a fundamental property of the median: it minimizes the sum of absolute distances.</note>.

These properties are also mutually dependent and apply to any arbitrary series of *a*; regardless of any particular <term>law of distribution</term> <note>The mathematical pattern or "shape" formed by the data points.</note>, just as is the case for the three main properties of the mean *A*.

The derivation of the second property from the first is self-evident and requires no explanation. However, the connection of the third property to them follows as such.

If the value for which the third property holds is initially set as an unknown $= x$, then the sum of the deviations with respect to $x$, according to their absolute value <note>The "absolute value" refers to the distance of a point from the center, regardless of whether it is positive or negative.</note>, is to be expressed as follows:

->$\Sigma \Theta = (a' - x) + (a'' - x) + \dots + (x - a,) + (x - a,,) + \dots$ (13)<-

To obtain the minimum of this sum, we must set its differential with respect to $x$ equal to 0; this gives:

->$- m' dx + m, dx = 0 ,$ (14)<-

consequently:

->$m' = m, ,$ (15)<-

which corresponds to the concept of the <term>central value<gloss>The median; the middle value in a data set where half the numbers are above and half are below.</gloss></term>.
I first proved this property of the central value in a treatise $^1)$ regarding the same and, by generalizing the method used there, drew more extensive conclusions, which I have no occasion to delve into here.

§ 81. One can assign the following significance to the central value for <term>collective measurement theory<gloss>Kollektivmaßlehre: The study of the laws governing variation within groups of similar objects.</gloss></term>.
If one imagined all specimens of a <note>original: "K.-G." abbreviation for "Kollektiv-Gegenstand" (Collective Object).</note> Collective Object placed into a large urn—for which one can regard the world itself—and a specimen were drawn at random, the probability would be equal that one would draw a larger or a smaller specimen than *C*. With a very large number of draws, this equal probability would indeed prove itself. In contrast, regarding values larger than *C*, the probability of drawing a smaller object outweighs, and regarding values smaller than *C*, the probability of drawing a larger specimen outweighs. Accordingly, one can call *C* the "probable value" of a Collective Object in the same sense that one calls the "probable error" of an observational average, insofar as the probability of exceeding or falling below it is equal.

The derivation of *C* from a series of values *a*, which are arranged according to their size, must in principle be done by counting an equal number of values from each end of the series toward the middle. ## § 83. The Most Dense Value *D*.

If we define the <term>most dense value<gloss>Known in modern statistics as the **mode**; it is the value that appears most frequently in a data set.</gloss> briefly as the one that occurs most frequently within a series of values (*a*), or the one where the greatest frequency (*z*) falls, we see that such a value cannot be derived from just any arbitrary series of *a* in the same way the previous two primary values were. It primarily holds relevance for <term>Collective Measurement Theory<gloss>A field of study, pioneered by Gustav Fechner, that applies statistical methods to groups of natural or social phenomena rather than individual measurements.</gloss>, though for that field it is very important^1). Indeed, if we were to arbitrarily set up the following series of five values (*a*):

->1, 3, 4, 6, 16,<-

we would find the arithmetic mean to be *A* = Σ *a* : *m* = 30 : 5 = 6; and the *central value* (found by meeting in the middle while counting from the left and right) would be *C* = 4. But which value should we take as the most dense value, since every value occurs only once, meaning all frequencies (*z*) are merely 1? Other series can be constructed where different frequencies occur for different values, but the same maximum frequency repeats across several values, making it impossible to decide which should be regarded as *D*. However, in the <term>distribution tables<gloss>Charts showing how often different measurements occur within a sample.</gloss> of Collective Measurement Theory with a large total count (*m*)—which meet the requirements for a successful investigation—such cases usually do not occur at all. Even if they do occur in <term>primary tables<gloss>Raw data tables before the numbers have been grouped into larger categories or "bins."</gloss> (examples of which can be found in the tables in Chapter VII), they can be resolved through the necessary <term>reduction<gloss>The process of grouping data into larger intervals to smooth out irregularities and reveal the overall trend.</gloss> in such a way that the maximum frequency falls on only one of the reduced values. In this case—

1) If the assumption—which has so far gone unchallenged—that <term>errors of observation<gloss>Minor deviations in measurements caused by human error or tool precision.</gloss> in unobjectionable observations have a symmetrical <term>probability<gloss>Abbreviated as *W.* (Wahrscheinlichkeit) in the original.</gloss> regarding the arithmetic mean of the observations should prove to be erroneous, then the great importance of the *D* (mode) would also extend to physical and astronomical measurement theories. <note>Regarding this, see Chapter XXVIII.</note>

From this, it further depends that, in order to obtain a simple distribution law for collective deviations, the deviations must be made dependent on it rather than on *A* or *C*. One can further add that *D* represents the most probable value of a Collective Object from the following point of view:

If one randomly picks a single specimen from the totality of values *a* in a Collective Object, the value *D* will be hit with a higher probability than any other. The values close to it will be hit with a probability nearly equal to its own, yet different, depending on whether they fall on one side of *D* or the other.

According to this, the importance of *D* for Collective Objects surpasses that of every other primary value from more than one perspective. However, this does not prevent the other values from remaining noteworthy for the properties they do *not* share with it, as they belong to the complete characterization of a Collective Object. Furthermore, *D* stands at a disadvantage compared to all others in that its most precise representation is cumbersome...

### § 84. The Dividing Value *R*.

The value that has an equal sum of <term>*a*<gloss>The individual measurements or data points in the set.</gloss> above it as below it. It serves as the dividing boundary between the smaller and larger values of *a* (when ordered by size), such that the sum of the smaller values produces the same total magnitude as the sum of the larger values.

<note>While the median (C) splits the *number* of cases in half, the Dividing Value (R) splits the *total sum* of the values in half. This is often used in economics to study wealth distribution.</note>

[It lies above <term>*C*<gloss>The central value or median.</gloss>. — Since the number of values of *a* lying above and below *C* is in both cases equal to $\frac{1}{2}m$ (according to the definition of *C*), it follows that:

->$\Sigma a < \frac{m}{2} C < \Sigma a'$<-
<note>$\Sigma a$ represents the sum of values below the median, while $\Sigma a'$ represents the sum of values above the median.</note>

Therefore, an equality between the lower and upper sums can only be reached at a value that is greater than *C*. Consequently, it also lies above <term>*A*<gloss>The arithmetic mean.</gloss> or above <term>*D*<gloss>The densest value or mode.</gloss>, depending on whether *A* or *D* is smaller than *C*. Conversely, it might possibly lie below one or the other of these two primary values if one or the other is larger than *C*. However, to determine its position first with regard to *A* (which is usually assumed to be already known), let it be assumed that *R* lies above *A*.]

One calculates $\sigma = \frac{1}{2} (\Sigma a'' - \Sigma a_{\prime\prime})$ moving upwards (that is, towards the larger values) starting from *A* in order to arrive at *R*.

->$\Sigma a, = \Sigma a_{,,} + \sigma.$<-
<note>Here, $\Sigma a,$ is the sum of values below the Dividing Value $R$. It is calculated by taking the sum of values below the mean ($\Sigma a_{,,}$) and adding an adjustment factor ($\sigma$).</note>

The upper sum with respect to $R$, however, is equal to:

->$\Sigma a' = \Sigma a'' - \sigma,$<-
<note>$\Sigma a'$ is the sum of values above $R$. It equals the sum of values above the mean ($\Sigma a''$) minus that same adjustment factor ($\sigma$).</note>

->$\Sigma a, = \Sigma a', \Sigma a_{,,} + \sigma = \Sigma a'' - \sigma,$<-
->$\sigma = \frac{\Sigma a'' - \Sigma a_{,,}}{2} .$ <span style="float: right;">(17)</span><-

->$\Sigma a_{,,} = \mu, A - \Sigma \Delta,$<-
->$\Sigma a'' = \mu' A + \Sigma \Delta',$<-
<note>$\mu$ represents the number of cases (frequency), and $\Delta$ represents the deviations from the mean $A$.</note>

we also have:

->$\sigma = \frac{(\mu' - \mu,) A + \Sigma \Delta}{2} .$ <span style="float: right;">(18)</span><-

These methods of determination apply regardless of any particular law of distribution, except that a rough and a precise determination can be distinguished in the usual way. [They remain valid even if $A$ <gloss>the arithmetic mean</gloss> lies above $R$; in that case, however, $\sigma$ becomes negative and must therefore—taken according to its absolute value—be counted downwards, i.e., toward the smaller values from $A$, in order to arrive at $R$.]

Determination: σ = ½ Σ Θ (relative to C <gloss>the median or central value</gloss>); starting from D <gloss>the "density value" or mode</gloss>, however: σ = ½ (m' - m,) D + ½ Σ δ. <note>These formulas allow the reader to find the adjustment factor σ using different starting points in the data set.</note> Moreover, R can also be found directly, without depending on a pre-determined other primary value. This is done by searching for the interval in which R lies by adding the values *a* from both ends of the distribution table, and then determining the "inclusion sum" *Y* in this specific interval such that the preceding sum, increased by the inclusion sum, equals half of the total sum of *a*. Using the designations defined in § 69, this leads to the formula:

-> R = g, + (½ Σ a - 𝔙) · I / (a₀ κ₀)      (19a) <-

or to

-> R = √(g,² + I / κ₀ (Σ a - 2 𝔙)),      (19b) <-

depending on whether—in accordance with the provisions made in § 72—the "inclusion measure" *x* (that is, the value by which R exceeds the lower limit *g,* of the interval *I*) is calculated according to the proportion

-> x : I = Y : a₀ κ₀ <-

or more precisely according to the equation:

-> Y = (g, + x/2) (κ₀ x / I) <-

and is then added to *g,*. <note>The variable *g,* refers to the lower boundary of the numerical class containing the dividing value, and *I* represents the width of that class.</note> ]

[Finally, it is worth mentioning that the position of R depends on the values *a* of the distribution table in a different way than the positions of A <gloss>the arithmetic mean</gloss>, C <gloss>the median</gloss>, and D <gloss>the mode</gloss>. If one increases every *a* by the same amount, then A, C, and D also increase by that same amount, so that their relative position within the table remains the same. In contrast, the specified increase causes R to approach C in such a way that, with an unlimited increase, R coincides with C. <note>In simpler terms: as a data set becomes more uniform or "dense," the point that splits the total sum (R) moves toward the point that splits the number of cases (C).</note> This follows directly from the fact that the sum of *a* located between C and R (that is, σ) is constantly equal to ½ Σ Θ (relative to C) and is therefore distributed over an increasingly smaller interval as *a* becomes larger.]

### § 85. The Heaviest Value *T*.

Every value *a* in a distribution table <gloss>a dataset or frequency table</gloss> suitable for our investigations yields, generally speaking, a different product *za* based on its size and the *z* <gloss>the frequency</gloss> of how often it occurs. We can now ask for the specific *a* for which this product reaches its maximum. At first, one might think that this coincides with the "densest value" <gloss>the mode, or the most frequent value, denoted as *D*</gloss>. However, for the mode, only the magnitude of *z* matters, not the product *za*. There are values for *a* that are larger than *D*, and although they occur less frequently than *D*, the larger size of *a* gives them an advantage regarding the product *za* they produce, up to a certain limit.

In any case, *T* can only lie on the positive side of *D* <gloss>meaning T is always a higher value than the mode</gloss>, because as the values of *a* decrease below *D*, both *a* and *z* decrease as well. According to a rough estimation in our example table, *T* would fall on the same value as *D* at *a* = 11, provided that the maximum *za* = 330 is found there. However, by a precise determination <gloss>scientific calculation rather than a simple table reading</gloss>, the two diverge. If the "double-sided Gaussian Law" <note>original: "zweiseitige G. G." refers to the Normal Distribution or Gaussian curve</note> is assumed to be applicable, one must use the following formula according to the proof provided below:

->$T = \frac{D + \sqrt{D^{2} + 2\ \pi\ \epsilon'^{2}}}{2}$ . (20)<-

From our example table in § 68, we find, according to the proportional method to be explained in the next chapter:

->$D = 11.6; \epsilon' = 1.9;$<-

and therefore

->$T = 12.1.$<-

Now one might ask: what is the empirical significance of the fact that the maximum of *za* falls on this determined value of *T*? In this regard, one must remember that upon closer inspection, every *a* in a distribution table actually represents an entire interval of the size *i* <gloss>the class width</gloss> of that table, of which the respective *a* is the center. Thus, with the value *T* = 12.1 for our distribution table, where *i* = 2, it is stated that among all

### Proof.
Since $T$ is greater than $D$ <gloss>the mode</gloss>, we set

-> $T = D + \partial,$ (21) <-

where $\partial$ <note>The Greek letter delta, here representing a small positive deviation</note> is a positive deviation from $D$, and we determine $\partial$ by setting

-> $za = z(D + \partial)$ (22) <-

differentiating this value to obtain a maximum equation with respect to $\partial$ and setting the differential to zero. For the sake of simplicity, we omit the small strokes <note>Fechner refers to prime marks (′) used in his system to distinguish values on the positive vs. negative sides of the distribution</note> above $z, a, \partial, e$ that should actually be applied to designate the position of these values above $D$.

We have, therefore:

-> $\frac{\partial(za)}{\partial \partial} = (D + \partial) \frac{\partial z}{\partial \partial} + z \frac{\partial \partial}{\partial \partial},$ (23) <-

of which the last value is $z$. In order to now find $\frac{\partial z}{\partial \partial}$, $z$ must be expressed as a function of $\partial$, which can be done by employing the probability ratios for $\partial$ on the positive side of $D$ according to the two-sided Gaussian Law <note>original: "G. G." (Gauß’sche Gesetz). Fechner developed a "two-sided" version of the Normal Distribution to account for asymmetrical data</note>. According to this, the probability $\phi \partial$ of a value $\partial$ is well known to be:

-> $\phi \partial = \frac{2h}{\sqrt{\pi}} \exp [-h^2 \partial^2],$ (24) <-

where $h = 1 : e \sqrt{\pi}$ <note>The "measure of precision" in 19th-century statistics</note>. Assuming the normally expected large $m$ <gloss>total number of cases</gloss>, however, $\phi \partial$ can also be expressed by $z : m'$, and consequently:

-> $z = \frac{2 m' h}{\sqrt{\pi}} \exp [-h^2 \partial^2],$ (25) <-

from which follows:

-> $\frac{\partial z}{\partial \partial} = \frac{2 m' h}{\sqrt{\pi}} \exp [-h^2 \partial^2] \cdot (- 2 h^2 \partial)$ (26) <-

## § 86. Heaviest Deviation Value *F*.

One can also speak of a characteristic deviation value, which is analogous to the heaviest *a*-value <gloss>the value T</gloss> and is to be calculated analogously; accordingly, it can be called the "heaviest deviation value." In the former case, one asked: for which *a* does the largest *za* <gloss>the product of frequency and magnitude</gloss> occur? Here, one asks: for which $\Theta$ <gloss>theta, representing deviation</gloss> does the largest *z$\Theta$* occur? And provided that, starting from a given primary value *H*, the value *a = H ± $\Theta$* is given simultaneously with $\Theta$, one asks: for which *a* does the largest *z$\Theta$* occur? This is a value that by no means coincides with the heaviest *a*-value <gloss>T</gloss>.

In the meantime, the analogy fails in the following points. The maximum of *za* is independent of the primary value one might prefer to favor, since this primary value changes nothing in the actual values of *a* and the *z* related to them; the only difference is that a simple calculation of the largest *za* is possible only by starting from *D* <gloss>the mode</gloss> according to our general distribution—

# XI. The Mode (The Most Frequent Value).

§ 87. [Since the <term>mode|The "most frequent value" or the value that appears most often in a set of data</term> serves as the starting value for the <term>distribution law|A mathematical rule that describes how often different measurements occur in a group</term> applied to <term>collective objects|A group of individual items, like a population of plants or a set of measurements, treated as a single statistical unit</term>, it holds a fundamental position in the theory of collective measurement. Therefore, a discussion of its mathematical significance and its calculation—based on that significance—is necessary. Here, it is essential to distinguish between the <term>empirical mode|The value that appears most frequent in the actual observed data (the "raw" numbers)</term>, designated as *Dᵢ*, which the table provides, and the <term>theoretical mode|The ideal peak of the data suggested by mathematical theory, representing the most probable value</term>, designated as *Dₚ*, which the distribution law requires, and to treat each separately.]

[The existence of *Dᵢ* is based on the fact that the frequencies (*z*) in the table—which indicate the number of individual specimens of a specific size (*a*) for a collective object—are not constant throughout, but rather rise and fall. Now, as long as we use a rough method of determination where the *z* values are taken as belonging directly to the recorded sizes (*a*), and measurements falling between those recorded sizes are ignored entirely, only the size (*a*) with the largest frequency (*z*) can be claimed as the mode. In such a case, if several successive sizes possess the same maximum frequency, there is no way to resolve the doubt of which size actually represents the "densest" or most frequent value ¹). However, if we take into account that the intervals between the measured sizes (*a*) are only due to the relatively small number of measured specimens and—

---

1) [The occurrence of two equal maximum frequencies (*z*) separated by lower intermediate values is not considered here. Such an occurrence would imply two different modes, which would indicate a mixture of two fundamentally different collective objects; in such cases, the standard laws of distribution cannot be directly applied.]
