## XIX. The Laws of Asymmetry.

§ 129. [In the two preceding chapters, the <term>Basic Law</term><note>The author uses "G. G." as an abbreviation for *Grundgesetz* (Basic Law), referring to the fundamental mathematical rule governing how data points are distributed.</note> was developed to the point that it stands ready for use as a suitable instrument for the calculation of distribution for <term>Collective Objects</term><note>A translation of *Kollektivgegenstände* (K.-G.), a term used in early statistics to describe groups of individual items—like heights of soldiers or weights of seeds—that are studied as a single whole.</note>, both in cases of substantial symmetry and substantial asymmetry of deviations. Experience teaches that the <term>Gaussian Law of Errors</term><note>Commonly known today as the "Normal Distribution" or "Bell Curve."</note> truly represents the correct law of distribution when individual values fluctuate only slightly around their mean. Even in cases of weak asymmetry—where it remains doubtful whether there is merely a disturbance of substantial symmetry or actual substantial asymmetry—the two-sided law offers advantages over the simple law. Thus, one can establish the two-sided Basic Law as the sufficiently proven law of distribution for Collective Objects with relatively weak fluctuations. This fundamental law of distribution for Collective Objects is then based solely on experience and requires no theoretical justification. From an empirical standpoint, the only remaining task is to derive the special laws of substantially asymmetrical distribution—which were previously mentioned in anticipation (in Chapter V)—as consequences of this Basic Law.]

[However, even though this Basic Law is sufficiently supported by experience, it is nonetheless of interest to develop theoretical assumptions regarding Collective Objects. The goal is to provide a theoretical basis for the two-sided Basic Law in a manner similar to how it was done for the simple law in the theory of errors. This shall be done in the supplement to this chapter, following the derivation of the special laws.]

<summary>This page introduces the laws of asymmetry, arguing that while the Gaussian Law of Errors works for symmetrical data, a "two-sided" Basic Law is better for data sets that fluctuate unevenly. The author notes that this law is currently based on observation but intends to provide a theoretical foundation for it.</summary>

<keywords>asymmetry, Basic Law, Collective Objects, Gaussian Law of Errors, distribution calculation, symmetry, theory of errors, empirical evidence</keywords>

[First, I will demonstrate that it is sufficient to assume the value $D_p$—determined according to the <term>Proportional Law</term> <note>The Proportional Law is Fechner's theory that in many natural datasets, fluctuations are proportional to the size of the object, leading to asymmetrical distributions.</note>—as the most probable value, in order to derive the two-sided Gaussian Law in the same way that the simple Gaussian Law is inferred in the <term>Theory of Errors</term> <note>The classic Gaussian or "Normal" distribution.</note> from the assumption that the arithmetic mean is the most probable value. [To prove this, let it be assumed that there are $m$ specimens $a$ of a Collective Object for which a value $D_p = a_o$ exists, determined according to the Proportional Law. ->$\frac{(a_o - a_1) + (a_o - a_2) + (a_o - a_3) + \dots}{(a' - a_o) + (a'' - a_o) + (a''' - a_o) + \dots} = \left(\frac{m_1}{m'}\right)^2$<-

->$m'^2 \delta_1 + m'^2 \delta_2 + \dots + m_1^2 \delta' + m_1^2 \delta'' + \dots = 0.\ \ \ \ \ (35)$<-

Let the probability of the deviations $\delta_1, \delta_2 \dots \delta', \delta'' \dots$ now be denoted by $\phi(\delta_1), \phi(\delta_2) \dots \phi(\delta'), \phi(\delta'') \dots$. Then the probability for the coincidence of all $m$ deviations is given by the product of the $m$ probabilities, thus by:

## XX. The Laws of Extremes.

§ 137. Among the elements usually considered in a <term>collective object<note>original: "K.-G." or *Kollektivgegenstand*. Fechner’s term for a group of individual items that belong to the same category but vary in measurement, such as the heights of individuals in a population or a series of temperature readings.</note></term> are the extreme values provided by its distribution table—that is, the measurements of the largest and smallest specimens. Dealing with these is of interest for several reasons. Out of mere curiosity, one might be interested in how large the tallest giant or how small the tiniest dwarf is that has ever appeared in a given country or at all; or what the greatest heat or cold is to which the temperature at a given location has risen or fallen, and so on.

However, specifying the extreme values of an investigated subject also has scientific value for our knowledge of it. By taking into account the number of specimens among which these extremes were observed, it helps characterize the subject. Furthermore, the expectation based on observed extremes—regarding the limits within which a future specimen is likely to be found, above which it will presumably not rise, and below which it will not sink—can sometimes become practically useful. For instance, the highest expected water level of a river can determine the height of a protective dam or the elevation of structures on its banks; similarly, the greatest expected cold can set a limit for the planting of certain crops, and so forth.

One must only not forget that the magnitude of the extremes is dependent on the number of specimens being observed. If, for example, the level of a river has not exceeded a certain height within 100 years, one cannot assume that this will not happen once in 1,000 years, since the latter provides a much larger scope for the development of extremes

<summary>This page introduces the "Laws of Extremes," explaining that while extreme values like the tallest giant or lowest temperature are often curiosities, they have scientific and practical importance for predicting future limits and building infrastructure. Fechner notes that the observed range of extremes is directly linked to the size of the sample or the length of the observation period.</summary>

<keywords>extreme values, collective object, distribution table, probability, statistics, sample size, infrastructure planning</keywords>

### The Laws of Extremes.

...is found, from which the interest in finding a law regarding the dependence of the size of the extremes on the number of specimens immediately becomes clear—an interest that is simultaneously practical and scientific. Directly, every empirical determination of extremes is significant only for the number of specimens from which the determination was made; however, it can serve as part of the empirical basis for a general determination of extremes with a modified number.

Hitherto, this point has frequently been overlooked; I find in more than one place that the magnitude of the absolute or relative deviation between the extremes: $E' - E$, or $(E' - E_r) : \Delta$ <note>These symbols likely refer to the difference between the maximum ($E'$) and minimum ($E$) values, or their relative deviation from a central value ($E_r$) divided by a measure of distribution ($\Delta$).</note>, which were obtained from different <term>m<note>The total number of individual cases or observations in a sample.</note></term> across different <term>collective objects<note>original: "K.-G." (Kollektivgegenstände). A term used by Fechner to describe a group of individuals or measurements that belong to the same category but vary in size or quality, like heights or temperatures.</note></term>, are used to compare the absolute or relative variability of the subjects in question—a practice that can lead to quite erroneous conclusions.

In this, the guiding insight seems to be the assumption that if one only determines the extremes from a large number, one can count on obtaining, if not the absolute possible extremes, then at least those very close to them; and in the absence of other points of reference, one can be satisfied with those found. But this assumption of an approximately reachable limit for the extremes as <term>m</term> increases has nothing to support it, either empirically or theoretically; rather, from both points of view, it is only true that the size of the extremes grows in a much smaller proportion than the size of <term>m</term>, but if <term>m</term> is thought to increase to infinity, the extremes continue to grow in a specifiable manner.

§ 138. [However, the establishment of a legal relationship between the size of the extremes and the number of values among which the extremes occur is opposed by a view—represented, for example, by **Dove** <note>Heinrich Wilhelm Dove (1803–1879), a prominent Prussian physicist and meteorologist.</note> and by **Encke** <note>Johann Franz Encke (1791–1865), a German astronomer known for his work on the periods of comets and error analysis.</note>—according to which extremes would elude any lawfulness.]

# The Laws of Extremes.

In the work "On the Non-Periodic Changes in Temperature Distribution on the Surface of the Earth," <note>This refers to the work of Heinrich Wilhelm Dove (1803–1879), a prominent Prussian physicist and meteorologist.</note> which specifies the extreme deviations that have occurred from monthly and annual temperature averages over a given number of years at various observation sites, the author explicitly notes (p. 351):
> "the numbers given here still have something very arbitrary about them, since a single unusually severe winter or a very hot summer can perhaps double the differences determined from a long series of preceding years,"

—a remark that Schmid also supports in his great meteorological work <gloss>1)</gloss>. Similarly, Encke <note>Johann Franz Encke (1791–1865), a German astronomer known for his work on the orbit of comets and the method of least squares.</note> notes in his treatise on the method of least squares <gloss>2)</gloss> (p. 275) based on the fact that in the well-known Besselian error series, <note>Refers to the work of Friedrich Bessel, whose "series of errors" describes how measurements deviate from a mean.</note> the extreme observation errors turn out to be somewhat too large compared to the theoretical requirement:
> "Moreover, this deviation is easily explainable by the circumstance that larger errors usually presuppose a quite unusual combination of disadvantageous influences, and are even frequently brought about by such an isolated event that no theory will be able to subject them to calculation."

Accordingly, there has indeed been no mention so far of either a theoretical or empirical investigation and determination of the lawful patterns of these values. Thus, the following investigation might not only fill a certain gap in this regard, but the factual removal of the suspicion—that extreme values are not subject to any laws at all—should in itself be of interest.

Now, it is certainly true that extremes or extreme deviations can sometimes arise from exceptional causes that fall outside the range of conditions under which a <term>collective object<note>original: "Kollektiv-Gegenstand." A term used by the author to describe a group of individuals or measurements that belong to the same category but vary in size or quality, like heights or temperatures.</note></term> is understood to exist and is subjected to investigation; for example, barrel-shaped distentions or decidedly <term>microcephalic<note>A medical condition characterized by an abnormally small head, used here as an example of a biological extreme that might be considered a statistical outlier.</note></term>...

# The Laws of Extremes.

...skulls, where healthy skulls are concerned. Such extremes are indeed unpredictable. But since the laws to be established only refer to such collective objects <note>The original uses the abbreviation "K.-G." for *Kollektiv-Gegenstände*, a term coined by Gustav Fechner to describe groups of individual items measured for statistical study.</note> that satisfy the requirements previously stated (Chapter IV), a deviation of extremes from the established lawful relationships can be considered an indication that these extremes are abnormal; such cases are to be excluded when dealing with normal conditions.

§ 139. Empirically, one can easily convince oneself of the change in extremes relative to the size of *m* <note>In this context, *m* represents the total number of individuals or measurements in a sample set.</note> in the following manner.

Determine from the totality of a primary list <term>primary list: a raw data set (*Urliste*) containing measurements in the order they were collected</term> of a given *m*, in which the measurements are contained in random order, the two extremes *E'* <note>the maximum value</note> and *E,* <note>the minimum value</note>. Then, without changing the random order of the measurements, divide the totality of these into a number of equal fractions—for example, if the total *m* were 1000, into 10 fractions of *m* = 100 each—and now determine the extremes of these fractions as well. Unless by chance—which can only happen exceptionally in a large total *m*—the same extremes already occur multiple times in the total set, you will not find them again in the fractions; instead, these fractions will, on average, yield only smaller *E'* and larger *E,*. If one repeats the process on each fraction of *m* = 100 by dividing it, for example, into 10 fractions of *m* = 10, the corresponding result will naturally occur. Now, one can consider the totality of measurements of a given *m* that one first had before them as itself a fraction of a totality of larger *m*. One can conclude that, if one had several such fractions of the same *m*, the *E'* and *E,* obtained from them would, on average, also be exceeded in the positive and negative directions <note>original: "in Plus und Minus"</note> by the *E'* and *E,* of the larger totality of all specimens.

One may notice that the extremes (*E*), which are obtained from fractions of the same size within the same totality, have somewhat differing magnitudes. <note>In this table, *m* represents the number of individuals in a subgroup, while *n* represents the number of subgroups. *E'* is the maximum value (upper extreme) and *E,* is the minimum value (lower extreme).</note>

This table gives rise to the following remarks.

Without exception, one can see that as *m* <note>the number of members in each group</note> grows, the average *E'* values rise and the *E,* values decrease. The natural consequence of this is that the difference between both extremes ($E' - E,$) grows as *m* grows; however, as one can see, it grows anything but proportionally with *m*. For example, when $m = 2$, the difference is $2.9$, but when $m = 360$, it is only $13.5$. At first, it may seem striking that the sum of both extremes ($E' + E,$) changes only very insignificantly as *m* grows. Furthermore—aside from the small irregularities at $m = 4$ and $72$, which are to be regarded as a matter of unbalanced random factors <term>unbalanced random factors: "unausgeglichene Zufälligkeiten," or statistical noise that hasn't smoothed out yet</term>—the change consists of a continuous decrease in $E' + E,$ as *m* increases. 

This is to be understood as follows: naturally, if *E'* increases as *m* grows and *E,* decreases, the possibility generally exists that both precisely compensate for one another. In that case, $E' + E,$ would have to remain constant as *m* grows—a result that, aside from unbalanced random factors, would be expected if there were a symmetry of deviations on both sides of the arithmetic mean <term>arithmetic mean: the standard average calculated by summing values and dividing by the total count</term>. Now, recruit measurements <term>recruit measurements: "Rekrutenmaße," historical datasets of soldiers' heights or physical dimensions, which were foundational to early social statistics</term> do approach such symmetry, but since they do not correspond to it entirely, the result for $E' + E,$ also does not quite correspond to the assumption of such symmetry.

<summary>This page presents a table demonstrating how maximum and minimum values in a dataset shift further apart as the sample size increases. It explains that while the gap between extremes grows, their combined sum remains relatively stable, suggesting a near-symmetrical distribution typical of biological data like recruit measurements.</summary>

[Although the values in Table I above clearly demonstrate the increase of the upper extremes and the decrease of the lower extremes as *m* <note>the number of members in a group</note> grows, they are nonetheless not suitable for proving the Laws of Extremes to be established in the following section (§ 141). This is because these laws are to be derived from the Gaussian Law <term>G. G.: *Gaußsches Gesetz*, or the Gaussian Law of Normal Distribution, which describes how data clusters around a central average</term>, which refers to the deviations from the arithmetic mean *A* or from the densest value *D* <term>densest value: the "mode," or the value that appears most frequently in a data set</term>. Consequently, the determination of extremes initially concerns the extreme deviations from the starting value, and not the extreme values *E'* and *E,* directly. The difference in the method of determination necessitated by this is illustrated by the observation that *E'* could very well lie below the starting value, and conversely, *E,* could lie above it; in such a case, the deviation of that extreme from the starting value represents the minimum value rather than the maximum value of the occurring deviations. The average values in the table above can therefore not be taken as the average values of the extreme deviations, since only the maxima of the deviation values are to be taken into account for that purpose. One could certainly object to this method by arguing that the extremes *E'* and *E,* attract interest in their own right, regardless of the primary value chosen as a starting point, and thus demand the establishment of directly applicable laws; however, this can only happen through the mediation of the laws valid for extreme deviations, since the distribution law to be used as a basis here refers to deviation values. Therefore, the theoretical determinations for the extreme deviations must first be empirically proven.]

-> $W[\Theta] = \frac{2h}{\sqrt{\pi}} \exp[-h^2 \Theta^2] d\Theta$. <- (1)

# The Laws of Extremes.

$m' - m_{,}.$ The asymmetry of the extreme deviations with respect to $D$ <note>The median or central value</note> thus follows the same direction as the asymmetry of the counts of deviations with respect to $D$. If one wishes to transfer this law to deviations with respect to the arithmetic mean $A$, one arrives at the reversal law—specified in the second part of § 33, point 7—based on the following reasoning. Since extreme deviations are large and subject to relatively large fluctuations, it is permissible to assume that the difference between the deviations does not change its sign when moving from $D$ to the relatively nearby value of $A$. However, the difference in the counts of deviations with respect to $A$ has the opposite sign as the difference in the counts of deviations with respect to $D$. Consequently, if that assumption holds true, the difference between the extreme deviations with respect to $A$ has the opposite sign of the difference between the counts of deviations with respect to $A$. Indeed, this reversal law finds its confirmation, for example, in Tables III and IV of Chapter XXV for the segments of <term>rye stalks: a common botanical dataset used by Fechner to demonstrate statistical variability</term> (with only one exception among 15 different cases). This can, however, only be regarded as an empirical law that generally applies in cases of significant asymmetry. In cases of insignificant asymmetry, on the other hand, it likely no longer holds true (compare § 181).

[3) If the asymmetry of the <term>K.-G.: shorthand for Kollektiv-Gegenstand, or Collective Law—the statistical distribution of a group of similar objects</term> disappears, then in principle, equal values must be required for the extreme deviations. In this case, the starting value is $A$ (which now coincides with $D$), and the simple <term>G. G.: shorthand for Gauss'sches Gesetz, the Gaussian Law or Normal Distribution</term> must be applied instead of the two-sided law. For this case, the formulas provided under point 1) remain valid, provided that $m'$ and $m_{,}$ are replaced by $\frac{1}{2}m$, and $e'$ as well as $e_{,}$ are replaced by $\eta$, which is equally valid for both sides. However, since in the case of substantial symmetry the distribution law relates to both sides of $A$ collectively when based on the total $m$, it is more appropriate to subject the positive and negative deviations together to the <term>determination of extremes: the process of calculating the most likely maximum or minimum values in a dataset</term>. ## XXI. The Logarithmic Treatment of Collective Objects.

§ 143. [The arithmetic treatment of collective objects <term>collective objects: Fechner's term (Kollektivgegenstände) for sets of items that vary around a central value, such as the heights of trees or dimensions of artifacts</term> considered exclusively until now, presupposes that the measurements possess a small proportional fluctuation around the principal values. However, there are also collective objects, such as the dimensions of gallery paintings and daily rainfall amounts, which—according to a remark in Chapter IV—offer a very strong mean deviation in relation to the principal values. This makes them unsuitable for the application of the arithmetic treatment; instead, they prove accessible to logarithmic treatment and enable a striking confirmation of the logarithmic law of distribution.]

[This gives rise to the task of going into more detail regarding logarithmic treatment in general, supplementing what was already stated in Chapter V (§ 35 and 36). There, the general viewpoints were developed which make it appear necessary to relate the law of distribution for collective objects fundamentally to proportional deviations rather than arithmetic deviations. From this, the direct conclusion followed that the Gaussian Law <note>original: "G. G." for *Gaußsches Gesetz*, the normal distribution or "bell curve"</note> should be based on the logarithms of the proportional deviations $\psi = a : H$—namely $\log \psi = \log a - \log H$—instead of the arithmetic $\Theta = a - H$. The application of logarithmic treatment was also communicated there in its essentials, and the notation was established. Accordingly, in general:

$\alpha = \log a; \psi' = \frac{a'}{H}; \lambda' = \log \psi' = \log a' - \log H; \psi, = \frac{H}{a,} \Bigg\} (1)$
$\lambda, = \log \psi, = \log H - \log a,$

§ 145. Based on the comparison between theory and experience carried out above, the logarithmic distribution law proves to be applicable for <term>Collective Objects<note>German: *Kollektiv-Gegenstand*. A term coined by Gustav Fechner to describe a collection of individual measurements or items that together form a statistical whole.</note></term> with strong relative fluctuation. Since this law—according to the discussions in Chapter V—markedly agrees with the arithmetic generalization of the <term>Gaussian Law<note>The "G. G." or *Gaußsches Gesetz* refers to the Normal Distribution or Bell Curve, named after Carl Friedrich Gauss.</note></term> when there is only a weak relative fluctuation of individual values around the principal values, it is to be claimed as the strictly valid distribution law for Collective Objects in general, as was already emphasized at the conclusion of the aforementioned chapter. Thus, the probability $W'$ or $W_r$, that a logarithmic deviation from the densest value $\mathcal{D}$ falls between the infinitely close limits $\lambda'$ and $\lambda' + d \lambda'$ or $\lambda_r$ and $\lambda_r + d \lambda_r$, is determined for every Collective Object by:

-> $W' = \frac{2 h'}{\sqrt{\pi}} \exp [-h'^2 \lambda'^2] d \lambda' \text{;} \quad \bigg\}$ <-
-> $W_r = \frac{2 h_r}{\sqrt{\pi}} \exp [-h_r^2 \lambda_r^2] d \lambda_r \text{;} \quad \bigg\}$ (4) <-

and the number of deviations between the specified limits is found to be:

-> $z' = W' \cdot m' \text{;} \quad z_r = W_r \cdot m_r \text{;} \quad$ (5) <-

where $h' m' = h_r m_r \text{;} \quad h' = 1 : e' \sqrt{\pi} \text{;} \quad h_r = 1 : e_r \sqrt{\pi}$ and $e'$, $e_r$, $m'$, $m_r$ <note>These symbols represent statistical constants including the precision measure ($h$) and the total number of observations ($m$).</note> are to be related to $\mathcal{D}$ as the starting value.

For the principal values $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{C}$, and $\mathcal{D}$ <note>These represent different types of averages: the geometric mean ($\mathcal{G}$), the median ($\mathcal{C}$), and the mode or densest value ($\mathcal{D}$).</note> of the logarithmic deviations, the same laws therefore apply as those discussed in Chapter XIX.

[The following theorems finally establish the relationship between the primary arithmetic values and those of the ratio deviations.]

For the logarithmic mean value $\vartheta = \Sigma \log a : m$, interpreted as a logarithm, there is a corresponding value denoted by $G$, the so-called <term>geometric mean<note>The geometric mean is the $n$-th root of the product of $n$ numbers. In statistics involving ratios or growth, it provides a more accurate "middle" than the standard average.</note></term> or <term>ratio value</term>. Regardless of the specific distribution law, this value is always slightly smaller than the <term>arithmetic mean<note>The standard average: the sum of all values divided by the count of values.</note></term> $A = \Sigma a : m$. According to a proof by <term>SCHEIBNER<note>Wilhelm Scheibner (1826–1908) was a German mathematician and colleague of Fechner at the University of Leipzig.</note></term> $^{1)}$, it has the following approximate relationship to $A$. This relationship is increasingly accurate the smaller the so-called <term>root mean square error<note>German: *quadratische Mittelfehler*. A measure of how much the data points vary or "spread" from the average.</note></term> relative to $A$ is (denoted by $q = \sqrt{\Sigma \varDelta^2 : m}$):

->$G = A \left( 1 - \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{q^2}{A^2} \right).$ (9)<-

According to this, one can approximately derive $G$ from $A$.

Between the logarithmic <term>mode<note>German: *dichtester Wert*. The most frequently occurring value in a data set.</note></term> $\mathfrak{D}$ and the logarithm of the arithmetic mode $D$, the following relationship exists:

->$\mathfrak{D} = \log D + \frac{e,^2 \pi}{2 \text{ Mod}}.$ (10)<-

In this formula, $e,$ represents the lower mean logarithmic deviation $= \Sigma \lambda, : m,,$ while "Mod" represents the modulus of our common logarithmic system $= 0.43429$, and $\pi$ is, as always, $3.14159$. This relationship is tied to the validity of the logarithmic generalization of the Gaussian Law <note>The "G. G." refers to the *Gauß’sche Gesetz* or the Normal Distribution, which Fechner is adapting for logarithmic data.</note> and can therefore be used to empirically verify this generalization.

[Proof. The logarithmic mode $\mathfrak{D}$ denotes that logarithmic interval which, among all intervals of the same size, contains the most values $z$. It is therefore determined by the maximum of the probability function (4) with constant $d\lambda'$ and $d\lambda,,$, which is to say, by the starting value of the deviations $\lambda'$ and $\lambda,$.]

### Logarithmic Treatment.

The **arithmetic mode** $D$<note>The "arithmetic mode" or "arithmetically most frequent value" refers to the value that appears most often in a standard dataset where intervals are measured in equal additions (1, 2, 3...) rather than ratios.</note>, on the other hand, lies within that arithmetic interval which, among all intervals of the same size, possesses the maximum $x$ <note>Here, $x$ represents the frequency or number of occurrences.</note>. Therefore, assuming the validity of the **logarithmic distribution law**, one finds this value as the maximum of the probability function (4) related to constant arithmetic intervals. Accordingly, let the arithmetic deviations of $a$ from the <term>ratio-mode<note>German: *dichtester Verhältniswert*. In a logarithmic distribution, this is the value around which the ratios of the data are most densely clustered.</note></term> $\mathcal{T}$ be denoted by $\Theta' = a' - \mathcal{T}$ and $\Theta, = \mathcal{T} - a,,$ so that $d\Theta' = da'$ and $d\Theta, = -da,,$. Based on the definitions, substitute $\lambda' = \log a' - \mathcal{D} = \log a' - \log \mathcal{T};$ and $\lambda, = \mathcal{D} - \log a, = \log \mathcal{T} - \log a,$ into the functions (4):

-> $d\lambda' = \frac{\text{Mod}}{a'} da' = \frac{\text{Mod}}{a'} d\Theta'$ <-
-> $d\lambda, = - \frac{\text{Mod}}{a,} da, = \frac{\text{Mod}}{a,} d\Theta, .$ <- (11)
<note>The term "Mod" refers to the **modulus** of the system of logarithms being used, a constant factor (approximately 0.4343 for common logarithms) used to convert between different bases.</note>

Then, for constant $d\Theta'$ and $d\Theta,,$ one obtains the following to determine the maximum of:

-> $W' = \frac{2 h' \text{Mod}}{\sqrt{\pi} a'} \exp [-h'^2 \lambda'^2] d\Theta' ; W, = \frac{2 h, \text{Mod}}{\sqrt{\pi} a,} \exp [-h,^2 \lambda,^2] d\Theta,$ <-

the equations:

-> $\frac{\partial W'}{\partial a'} = - \frac{W'}{a'} (1 + 2 h'^2 \lambda' \text{Mod}) = 0;$ <-
-> $\frac{\partial W,}{\partial a,} = - \frac{W,}{a,} (1 - 2 h,^2 \lambda, \text{Mod}) = 0.$ <-

However, the values $\lambda'$ and $\lambda,$ are by their nature positive. Therefore, only the second of the two equations offers a maximum for:

-> $\lambda, = \frac{1}{2 h,^2 \text{Mod}}$ (12) <-

If one sets the $a$-value belonging to $\lambda,$ here to be denoted by $D$:

-> $\lambda, = \mathcal{D} - \log D; \text{ furthermore } h,^2 = \frac{1}{\epsilon,^2 \pi},$ <-

one indeed obtains the relationship represented by (10).

# Logarithmic Treatment.

§ 146. [Supplement. If, in accordance with the explanations in § 35, the principle is established that the changes in size of the individuals within a <term>Collective Object<note>German: *Kollektiv-Gegenstand* (K.-G.). In Fechnerian statistics, this refers to a group or population of individual items—such as leaves on a tree or measurements of a star—that together form a unified dataset for analysis.</note></term> are essentially dependent on the size of the individuals themselves undergoing those changes, then the modification to be applied to the hypothesis developed in the supplement to Chapter XIX (§ 136) follows immediately, in order to make it applicable to the **logarithmic distribution law**.]

[Namely, to derive the logarithmic law—just as with the arithmetic one—specific influences or circumstances, or "forces" for short, can be assumed as the causes of these changes in size. Their number is assumed to be indefinitely large, denoted as *n*, and a **probability**<note>Original: *W.*, abbreviation for *Wahrscheinlichkeit* (probability).</note> *p* is assigned to each for its occurrence, while the probability *q = 1 — p* is assigned for the absence of its effect. However, the result of their occurrence is no longer to be understood as an additive increase, but rather as a **multiplication**; thus, instead of *a + i* and *a + xi*, we use *ai* and *ai^x*. Consequently, based on this modification, one obtains for an individual of size *ai^x* the same probability that, according to the previously developed hypothesis, belonged to an individual of size *a + xi*, so that now:

-> W[*ai^x*] = \frac{n!}{x! (n - x)!} p^x q^{n - x}. (13) <-

If, however, one sets *a = log a* and *i = log i*, then *a + xi = log (ai^x)*, and one obtains the following as the expression for the probability that the logarithm of an individual's size is equal to *a + xi*:

-> W[*a + xi*] = \frac{n!}{x! (n - x)!} p^x q^{n - x}. (14) <-

According to this, the earlier developments apply in the same manner and to the same extent to the logarithmic distribution law, provided that everywhere *a* is replaced by *a = log a* and *i* by *i = log i*.]

<summary>This page explains the transition from an arithmetic to a logarithmic distribution by shifting the underlying assumption of change from addition to multiplication. It demonstrates that if individual variations are proportional to their current size, the resulting data follows a logarithmic rather than a linear pattern.</summary>

<keywords>logarithmic distribution law, Collective Object, probability, multiplicative change, binomial distribution, statistical derivation</keywords>

## XXII. Collective Treatment of Ratios Between Dimensions. Mean Ratios.

§ 147. Following this, I wish to say something about a task which plays a significant role in <term>Collective Measurement Theory<note>German: *Kollektivmaßlehre*. This was Fechner's term for the statistical study of "Collective Objects"—groups of similar items (like leaves or skulls) that vary around a central value.</note></term>, and the discussion of which can appropriately find a place here, since it too directly suggests the need for a logarithmic treatment.

As has been noted, not only can simple dimensions of an object be treated collectively, but also the ratios between them. I have already mentioned this (Chapters I and III) in regard to the ratios between the skull dimensions of a given race and the stem sections—so-called joints or internodes—of a **grass plant** <note>Original: *Graminee*. A member of the grass family, Poaceae.</note>, for which plenty of other examples can be found. Let us focus on the ratio between the vertical dimension *a* and the corresponding horizontal dimension *b* of the skull of a given race, which is to be determined for comparison with other races. In doing so, we usually place *a* in the numerator and *b* in the denominator, although the ratio could just as well be taken in reverse. Now, the ratio *a:b* already varies somewhat even among specimens of one and the same race; however, for the purpose of comparative characterization against other races, unified results are required instead of these varying individual measurements. One can therefore only demand a **mean ratio** between *b* and *a*, which is generally designated as *M[a:b]*. Depending on whether one has the arithmetic or geometric mean in mind, *A* or *G* takes the place of *M*. The corresponding task regarding the dimensions belonging to one another...

§ 148. A mean ratio can be obtained in several different ways; specifically in the following ways, where corresponding values of *a* and *b* shall be designated with the same index <note>i.e., $a'$ corresponds to $b'$, $a''$ to $b''$, etc.</note>. The examples established for the ratio *a : b* can, of course, be transposed for the ratio *b : a*.

1) The *arithmetic mean* of ratios *A [a : b]* is obtained by adding all individual values of *a : b* and dividing by their total number; thus:

-> $A [\frac{a}{b}] = (\frac{a'}{b'} + \frac{a''}{b''} + \dots) : m = \frac{1}{m} \Sigma \frac{a}{b} .$ (1) <-

2) I designate as the *summary mean* that which is obtained when one divides the sum of all *a* by the sum of all *b* or—what amounts to the same thing—divides the arithmetic mean of all *a* by the arithmetic mean of all *b*, according to the formula:

-> $M_s [\frac{a}{b}] = \frac{a' + a'' + \dots}{b' + b'' + \dots} = \frac{\Sigma a}{\Sigma b} = \frac{A}{B} .$ (2) <-

One might argue against the use of this mean, claiming it is more a ratio between means than a mean of ratios; but while it is the former, it is simultaneously the latter within the broader concept of the "mean" that we are using here. This is because it falls between the individual values of *a : b* according to a specific principle and, aside from entirely exceptional cases, falls near the other types of means.

3) *Proportional Mean.* <note>Original: *Prozentisches Mittel*. Literally "percentile mean," but here referring to the relative proportion of a part to a whole.</note> To obtain this mean, one forms the values *a : (a + b)* and *b : (a + b)* and divides the sum of the one by the sum of the other according to the formula:

### Dimensional Ratios

...to state which factors might decide the choice of one method of determination over the other.

In this regard, one can generally say that the arithmetic and percentage means are inferior to the other two mean values in every respect; generally speaking, the geometric mean should deserve preference, though the summary mean can also find useful application under certain circumstances.

In fact, the arithmetic mean of ratios suffers from the following disadvantages:

a) To be able to add the individual fractions $a : b$, one must first reduce each one to a decimal fraction, which is very laborious when there are many values of $a : b$.

b) In itself, it is indifferent whether one wants to use the direct values $a : b$ or the reciprocal values $b : a$ <note>Reciprocal values are essentially "flipped" fractions (e.g., 2/3 becomes 3/2).</note> to calculate the mean in order to determine the average ratio of $a$ and $b$; and one should, of course, obtain a consistent result by both methods. However, this method does not grant this, as shown when one reverses the mean obtained from the reciprocal values—thereby obtaining the so-called <term>harmonic mean</term> <note>The harmonic mean is a specific type of average often used for rates and ratios; here, Fechner shows it doesn't align with the arithmetic mean when proportions are inverted.</note> relative to the one obtained from the direct values; the two do not agree. In short, $A [a : b]$ is not equal to its corresponding harmonic mean $1 : A [b : a]$. Let us take, for example, a very simple case of only two ratios:

-> $\frac{a'}{b'} = \frac{1}{2}; \frac{a''}{b''} = \frac{3}{4},$ <-

then:

-> $\frac{b'}{a'} = \frac{2}{1}; \frac{b''}{a''} = \frac{4}{3}; A \left[ \frac{a}{b} \right] = \frac{10}{16}; A \left[ \frac{b}{a} \right] = \frac{10}{6}; 1 : A \left[ \frac{b}{a} \right] = \frac{6}{10},$ <-

However, $\frac{10}{16}$ is $= 0.625$, while $\frac{6}{10} = 0.600$. If one takes fractions that deviate even further from each other than in our example, the difference between the direct and harmonic mean becomes even larger. In the case of such <term>K.-G.</term> <note>Abbreviation for *Klasse von Gegenständen* (class of objects), referring to the group of items being measured, such as the visiting cards mentioned on the previous page.</note> where most values of $a : b$ do not deviate very far from a central value, the difference is usually very small, but nonetheless not to be neglected everywhere.

c) If one has to determine the middle ratios between three types of values *a*, *b*, and *c*, then three ratios (*a* : *b*, *b* : *c*, *a* : *c*) along with their reciprocal <note>The "flipped" version of a fraction; for example, the reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2.</note> values are possible, and one might wish to be able to derive the third ratio directly from two of these ratios (whether direct or reciprocal). However, this method does not achieve this, in that one cannot, for example, obtain the mean of *a* : *c* (written as *A* [*a* : *c*]) by multiplying the mean of *a* : *b* by the mean of *b* : *c*.

The percentage mean <note>An average calculated using percentages rather than raw numbers.</note> shares all these same disadvantages of the arithmetic mean. Nevertheless, one occasionally finds both the one and the other being used.

The summary mean and the <term>geometric mean</term> <note>The geometric mean is calculated by multiplying values together and taking the nth root, rather than adding them; it is often used in growth rates or proportions.</note> are, on the other hand, free from all these disadvantages. If, however, one still wished to place special trust in the direct arithmetic mean and the—in principle—equally valid but different <term>harmonic mean</term>, one could only rely on the arithmetic or geometric mean of those two values. But since one would also be free to start from *b* : *a* as the direct ratio instead of *a* : *b*, an ambiguity would remain here as well. Even when choosing the arithmetic mean, the question would again arise whether one should prefer the direct or the harmonic version; thus, the ambiguity would not be resolved from this side either. However, according to a proof for which I am indebted to Prof. SCHEIBNER <gloss>1)</gloss>, the geometric mean value of given ratios falls—in the case that usually occurs in <note>Likely referring to "Körper-Gestalten" or Body-Forms, a context for these measurements.</note>—between the arithmetic and harmonic means.

§ 149. Finally, the question likely only concerns to what extent the summary mean or the geometric mean is preferable.

The summary mean <note>Also known as the aggregate mean; it is calculated by dividing the sum of all numerators by the sum of all denominators.</note> recommends itself above all through the ease of its calculation, as it only requires summing all *a* values and all *b* values and dividing one sum by the other, whereas obtaining the <term>geometric mean</term> <note>A type of average where you multiply the numbers together and then take the nth root; it is useful for sets of numbers that vary significantly in scale.</note> requires first translating all *a* and *b* values into logarithms. Both, however, have the following fundamental difference in meaning.

Suppose a summary mean:

->$\frac{a' + a'' + a''' + \dots}{b' + b'' + b''' + \dots}$<-

is given. It is evident that if, for example, one specimen—based on its two components *a'* and *b'* included in the ratio—were very large compared to the others, the mean ratio would noticeably depend almost entirely on the ratio *a'* : *b'*. In that case, $a'' + a''' + \dots$ would vanish against *a'*, and $b'' + b''' + \dots$ against *b'*. In general, larger specimens gain more influence on the mean in proportion to their size. This is perfectly in order if one assigns more weight to larger specimens for the determination of the mean than to smaller ones, which under certain circumstances may very well be the case. At any rate, nothing prevents us from seeing a characteristic ratio of the given <term>K.-G.</term> <note>Original: "K.-G."; likely an abbreviation for *Körperformen-Gattung* (body-type category or class of forms).</note> in the summary mean, which carries this circumstance with it, just as well as in any other mean ratio that does not, since it simply characterizes the object in a different sense.

On the other hand, it may certainly be the intention to let large and small specimens contribute to the mean with equal importance—for example, not to treat the ratio between horizontal and vertical dimensions in larger heads as more significant than in smaller ones. The geometric mean corresponds to this intention, which is likely more frequently desired.

# Dimensional Ratios

The summary mean shares an advantage with the geometric mean that the arithmetic and percentage means lack: if two of three ratios, *a*:*b*, *b*:*c*, and *a*:*c*, are determined as means, the mean of the third follows directly from them. According to both methods, we have:

->*M*[*a*/*c*] = *M*[*a*/*b*] · *M*[*b*/*c*] (5)<-

However, the summary mean has the following advantage over the geometric mean. Suppose that for a multi-part object—for example, stalks of grain of a given type—one has determined the <term>summary mean</term> <note>Calculated by dividing the sum of all numerators by the sum of all denominators.</note> ratio of each part's length to the total length of the stalk. In this case, one only needs to add these ratios for any two parts to obtain the mean ratio of the combination of those two parts to the total length. This is not the case with the geometric method, as can easily be proven. To put it briefly: according to the summary method, the determinations of ratios for the parts and the whole relate more rationally than according to the geometric method or, indeed, any other.

Furthermore, the following case must be considered. Let us assume that in a <term>collective object</term> <note>original: "K.-G." is an abbreviation for *Kollektiv-Gegenstand*, a term used by Gustav Fechner to describe a group of individual specimens studied as a single statistical population.</note> instances occur where one or the other of the two values, *a* or *b*, is zero. For example, when determining the mean ratio between the weights of the solid and soft parts of various animals, some animals may completely lack solid parts. In this case, the <term>geometric mean</term> <note>A type of average where you multiply the numbers together and take the nth root; it fails if any value in the set is zero.</note> becomes unusable because the mean becomes zero or infinite depending on whether the zero value appears in the numerator or denominator. One can then only rely on the summary mean, unless one wishes to establish the principle that such cases—where one value is zero—should not be combined under the same mean as those where *a* and *b* always maintain finite values.

# Dimensional Ratios

It is characteristic of a thorough analysis that both types of means are determined, though this does not prevent one from preferring one over the other depending on the circumstances. Determining both means—beyond contributing to the general description of a given <term>collective object</term> <note>original: "K.-G." for *Kollektiv-Gegenstand*, a statistical population of individual items.</note> with components *a* and *b*—offers the advantage that several important specific characteristics are linked to the relationship between these two means, namely:

1) If the ratio of *a* to *b* remains the same for all specimens regardless of the absolute size of *a* and *b*—meaning it is the same for large specimens as it is for small ones—then the <term>summary mean</term> <note>The sum of all 'a' values divided by the sum of all 'b' values.</note> is equal to the <term>geometric mean</term>.

2) If *a* and *b* always grow or shrink together, but not generally in the same proportion, it may be that the ratio *a : b* increases as the absolute size of *a* and *b* grows, or it may decrease. The former is the case if the geometric mean of the ratios is smaller than the summary mean; the latter is the case if it is larger.

3) If the relative <term>fluctuation</term> <note>Proportional variation.</note> of the *a* values around their <term>arithmetic mean</term> *A* is equal to the relative fluctuation of the *b* values around their arithmetic mean *B*, then the geometric mean is equal to the summary mean. The measure of relative fluctuation here, relative to *A*, is the simple or quadratic <term>mean deviation</term> of *A* divided by *A* (namely $\epsilon_\alpha : A$ or $q_\alpha : A$); let us call this *P*. Correspondingly, $\epsilon_\beta : B$ or $q_\beta : B$ (or *Q*) represents the fluctuation relative to *B*.

4) Depending on whether the relative fluctuation of the values is stronger around *A* or around *B*, the geometric mean will be smaller or larger than the summary mean.

5) From a combination of points 1) and 2) with 3) and 4), it follows that—

-> $\frac{a' + a'' + \dots}{b' + b'' + \dots}$ <-

However, to the extent that the equality between the individual values of $a : b$ ceases, generally speaking, the equality between the two means also ceases. It may then be that $a : b$ partly increases and partly decreases with a change in the absolute size of *a* and *b*, in which case nothing general can be established. # XXIII. Dependency Relationships.

§ 152. One may ask whether the average temperatures of consecutive years vary according to the laws of pure chance or exhibit a certain dependency upon one another in their sequence; a question that can be applied to many analogous cases. Now, these dependency relationships can take various forms, and the investigations into them must be conducted accordingly. One of the simplest questions and methods of investigation, however, stems from the following observation.

I take a list of drawn lottery numbers. Such a list begins, for example, with:

->26 826 —<-
->21 460 +<-
->31 094 —<-
->22 120 —<-
->16 226 (+)<-

As shown above, I designate every decrease from one number to the next with a — and every increase with a +. Without referring back to the very first number <note>The author is looking at the direction of change *between* numbers. The first number has no preceding value to compare it to.</note>, I obtain the following series: — + — —. From this series, and again without referring back to the first sign, I find two <term>sign changes</term> <note>original: "Zeichenwechsel"; occurring when a + is followed by a — or vice versa.</note> and one <term>sequence</term> <note>original: "Folge"; a "run" or repetition where a sign is followed by the same sign, such as — followed by —.</note> of identical signs. Alternatively, if I refer back to both the numbers and the signs <note>This implies a method of "closing the loop" or counting the initial transition to provide a complete set of comparisons.</note>: — + — — + which contains four changes and one sequence. Generally, if I call the total number of items *m* and the total number of changes and sequences *z*, in the first case *z* = *m* — 2, and in the latter case *z* = *m*. Let the former be called Method *a*, and the latter Method *b*.

Whether I apply Method *a* or Method *b*, I find that with a large *m* <note>A large sample size.</note>, the number of sign changes is approximately equal to the...

# Dependency Relationships.

...double the number of sign sequences, so that I can assume the <term>probability</term> <note>original: "W." (Wahrscheinlichkeit)</note> of the one to the other is as 2 : 1.<sup>1)</sup> This is the law of pure chance.

If, however, a dependency of consecutive numbers were to exist such that they rose and fell in a continuous manner through a certain interval, the number of <term>sign sequences</term> <note>original: "Zeichenfolgen"; here meaning "runs" or "repetitions" where the direction of change remains the same, such as two consecutive increases (+ +).</note> would increase beyond the previously mentioned ratio. Indeed, if the dependency always proceeded in the same direction, one would obtain nothing but sign sequences according to method *a*, and according to method *b*, *m — 2* sequences and 2 changes.

Let us remain with method *a* and call the number of changes *w* and the number of sequences *f*. In this case, full independence is characterized by *f* = 1/3 *z*, full dependency by *f* = *z*, and partial dependency by values of *f* falling between these two. One can find a measure of partial dependency for a given *f* and *z* in the ratio by which the excess of *f* over the measure of full independence stands to the total excess of full dependency over full independence. That is, if we denote this measure as **Dep.** <note>original: "Abh." (Abhängigkeit)</note>:

-> Dep. = (3*f* — *z*) / 2*z* . (1) <-

Meanwhile, *f* remains uncertain because of the finite number *m*, and the calculation of **Dep.** shares in this uncertainty. The determination of this uncertainty—

---

1) [Theoretically, one derives this ratio from the observation that three values *a*, *b*, *c*, which are free from any <term>succession dependency</term> <note>original: "Successionsabhängigkeit"; the tendency of one value to influence the next.</note>, can appear with the same probability in each of the six possible <term>successions</term> <note>original: "Successionen"; permutations or orders of appearance.</note>:

-> *a, b, c,* <-
-> *c, b, a,* <-
-> *b, a, c,* <-
-> *c, a, b,* <-
-> *a, c, b,* <-
-> *b, c, a* <-

such that, if for example *a < b < c*, the first two successions each result in a sign sequence <note>In *a, b, c*, the values only increase (+ +); in *c, b, a*, they only decrease (— —).</note>, while the last four each result in a sign change <note>For example, in *b, a, c*, the values first decrease (b to a) and then increase (a to c), creating a change from — to +.</note>. Consequently, the probability of a sign sequence is to be set at 1/3, and the probability of a sign change at 2/3.]

...is to be included in the value of **Dep.** <note>original: "Abh." (Abhängigkeit); the measure of dependency.</note> as the <term>probable error</term> <note>A statistical term for the deviation within which there is a 50% chance the true value lies.</note>.

[This determination is achieved by calculating the probable limits resulting from the inversion of the so-called **BERNOULLI**-an theorem <note>Named after Jacob Bernoulli; a foundational principle describing the results of performing the same experiment a large number of times.</note> for the probability of a sign sequence, based on the observed values of *f* <note>The number of sign sequences.</note> and *z* <note>The total number of intervals.</note>. If one sets the unknown probability for the occurrence of a sign sequence equal to *x*, and the probability of a sign change equal to 1 — *x*, then according to the cited theorem of the <term>calculus of probability</term><sup>1)</sup>, the probability:

-> $W = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_0^c \exp[-t^2] dt$ (2) <-

exists for the value of *x* to lie between the limits:

-> $\frac{f}{z} - c \sqrt{\frac{2f \cdot w}{z^3}}$ and $\frac{f}{z} + c \sqrt{\frac{2f \cdot w}{z^3}}$ (2a) <-

Since the value of *c* becomes 0.47694 for $W = \frac{1}{2}$, the probable limits of *x* are equal to:

-> $\frac{f}{z} \pm 0.67449 \sqrt{\frac{f \cdot w}{z^3}}$. (3) <-

Accordingly, the probable limits of **Dep.** are equal to:

-> $\frac{3f - z}{2z} \pm \frac{3}{2} \cdot 0.67449 \sqrt{\frac{f \cdot w}{z^3}}$. (4) <-

It is therefore an even bet (1 against 1) that the measure of dependency, as defined above, is no smaller than the lower and no larger than the upper of the two specified limits.]

§ 154. [Another method for investigating successional dependency <note>This refers to whether the order of data points shows a pattern, such as "persistence," where one high value is likely to be followed by another.</note> was indicated in § 20, alongside the method discussed thus far. It is based on the observation that, given complete independence and assuming no disruption by unbalanced random occurrences, the number of sequences of two values both above or two values both below the center value *C* should be equal to the number of changes between values situated above and below *C*. Specifically, if values above *C* are designated by $+$ and values below *C* by $-$, the probability <note>original: "W." (Wahrscheinlichkeit)</note> of a positive value is just as great as the probability of a negative one; therefore, under complete independence, each of the four possible successions—$++$; $--$; $+-$; $-+$—is equally likely. The first two each result in a sign sequence, while the last two each result in a sign change, so that the probability for both a sign sequence and a sign change is $\frac{1}{2}$. If one now finds $f$ sign sequences and $w$ sign changes for a series of values treated in this manner, given a sufficiently large number of $z = f + w$ successions of signs, the probable limits for the unknown probability $x$ of a sign sequence can be found—just as above—from the inversion of the <term>Bernoulli’s Theorem</term> <note>A fundamental rule in probability describing the outcome of repeated independent trials; here used to calculate the margin of error.</note> as:

->$\frac{f}{z} \pm 0.674\,49 \sqrt{\frac{f \cdot w}{z^3}}$<-

Here, if partial successional dependency exists—which reveals itself as a clustering of sequences compared to changes—the value $f:z$ will remain between $\frac{1}{2}$ (which applies to complete independence) and 1 (which indicates full dependency where $f = z$). ## XXIV. On the Spatial and Temporal Connection of Variations in Recruit Size.

§ 156. Depending on the conditions of the <term>vintage years</term> <note>original: "Jahrgänge"; referring here to specific harvest years or birth cohorts</note>, field crops do not only produce a varying yield, but also grow to different heights in different years; this depends mainly on the temperature and moisture conditions of those specific years. Insofar as these conditions are shared across larger stretches of land, their influence on the growth of crops also manifests collectively for all parts of such regions. However, this growth changes from one stretch of land to another as these environmental conditions themselves vary.

The question arises whether something corresponding occurs regarding the height of people born in the same years—whether their height also changes according to the nature of those years across contiguous regions, or perhaps even changes in connection with the growth of plants. Now, to be sure, one can hardly assume a direct influence of temperature and moisture conditions on the growth of humans in the same way as on plants. Humans do not grow anew from a seed every year like <term>field crops</term> <note>original: "Feldfrüchte"</note>, nor do they conclude their existence within a single year, which would allow us to focus only on the conditions of that one year. Nevertheless, it is conceivable that the fertility of a particular year might exercise an indirect influence on the growth of the child. This could happen by influencing the nutritional conditions of the parents at the time of the child's conception, during <term>pregnancy</term>, or by affecting the nutrition of the child itself during the period of growth—especially the earliest stages—an indirect influence on the growth of the child

In short, one is not at a loss to find possible causes for the average height of people born in the same year changing across larger stretches of territory in connection with one another just as well as that of plants—whether this happens with or without a direct relationship to the plants themselves. The primary question, however, is whether the fact of such a connection over larger or smaller stretches of land is demonstrable; and the following investigation will prove that it is the case.

In any case, for the investigation of the questions to be treated here, recruit measurements combine several of the most favorable conditions; one might say they are tailor-made for it. Indeed, they are the only material available to date for such an investigation. Firstly, the recruit measurements of each <term>birth cohort</term> <note>original: "Jahrgänge"; referring to the group of men born in the same year</note> are taken from individuals who were also born in that same year—18, 19, or 20 years earlier, depending on the specific regulations of different countries. Secondly, recruit measurements extend across all civilized countries over long periods and are specified by entire countries, provinces, districts, and cities. This provides the opportunity to comparatively investigate the effects of general and specific influences on a larger scale. Thirdly, the number of individual measurements is already very large for every birth cohort, even for just a modest district—and much more so for an entire province or country. As previously noted, this results in the compensation of a disadvantage that would otherwise appear very concerning: namely, that individual measurements are often very inaccurate.

On my part, the entire investigation regarding the previous questions was conducted only on the basis of the very limited material available to me in the Saxon and Belgian measurements. This was partly due to the fact that I did not find other usable material, and partly because this investigation was conducted merely as a secondary study. For Saxony, I likely could have subsequently obtained original lists for other parts of the country and later birth cohorts; however, the processing of the material used so far was already exhausting of both time and patience. **§ 157.** Accordingly, regarding the general description of the method of investigation:

Let us generally call the change of a value from one birth cohort to the next the *movement* of that value. We speak of a **parallelism** in the movement of two values—for example, the annual means of recruit measurements in two neighboring parts of the country—if the movements on both sides have the same direction of decrease or increase. This does not require, as would be demanded in the mathematical sense of the word parallelism, that the change in both compared values be equally large or proportional to one another; it is enough if they simply correspond in direction. A case of parallelism shall be denoted by **||**, and a case of non-parallelism or, as we shall call it, **anti-parallelism**, shall be denoted by **$\times$**. The number of parallelisms among a given number *z* of compared cases of movement shall be denoted by *p*, and the number of anti-parallelisms by *q*. Should no dependency of the two values on one another or on a common cause exist, then in the course of a larger series...

# Variations in Recruit Height

...of years and thus of cases of movement, the parallel cases (||) <note>Parallelism (||) refers to when two different datasets—such as heights in two different provinces—move in the same direction (both increasing or both decreasing) from one year to the next.</note> alternate indifferently with the cross-cases (X) <note>Cross-cases or anti-parallelism (X) refers to when one dataset increases while the other decreases.</note>, and the number of both must be close to each other—that is, equal, except for unresolved chance occurrences. Should all cases turn out parallel, one would have to conclude that a cause or a combination of several causes, which affects the movement of both values, steadily outweighs all those acting in the opposite sense. Should only a significant preponderance of parallelisms (||) over cross-cases (X) occur, one could—in proportion to the size of that preponderance—find it more probable that a common influence is indeed taking place in that regard, but one that occasionally gives way to the prevalence of opposing influences. Finally, should the cross-cases (X) occur exclusively or very predominantly, this would not prove an independence of both values from each other, but rather that the same influence that works to increase one value works to decrease the other.

In addition to parallelism and anti-parallelism in the sense indicated—where the magnitude of the movements is not considered—one can now also take this magnitude into account. The <term>probability</term> <note>original: "W." (Wahrscheinlichkeit)</note> of a dependency or a common influence is significantly strengthened if it is primarily the strong movements in which parallelism or (in the case of opposing effects) anti-parallelism shows itself without exception or very predominantly. Meanwhile, in the case of weaker movements, one must account for the influence of unresolved chance occurrences. Therefore, in cases where a larger series of birth cohorts is available (as in Table III, see § 160), it is practical to first list the movements according to the sequence of birth cohorts to see whether the ratio of || and X changes conspicuously over time. After this, one should list them once more according to the order of the *magnitude* of movement of one value or the other. In this arrangement, the cases corresponding to the assumption of a common influence must be found primarily on the side of the larger movements, while the non-corresponding and indifferently alternating cases must be found on the side of the smaller movements, if such an influence is to be considered acceptable.

# Variations in Recruit Height

Here, the question arises whether the weight one should assign to a case of parallelism (||) or anti-parallelism (X) should be proportional to the sum or to the product of the magnitudes of movement <note>Movement refers to the change in value from one year to the next.</note> involved. Indisputably it is the product; for if one of the two movements occurring in a single case is zero, the weight of the case—being undecided between || and X—must be zero. Furthermore, parallelism between two positive movements (both increasing) counts the same as parallelism between two negative movements (both decreasing), which can only be achieved by taking the product of both movements. <note>In mathematics, multiplying two positive numbers or two negative numbers both result in a positive product, signaling they moved in the same direction.</note>

Having established this, one will obtain an even more certain judgment than from the mere number of parallelisms and anti-parallelisms by considering the weights as follows. Let us take the products of movement for the corresponding values for both the parallel cases (||) and the anti-parallel cases (X) separately; let the sum of the former be $P$ and the latter be $Q$. Now, instead of judging by the ratio or proportional difference between $p$ and $q$ <note>$p$ and $q$ refer to the raw count of cases, while $P$ and $Q$ refer to their weighted sums.</note>, we judge by that of $P$ to $Q$. If a common influence is to be accepted, there must not only be a significant proportional preponderance of one of the two values $P$ or $Q$ over the other, but the proportional difference of $p$ to $q$ must also be exceeded by it. In short, the absolute value of $(P - Q) : (P + Q)$ must be greater than $(p - q) : (p + q)$, because in the latter ratio, the greater weight of the strong cases in favor of the influence is not taken into account. It is therefore useful in every case to determine both $p$ and $q$ as well as $P$ and $Q$. If the conclusion drawn from the behavior of the former is not further reinforced by the behavior of the latter, one should consider the common influence to be doubtful.

The certainty of the conclusion generally increases, on the one hand, with the total number of cases of movement $z$, and on the other, with the magnitude of the proportional differences:

->$\frac{p - q}{p + q}, \frac{P - Q}{P + Q}$<-

No noteworthy result can be drawn from a $z$ that is too small or from relative surpluses that are too minor. However, the more both increase, and the more the second ratio increases relative to the first, the closer the <term>probability</term> <note>original: "W." (Wahrscheinlichkeit)</note> of a...

### On the Spatial Correlation of Variations in Recruit Height.

§ 159. In itself, there is nothing striking about the fact that average recruit heights vary in the same location; after all, given the multitude of accidental circumstances on which the growth of individual human beings depends, who can expect that these differences would balance out to the exact same values year after year through the calculation of a mean? <note>The "mean" or "average" is calculated by adding all values and dividing by the total number of individuals.</note> However, it may indeed seem striking that the fluctuations in the average recruit height between different years are large enough to be noticeable even without calculating a mean to those tasked with measuring the recruits. For instance, at the Leipzig Quartermaster’s office, where I obtained the lists for the Leipzig recruits, I was told that they speak of "good" and "bad" year-classes in this respect. Likewise, a high-ranking Austrian officer, who had presided over recruit measurements for many years, declared—when told of my observations on this matter—that there could be no doubt whatsoever that recruit height changes according to the year-class. I myself had noticed, while calculating the arithmetic means from the seventeen year-classes of the Leipzig city measurements for my general study, that the last year-class of 1862 yielded the maximum and the penultimate year of 1861 yielded the minimum of all seventeen years. The difference of 1.17 inches <note>At the time of Fechner's writing, Saxony used its own "inch" (Zoll) measurement, which was approximately 2.36 centimeters.</note> seemed so remarkable due to its size that I sought to get to the bottom of it. This observation served as the starting point for the entire investigation that follows.

Initially, a suspicion arose that this large difference was based on a constant <term>measurement error|an inaccuracy in data collection that consistently shifts results in one direction, such as a miscalibrated measuring rod</term> in opposite directions for the two years. If that were the case, one would not expect to find a corresponding difference in recruits stationed and measured somewhere other than Leipzig. # Variations in Recruit Height.

# Variations in Recruit Height.

If we first compare the height fluctuations for the entire Annaberg District <term>Amtshauptmannschaft</term> <note>A regional administrative district in the Kingdom of Saxony.</note> with those for the entire Borna District according to the final results of Tables I and II, we find: 1) that for Annaberg, the years 1860 and 1861 do not differ, or only by an insignificant negative fraction when considering the third decimal place; however, 1861 and 1862 differ much more significantly—by $+0.18$. 2) These movements truly run parallel to those of the Borna District; thus, in both respects, a common influence reveals itself. It is only that the influence for the Annaberg District is much smaller, or perhaps more outweighed by influences of an opposite nature, than for the Borna District, where the corresponding movements were $-0.09$ and $+0.98$. Yet, $+0.18$ is still twice as large as the probable difference of $\pm0.09$ calculated from the data <note>original Latin: "Datis"</note> ¹). This parallelism <note>The tendency for data sets from different areas to trend up or down in sync.</note> is also found again between the towns and villages of the Annaberg District in the years 1861 and 1862; it is only missing in the years 1860 and 1861, which are generally not to be relied upon with certainty.

Insofar as any conclusion can be drawn at all from the previous, still very limited data, it would be that in the years in question, a very general influence in the same direction did indeed extend over the whole of Saxony regarding height movement, but that this could only take effect to a greatly reduced degree in the Annaberg District due to local counter-effects. Furthermore, the fact that different conditions for physical development exist in the Annaberg District than in the Borna District follows directly from the fact that the average heights <note>original: "Mittelmaße"</note> in the former are absolutely smaller than those found in the latter.

# Variations in Recruit Height.

One sees first of all, in general, that the parallel cases far outweigh the anti-parallel cases; <note>In this context, "parallel" means the average height of both groups moved in the same direction—either both increasing or both decreasing—compared to the previous year. "Anti-parallel" means one group grew taller while the other grew shorter.</note> and if one rearranges the table according to the numerical sequence of the measurements, then, when ordered by the Leipzig measurements, the first six movements are parallel without exception; according to the students, the first ten are parallel with the sole exception of 1851. Only from that point onward do parallel (||) and anti-parallel (✕) movements alternate somewhat randomly, which explains the high ratio of *P* to *Q*. <note>The author uses *P* and *Q* as statistical variables to represent the total counts of parallel and anti-parallel instances.</note> It is, however, striking that the strongest movement among the students from 1851–52, equaling — 1.02, corresponds to only a very insignificant movement among the Leipzigers, though in the same direction, equaling — 0.11. Through careful revision, I have convinced myself that this does not result from a calculation error on my part. Moreover, it should not be ignored that the relatively small *m* <note>In statistics, *m* typically denotes the sample size, or the number of individuals measured in a specific group.</note> of each year’s class among the students weakens the certainty of the determination.

Instead of tracking the movement from one year to the very next, as in the previous table, one can also track it from an initial year to each subsequent year. The results for this can be very easily derived from a table like the previous one by adding the movements through the relevant years algebraically—that is, taking the plus and minus signs into account. In this way, one obtains the following movements:

If, on the other hand, one adds the positive (+) and negative (–) movements separately for each side, one discovers the total amount of variation in height in both directions. For the Leipzig city measurements, this yields +3.07 and –2.01, indicating a not insignificant overall growth. In contrast, the students show +3.85 and –4.03, suggesting an almost perfect balance between increase and decrease.

Indisputably, one would expect that in years that produce a larger average measure *A* <note>The author uses *A* to represent the arithmetic mean or average height.</note>, more giant-like results would also appear as upper extremes *E'* <note>The "upper extreme" refers to the tallest individuals in a given year's sample.</note>; in general, *A* and *E'* should predominantly move in parallel. This was specifically confirmed for both Leipzigers and students by taking the average of the three highest extremes for each year (to better compensate for random outliers). For the Leipzigers, across 16 movements between 17 year-groups, the results were *p* = 10.5^1); *q* = 5.5; *P* = 18.03; *Q* = 1.23. For the students, across 19 movements between 20 year-groups, *p* = 11; *q* = 8; *P* = 21.33; *Q* = 6.84. <note>In this statistical method, *p* and *q* represent the frequency of directions matching or differing, while *P* and *Q* represent the weighted strength of those movements.</note> Furthermore, one would expect that in years with a larger *A*, the lower extreme *E* <note>The "lower extreme" refers to the shortest individuals in the sample.</note> would also increase—that is, as the average height grows, the shortest recruits would also be taller. This was indeed found to be the case among the students after averaging the three minimum measurements for each year: *p* = 14; *q* = 5; *P* = 19.73; *Q* = 10.99. Most remarkably, however, the Leipzigers provided the exact opposite result: *p* = 4.5; *q* = 11.5; *P* = 3.23; *Q* = 22.62. This means that as the average height rose, the smallest recruits, on the whole, became much smaller rather than larger. This result, appearing with such great decisiveness, seems remarkable to me, and for the time being, I can offer no explanation for it.

# Variations in Recruit Height.

The Belgian measurements provided a welcome point of reference for this study. For a long period, these measurements were recorded in a consistent manner—not only for the entire country but also for individual provinces (departments)—in the "Statistical Documents" of Belgium and a previous report <gloss>1)</gloss>. However, since years with weak movement in the average height (*A*) or the central value (*C*) <note>*A* represents the arithmetic mean, while *C* likely refers to the median or a central distribution point in the author’s data.</note> do not allow us to expect a reliable "parallelism" <note>The tendency for height trends to move in the same direction across different regions simultaneously.</note> across individual parts of the country, I have only conducted the comparison for stronger movements where they can be found for all of Belgium. To that end, I chose the movements between the following years and eras:

1) 1852 and 1858;
2) the two five-year eras of 1851–1855 and 1856–1860;
3) two sub-eras of the first of these five-year periods, namely 1851–1853 and 1854–1855.

As for group 1), although 1852 and 1858 are far apart, there is, as noted, nothing to prevent us from observing the movement of height even between distant year-groups. Those specific years were chosen because the first contains the maximum and the last contains the minimum of the *C* and the ratio of tall to short recruits (*g : k*) <note>original: "g : k"; likely 'groß' (tall) to 'klein' (short/small).</note> within a long sequence of years. Consequently, the parallelism of height movement between different parts of the country—if such a thing existed at all—ran the least risk of being overshadowed or hidden by unresolved random coincidences. Regarding group 2), these eras are also distinguished by the fact that their *C* values, as well as their *g : k* ratios, differ quite significantly. Group 3) is a more specific breakdown of the first part of group 2).

For 1), only the *g : k* ratios are determined; for 2), the *C* and *g : k* are determined; and for 3), the *C* and the ratio of tall to medium recruits (*g : m*) <note>original: "g : m"; likely 'groß' (tall) to 'mittel' (medium).</note> are determined. The calculation of these values for groups 2) and 3) was done summarily for the years included in each era by combining the measurement figures belonging to the same measurement intervals (not individually as an average of the determinations from single years); the same applies to the final *C* value of each era.
