The absolute value of *C* <note>The author uses *C* to denote a central value, likely the median height of the group.</note> or the ratio of tall to short recruits (*g : k*) <note>original: "g : k"; representing the ratio of *groß* (tall) to *klein* (short) individuals.</note> is provided only for the first of the compared years or eras. For the second period, only the relative movement (the increase or decrease) is shown. For example, a listing in the first table of 1.776 | – 0.182 indicates a change from 1.776 to 1.594.

Whether we observe "parallelism" or "anti-parallelism" <term>parallelism: the phenomenon where different groups or regions show the same statistical trend (e.g., all increasing in height) at the same time.</term> between the various provinces depends on whether the mathematical signs of the movements (positive or negative) match within the same column. Looking at the 27 movements recorded in the following three tables for the nine provinces of Belgium, only a single case (Liège in the 3rd table) deviates from this parallelism. I have re-checked my calculations and could find no error regarding this exception; therefore, the existence of a common influence on height movement across all of Belgium is beyond doubt.

However, the magnitude of these parallel movements varies greatly between the different provinces. In some places, the change is so slight that it is easy to see how "anti-parallel" cases (where provinces move in opposite directions) would frequently occur if one tried to track movements during periods when the trend for Belgium as a whole was weak. This would naturally also happen if one tried to track the data year-by-year, as was done with the Leipzig students, though a majority of parallel cases would still be expected.

In any event, it would be quite interesting to carry out this comparison for the provinces of Belgium in such a way, as it might reveal many characteristic differences between them. The *Statistical Documents* <note>original: "Documents Statistiques"; refers to the official Belgian national statistics publications.</note> offer sufficient material for this; however, I cannot personally embark on this expansion of the investigation, as it would lead too far afield, despite being quite simple to execute in principle.

## On the question of a temporal connection
## regarding variations in recruit height.

§ 162. How this question is to be understood is indicated in § 156. Let us first examine it in relation to the Saxon measurements available to us, namely those of the Leipzigers <note>Residents of the city of Leipzig.</note> and the students. The general summary <term>average A</term> <note>original: "A" refers to the "Arithmetisches Mittel" or arithmetic mean.</note> of the former is 69.61, with which the individual average agrees. If we now designate the successive 17 years from 1846 onwards with a $+$ or $-$ sign, depending on whether their average *A* stands above or below this mean, we find the following series of signs:

->$- - - - - - + + - + + + + - + - - - - + .$<-

Among the students, the summary average *A* of the twenty year-groups is 71.76; with which the individual average likewise agrees. The sequence of signs for this is as follows:

->$+ - + + - + - - + + - + + + + + - + - - - - + .$<-

Now, according to the <term>probability calculus</term> <note>The mathematical study of randomness and chance.</note> of pure chance, one would expect just as many <term>sign changes</term> <note>When a year's height moves from above average to below average, or vice versa.</note> as <term>sign sequences</term> <note>When a year stays on the same side of the average as the previous year.</note>, as one can see for oneself by taking a primary list of recruit measurements in which the measurements follow each other by chance, and marking the individual measurements in order with $+$ or $-$ depending on whether they are larger or smaller than the average *A* of the list¹). In the case of the Leipzig measurements, however, the number of sign sequences is 9 and the number of changes is 7; for the students, the number of sign sequences is 7 and the number of changes is 13. From this, no temporal connection can be inferred, for if such a connection existed, the sign sequences would have to decisively predominate.

In contrast to this, a very striking connection emerges from the Belgian measurements (see Table VIII below). The individual <term>central value C</term> <note>original: "C" refers to "Zentralwert," known today as the median.</note> of all 33 year-groups from 1843 to 1875 inclusive is 1645.8 mm.

# Variations in Recruit Height.

One can see that, apart from the cohorts of 1857 and 1870, the trend of the *g*:*k* values <note>The ratio of "greater" heights to "lesser" heights relative to the middle range.</note> runs parallel to the trend of the *C* values <note>The central value or median height of the group.</note> in terms of both decrease and increase throughout.

It should be noted that only the values from the 1849 cohort onward are determined by direct measurements of 19-year-old recruits. The values of the first six cohorts (separated by a line in the table) were adjusted from measurements of 18-year-old recruits who had been conscripted one year earlier. Thus, for example, the *C* = 1642.1, which is listed in the table as valid for 19-year-old recruits of the year 1843, was derived from a *C* = 1632.5, which was obtained directly from measurements of 18-year-old recruits in the year 1842<sup>1</sup>). The following explanation is provided regarding this.

Until the year 1847 inclusive, as noted, recruits were measured at a full 18 years of age, and were naturally smaller than if they had been measured a year later at 19 years of age. In order to adjust them to this standard, I determined the singular mean <note>A statistical method of calculating an average from individual data points rather than grouped summaries.</note> of the six *C* values, as well as the *g* : *k* ratios, for the cohorts of 18-year-old recruits from 1842 to 1847 inclusive; I found the former to be 1631.6 and the latter to be 1.033. On the other hand, I sought the corresponding values for the 13 cohorts of 19-year-old recruits from 1849 to 1861 and found them to be 1641.2 and 1.373 respectively. Based on this, the *C* values of the 18-year-old recruits were multiplied by 1.0059 (1641.2 : 1631.6) and the *g* : *k* values by 1.329 (1.373 : 1.033) to adjust them to the values they would have had if they had been measured one year later.

The reason I took only 13 cohorts of 19-year-old recruits for comparison with the six cohorts of 18-year-old recruits to determine the reduction factor <note>The multiplier used to account for the physical growth that occurs between ages 18 and 19.</note>, while 27 were available, was primarily because at the time of undertaking this...

## XXV. Structure and Asymmetry of Rye

->(*Secale cereale*).<-

§ 164. Regarding the terminology, I note at the outset that by "panicle" <note>original: *Rispe*. While *Rispe* usually refers to a branched cluster of flowers (panicle), Fechner specifically defines it here as the fruiting spike or "ear" of the rye.</note> I will understand the fruiting spike—that is, the uppermost part of the stalk which contains the grains. By "first, second, third segment," etc., I mean the segments or so-called <term>internodes: the sections of a plant stem between the joints or nodes</term>, counted in order from the top downward. By "stalk" <note>original: *Halm*</note> I mean the entire length: the sum of the panicle and the segments down to the root, excluding the root itself.

Around July 24, 1863, from a field planted with rye at Leutzscher Pflege <note>A historical district or agricultural area near Leipzig.</note> near Leipzig—to be denoted briefly as L.—a sheaf of mature stalks was pulled up with the roots for harvest. The majority of these, numbering 217, had 6 segments; 138 had only 5 segments; 10, by contrast, had 7 segments; and 6 of a rather stunted appearance had only 4 segments. The following main investigation regarding the proportions of asymmetry and asymmetrical distribution refers to the 217 six-segmented and 138 five-segmented stalks from this site, with a primary focus on the former.

Meanwhile, it seemed of interest whether ears from other locations (around Leipzig) behave similarly to those from Leutzscher Pflege regarding the proportions of their segmentation. For this purpose, a smaller number of stalks had to suffice, as the investigation would otherwise have been unfeasible for me to complete. Therefore, around the same time, smaller bundles of stalks were taken from the following locations around Leipzig, containing the following number of stalks: At Stünz (St.) on July 16: 22 pieces, consisting of 20 six-segmented and 2 five-segmented; at Täubchenweg <note>A well-known street and area in Leipzig.</note>

<meta>This page continues the botanical study of rye stalks (*Secale cereale*) introduced on the previous page, moving from the general sample size to the specific methodology used for measuring the segments and the challenges of accurately recording botanical data.</meta>

### Structure and Asymmetry of Rye.

(Tbch.) <note>Likely an abbreviation for a specific field site or "Tagebuch" (Diary).</note> July 20: 24 pieces, 4 with six segments, 20 with five segments; at Schönefeld (Sch.) July 15: 22 pieces, 18 with six segments, 4 with five segments. The stalks originated from a field that had already been half-harvested.

For all stalks, the panicle <note>Fechner uses *Rispe* (panicle) to refer to the grain-bearing ear or spike of the rye.</note> and the individual segments were measured separately up to the center of the nodes. The total length of the stalk (that is, including the panicle but excluding the root) was obtained only by adding the lengths measured individually, as it is practically difficult to measure the whole stalk in one piece—not only because of its often great length but also because the segments often meet at <term>obtuse angles: angles greater than 90 degrees, causing the stalk to zigzag rather than grow perfectly straight</term>. Consequently, the determination of the total stalk is relatively somewhat less accurate than that of its individual parts, because the errors in individual measurements partially compensate for each other during addition, but partially also add up. The bottommost segment is also usually not accurately measurable, and the determinations regarding it are of much lower value than for the other segments because it is mostly stunted, such that it could only be measured roughly over the top with the measuring tape; and I would have even set these determinations aside entirely if, on the one hand, a noticeable gap in the total context of the data had not resulted, and if, on the other hand, the roughly obtained measurements had not generally fit quite well into the overall sequence. At times, one may be in doubt whether the bottommost segment should be counted as part of the root rather than the stalk, as small roots occasionally appear to descend from its upper node; however, as long as a single, albeit stunted, <term>internode: the section of a plant stem between two joints or nodes</term> runs from this node down to the branched root, it was always counted as the lowest segment of the stalk. The ripe panicle can also easily be measured as too short due to the loss of the lowest grains, and the first segment adjacent to it measured as correspondingly too long; however, the length of the panicle could still be determined by a small projection, more easily felt with the finger than visible to the eye, which separates it from the first segment. The <term>awns: the bristle-like appendages growing from the ear of the grain</term> of the panicle were not included in the measurements.

<meta>This page continues the methodological discussion regarding the measurement of rye stalks. ### Structure and Asymmetry of Rye.

For the measurements, I used a measuring tape precisely divided into centimeters <margin>1) Commercially available measuring tapes are often inaccurately divided.</margin>, which was kept as uniformly taut as possible during the process. Millimeters, and occasionally even half-millimeters, were estimated. Marking millimeters directly on the measuring tape would have provided no significant advantage; aside from the fact that the constant, sharp focusing required would have strained the eyes too much, one can estimate tenths of a centimeter accurately enough. One must simply guard against inconsistent estimation, for which recruitment measurements <note>Refers to the anthropometric data taken from military conscripts, a common source of large-scale statistical data in the 19th century.</note> and skull measurements (see Chapter VII) have provided examples of bias. 

However, after the entire bundle had been measured in groups, all sections of the stalks were measured a second time. This was done not so much to gain a slight increase in precision from the average of the two measurements, but rather to identify and correct major errors in perception and recording by cross-checking two independent sets of records. Such errors are harder to avoid entirely during such a large number of tiring measurements and recordings than one might think. From the two measurements of the same length, one could have taken the average; however, for the sake of simplicity, I preferred to leave the sum of both measurements undivided by two. All subsequent data refers to this arrangement, which simply means that in the following text, the unit of measurement is the half-centimeter instead of the whole centimeter.

§ 165. [In this way, the primary tables for the panicle <note>The branching grain-head of the rye plant.</note> and the individual segments of the stalk were obtained, of which Table IV in Chapter VII (for the topmost segment of the 217 six-segmented stalks) provides an example. From these, the following tables were then derived.]

Since the unit of measurement $\delta$ <note>original: "$\delta$"; the Greek letter delta, here representing the smallest unit of deviation or measurement used in the study.</note> for the rye is everywhere 1/2 cm, I will omit any special mention of it in the following sections.

§ 166. The results of the greatest general interest which can be drawn from the preceding tables seem to me to be the following two:

1) That specific, regular structural proportions exist in rye of such a kind that they can be regarded as characteristic of the plant. These undoubtedly provide a reason not only to investigate different types of grain and grasses <note>original: *Gramineen*</note> in the interest of their comparative characteristics, but also to study the influence of external circumstances—such as soil quality and annual weather conditions—upon these proportions.

2) That from these results emerge decisive evidence for the existence of an essential asymmetry and a foundation for testing its laws.

# Structure and Asymmetry of Rye.

Let us first investigate the former objective of the study.

One might find it questionable whether the variations shown by individual rye stalks in terms of their length and structural proportions depend more on a random diversity of the seeds or on the nature of the soil surrounding each individual plant. It is likely due to both causes, though it cannot yet be decided empirically. In any case, the following collective relationships <note>Fechner uses "collective relationships" to refer to statistical patterns found within a group or "collective" of samples.</note> occur:

1) Despite the fact that the average length *A*~1~ <note>The arithmetic mean.</note> of the entire stalks fluctuates between 344.7 and 222.1 depending on the location (for which the data under Table I should be consulted), the proportions of the segments (according to their arithmetic means) relative to the total length remain independent of this and are to be seen as variable only according to the number of segments. In short, for a given number of segments, they can be considered constant and therefore characteristic of rye. Table I contains the evidence for this, insofar as all segments, as well as the panicle <term>panicle: the branched flowering part at the top of the rye stalk</term>, are reduced to the ratio of the stalk (set at 100). Since, besides Leutzsch with *m* = 217 and 138 <note>The variable *m* represents the number of stalks measured in each sample group.</note>, the other locations only have an *m* of 10, 18, and 20, I would not have believed that—given the uncertainty caused by such a small *m*—the agreement of the relative segment lengths for a given number of segments could have gone as far as it has. Only in Schönefeld (with *m* = 18) do some larger differences from the other locations appear for the six-segmented stalks; but compare, on the other hand, for the six-segmented stalks, the surprising agreement of the segment proportions between L. (Leutzsch, *m*=217) and St. (Stötteritz, *m*=20) <note>L., St., Sch., and Tbch. (Taucha) refer to different agricultural trial locations near Leipzig.</note> despite the very different total lengths of 275.2 and 344.7. One should also note the no less remarkable agreement for the five-segmented stalks between L. (138) and Tbch. (20) with different total lengths of 261.1 and 222.1. Indeed, even Sch. five-segmented with *m* = 4 matches this remarkably well, and only Tbch. six-segmented with *m* = 4 and L. four-segmented with *m* = 6 show significant deviations; however, comparisons with such a small *m* cannot be authoritative at all and were therefore omitted in the previous table. 2) If one compares the columns for the seven-, six-, and five-segmented stalks in Table I, one generally finds that as this number of segments decreases, the first three segments increase in relative length, while the last ones decrease. # Structure and Asymmetry of Rye.

The extreme deviations, which are not explicitly stated in Tables III and IV but can be easily found using the formulas *U'* = *E'* — *A* and *U,,* = *A* — *E* <note>In these formulas, E' and E represent the upper and lower extreme values, while A is the arithmetic average. These calculations help determine how far the longest and shortest stalks stray from the average.</note>, depend only on unbalanced chance occurrences and vary randomly in size and sign between the segments of the stalks. However, if we track the difference *u* <note>The variable *u* refers to a specific measure of asymmetry—the difference between the arithmetic mean and the most frequent value (the mode) or median.</note> downward through the series of segments, we see that its value, which is positive for the first segment, continuously decreases in size and, from a certain segment onward, turns negative. For six-segmented stalks, this shift happens at the fourth segment; for five-segmented stalks, it occurs only at the fifth segment. If we do the same with the difference *U'* — *U,,*, we find the corresponding result with reversed signs, though here, even in the six-segmented stalks, the reversal does not begin until the fifth segment. At the same time, these tables provide an opportunity to confirm the general rule (§ 33; 142) that *U'* — *U,,* has the opposite sign of *u'* — *u,,*, which can only suffer a sensory exception through unbalanced chance when *u* and *U'* — *U,,* are very small; an example of this can be found here in the fourth segment of the six-segmented stalks. For the panicle <term>panicle: the branched, flowering head of the rye plant</term> in both six- and five-segmented stalks, *u* is negative and *U'* — *U,,* is positive; for the entire stalk, the former value is positive and the latter is negative.

It would now be very interesting to investigate whether the legally defined progression of *u* and *U'* — *U,,*—which has been proven here for only a single location (Leutzsch) and the weather of a specific year (1863) with a sufficiently large sample size *m*—can also be found at other locations and in other years. It is quite possible that different locations and weather conditions during the growth of the stalks might lead to different proportions in this regard. Now, while I do have data for other locations (St., Tbch., Sch. <note>These are likely abbreviations for villages near Leipzig: Stötteritz, Thonberg, and Schönefeld.</note>), the sample size *m* is only 18 to 20, which is far too small to expect reliable results. The comparison between theory and experience shows a sufficient agreement, which is all the more satisfying as the sample size *m* = 217, upon which the determinations are based, is relatively small. In particular, one can notice that the second segment corresponds well to the requirements of the theory; in this, of course, no distinguishing feature compared to the other segments is to be found, but rather only a matter of chance <note>The author suggests that the high level of agreement in the second segment is a statistical coincidence rather than a unique biological property.</note> related to the specifically chosen reduction level and reduction position. At the same time, the presence of essential asymmetry is thereby placed beyond question. However, in order to check the conclusions regarding the decrease and reversal of asymmetry for descending segments—which are suggested by the regular progression of the *u*-values in Tables III and IV—it is appropriate to compare the *u* values in Table III relating to *Aᵣ* with the corresponding *u* values in the table above relating to *Dₚ*. ### Dimensions of Gallery Paintings.

...show. Finally, I will share (§ 175), again from the *Propaedeutic of Aesthetics* <note>original: *Vorschule der Ästhetik*</note>, data regarding the ratio of height to width and regarding the surface area of the gallery paintings.]

§ 171. The classes of paintings are distinguished as religious, mythological, genre, landscape, and still life:

a) **Religious paintings**, that is, paintings with Old Testament and Christian-religious content. Included here were not only compositions with multiple figures, but even individual heads and figures, such as heads of Christ, images of saints, depictions of martyr stories, and even landscapes with sacred <term>staffage</term> <note>Small figures or animals added to a landscape painting to provide scale or a narrative element</note>; thus, this class is actually a poorly defined hodgepodge; consequently, a very irregular distribution in terms of measurement and number took place within it.

b) **Mythological paintings**, that is, paintings with content from the Greek and Roman world of gods and heroes, categorized broadly and therefore also poorly distributed.

c) **Genre paintings**, in the usual sense, excluding scenes of war and hunting.

d) **Landscapes**, with the inclusion of <term>marines</term> <note>original: *Marinen*; paintings depicting the sea or maritime scenes</note>, though excluding views of harbors and cities.

e) **Still lifes**, that is, paintings with inanimate objects (aside from architecture, which is excluded here), such as arrangements of food, utensils, as well as flower and fruit pieces—with the exception of those that include human figures, but including those in which animals appear incidentally.

Secular historical paintings, architectural paintings, portraits, and generally any paintings not comprised in the previous classes were not included in the investigation. Excluded everywhere are frescoes and tapestries, <term>diptychs</term> <note>Artworks consisting of two hinged panels</note> and <term>triptychs</term> <note>Artworks consisting of three hinged panels</note>, as well as panels on which different depictions were contained in sections marked off from one another.

Naturally, doubts could often arise as to whether a painting should be included as a genre painting under c) or set aside as a secular historical painting, or whether a painting as a landscape...

### Dimensions of Gallery Paintings.

A completely sharp principle of separation cannot be established here at all; I followed the general impression <note>original: *Aperçu*</note> of the painting descriptions as they appeared in the catalogs.

There are several cases where two or even a series of images related by content and sharing the same format are listed one after another in the catalogs. For example, in the third section of the Louvre catalog: *French School* <note>original: *École française*</note> page 342 ff., from numbers 525 to 547 under the collective title: "The Principal Events in the Life of Saint Bruno" <note>original: *Les principaux traits de la vie de St. Bruno*</note>, there are 22 paintings by LE SUEUR which, with the exception of number 533, all have the same dimensions: *h* [height] = 193 cm; *w* [width] = 130 cm.

The question arose whether, in such cases, all examples should be included and calculated in the distribution table as a single entry or recorded as many times as they occurred.

If the objective were to determine the actual average values and the actual distribution ratios of paintings of a given type contained in specific galleries—though this would likely be of little interest—then naturally only the latter method could be followed. However, since one could not count on the same dimensions recurring on average in the same proportions in other galleries, one would obtain an inappropriate contribution to the determination of general averages and would find the general distribution ratios significantly altered. Thus, the following numbers of religious paintings were found in the following size intervals of height:

### Dimensions of Gallery Paintings.

...which numbers closely coincide, as is to be expected with adjacent intervals. However, in this instance, all 22 of Le Sueur’s paintings—each 193 cm in height—were counted only twice. Had one chosen to count them 22 times, then instead of the consecutive numbers 91; 89; 93, one would have obtained: 91; 109; 93; which would have made the distribution very irregular. The same applies in other cases. Since a majority of related paintings with the same dimensions suggests a certain strong preference for those dimensions and therefore claims an increased statistical weight, I have decided, as a simple rule of thumb, to count all cases where two or more related paintings of the same dimensions exist exactly twice—but no more than twice—in the distribution table.

Therefore, when the total number of paintings examined is given as 10,558 in the following sections, this number is not strictly precise. As per the previous remark, a larger number of related paintings with the same dimensions are only ever counted as two; on the other hand, landscape paintings that feature religious or mythological <term>staffage</term> <note>Figures or animals added to a landscape painting to provide scale or narrative interest; from the German *Staffage*</note> are recorded twice: once among the landscapes and once among the religious or mythological paintings. However, since the influence of both these circumstances is not significant and, moreover, they work in opposite directions, the above number remains accurate enough.

Religious and mythological paintings show a very similar progression to the genre, landscape, and still-life paintings, except that in these classes—indisputably due to the unfavorable grouping of the paintings included under them—some very large irregularities remain in the progression. These are unlikely to be balanced out even by an increased sample size (*m*) <note>The variable "m" refers to the total number of observations or items in the statistical sample.</note>; therefore, these classes are not suitable for testing the laws of distribution and have not been analyzed by me as extensively as the others. For still-life paintings where width exceeds height (*b* > *h*), relatively significant irregularities also remained, such that a full, detailed analysis would not have been worthwhile.

# Dimensions of Gallery Paintings.

In this respect, providing more detail would simply cost too much space relative to its significance. If we stick to the overall results of the twenty-two galleries, the five investigated classes follow this order of frequency (without distinguishing between the $h > b$ <note>Height greater than breadth (Portrait orientation)</note> and $b > h$ <note>Breadth greater than height (Landscape orientation)</note> categories) according to their combined values: **Religious**, **Landscapes**, **Genre**, **Mythological**, and **Still Life**. The ratio of landscapes to genre paintings in particular (2076 : 1477) slightly exceeds a ratio of 4 : 3.

Among **genre paintings**, those whose height is greater than their width ($h > b$) are slightly more numerous than those whose width is greater than their height ($b > h$). In contrast, among **landscapes**, the wide format ($b > h$) is more than six times as numerous as the tall format ($h > b$). It may be of some interest that among **religious paintings**, the tall format ($h > b$) is approximately twice as numerous as the wide format ($b > h$); this is undoubtedly because **heaven** <note>In religious art, "heaven" (Himmel) refers to the upper portion of a canvas where divine figures or celestial light are depicted, requiring vertical space.</note> is often included at a great height in the representation. Conversely, in **mythological paintings**, the width is preferred, with the wide format ($b > h$) being almost twice as frequent (609 versus 350) as the tall format ($h > b$).

The average size can be seen from the values $A_1$ <term>Arithmetic Mean: The standard average calculated by adding values and dividing by the total count.</term> or $G_1$ <term>Geometric Mean: An average calculated by multiplying values together; often used in aesthetics to find a "typical" proportion.</term>, and the average fluctuation can be seen from the $\eta$ <term>Mean Variation: A statistical measure showing how much the individual paintings typically deviate from the average size.</term> values applicable to $A_1$. The comparison of $\eta$ and $A_1$ specifically shows that as the average size increases, the average fluctuation also grows; however, the relative fluctuation ($\eta : A_1$) does not show very strong differences across classes and categories.

To account for extreme fluctuations alongside the average fluctuation, I provide the extremes $E'$ <note>The highest value in the data set.</note> and $E,$ <note>The lowest value in the data set.</note> in the following table, as well as the difference $U' - U, = (E' - A_1) - (A_1 - E,)$. The additional values $E''$ and $E_{,,}$ represent the values in the distribution table immediately preceding and following the extremes $E'$ and $E,$.

To judge the asymmetry, the $u$-values <note>In this context, $u$ likely refers to a specific statistical measure of skewness or deviation used by the author.</note> of Table III are most useful. According to them, the asymmetry regarding $A$ <note>The arithmetic mean, or average.</note> is everywhere negative and strongly pronounced. One can also observe based on those values that $h$ <note>Height.</note> corresponds with the associated $b$ <note>Breadth or width.</note> in its asymmetry, as the small differences shown between them in the table can be considered accidental. Only in the case of Religious paintings is the difference in this regard somewhat larger; however, the great irregularities of this class do not permit any reliable legal rules to be derived from them.

The values $U' - U$ in Table IV confirm the presence of significant asymmetry and at the same time validate the law of reversal <note>The "Umkehrgesetz," a principle where the signs or directions of statistical values flip under certain conditions.</note> for the asymmetry of $u = \mu' - \mu$ and $U' - U$, as both series of values here consistently have opposite signs.

Moreover, the wide divergence of the values $A$ and $C$ <note>The median, or middle value.</note> in Table III, as well as the position of $C$ below $A$, already reveals the presence of strong asymmetry in a negative direction. Furthermore, a comparison of $G$ <note>The geometric mean.</note> with $C$ teaches that the asymmetry regarding $G$ is far lower, and for Still Life where $h > b$, it is even in the opposite direction than regarding $A$. This is related to the fact that $G$ is necessarily smaller than $A$ and, since $C$ is also smaller than $A$, $G$ lies either above or below $C$, but in any case is closer to the latter value than to $A$.

| *Landscape* . | 1.25 | 1.38 | 1.28 |

These findings contain what seems to me a very interesting result: that the ratio of the larger to the smaller dimension has nearly the same value across the various classes of paintings—for the differences in the table may be regarded as incidental—but this value differs depending on whether *h > w* or *w > h*. This value deviates significantly from the <term>golden ratio</term> <note>Approximately 1.618; a proportion often theorized to be the most aesthetically pleasing, though Fechner's data suggests artists actually preferred "squat" ratios like 1.25 or 1.33.</note>. In cases where the height is greater than the width (*h > w*), the height relates to the width almost exactly as 5 : 4; where the width is greater than the height (*w > h*), the width relates to the height approximately as 4 : 3.

Furthermore, one may notice that while height and width deviate from one another by such a considerable ratio in the two separate groups (*h > w* and *w > h*), the ratio in the combined categories for *Genre* and *Still Life* settles almost into equality (the value of 1). One might assume that because height deviates from width to a lesser degree in the *h > w* group than in the *w > h* group, the latter would tip the balance in its favor when combined; however, this is roughly compensated for...

## XXVII. Collective Objects from the Field of Meteorology.

§ 176. [**Daily Rainfall Amounts for Geneva.** — An investigation of the rainfall conditions in Geneva has already been provided by **PLANTAMOUR** in his *New Studies on the Climate of Geneva* <note>original: "Nouvelles études sur le climat de Genève"</note> in the section "on rain" <note>original: "de la pluie"</note> 1). He bases this on fifty years of observations of rainfall amounts and rainy days during the years 1826–1875. However, since he uses only monthly values for the frequency and quantity of rain as the basis for his calculations, and his goal is the regular distribution of rain over the course of the year, as well as the character of individual months regarding their dryness or humidity, the following investigation cannot be conducted in imitation of Plantamour’s. This is because we are concerned here with the proof of <term>asymmetry</term> <note>In statistics, asymmetry (or skewness) refers to a distribution where the data is not mirrored perfectly on both sides of the average, but instead leans or "tails" off in one direction.</note> and the validation of the **logarithmic law of distribution** for rainfall amounts. For this purpose, the 50-year monthly values are by no means sufficient, given the exceedingly large fluctuations between individual values. Instead, one must go back to the daily rainfall amounts.]

[The research material is found in the *Archives of Physical and Natural Sciences* <note>original: "Archives des sciences physiques et naturelles"</note> of the *Universal Library of Geneva* <note>original: "Bibliothèque universelle de Genève"</note> among the meteorological tables provided every month. There, for every rainy day, the rainfall amount is recorded in millimeters, even down to tenths of a millimeter, under the heading: "Water fallen in 24 hours" <note>original: "Eau tombée dans les 24 heures"</note>. Regarding the form of the <term>precipitation</term> <note>Any form of water—liquid or solid—falling from the sky, such as rain, snow, or hail.</note>, whether

In fact, all months show the densest clustering in the 0–1 mm interval, but from 2 mm onward, one finds a rapid decrease in values. After a period of undecided fluctuation, these values form very irregular end sections with scattered *a* <note>original: "a"; referring to the observed measurement values of rainfall height.</note>. For the month of January, the boundaries of this end section are 12 mm and 40 mm.

These general details already reveal the presence of an extremely strong asymmetry <term>Asymmetrie</term> <note>In statistics, asymmetry (or skewness) refers to a distribution where the data is not mirrored evenly around the center; here, Fechner is noting that light rain is much more frequent than heavy rain.</note> for all months of the year. Furthermore, the progression of *m*, *A*, and $\eta$ <note>the mean deviation, which measures how much the data varies from the average</note> in the table above deserves attention. From the *m*-values, it follows that the frequency of rain has two cycles over the course of the year, whose low points (minima) are the months of February and July, and whose high points (maxima) are the months of May and October, while a steady rise or fall takes place in between. Only September breaks this regularity; however, this disruption is to be considered accidental, since it is absent for the *m*-values of the years 1826–1875 taken from Plantamour's tables¹, where the month of January instead appears as the disruption. This can be seen from the following comparative compilation of *m*-values for the periods 1826–1875 and 1845–1892, where the order of values from left to right corresponds to the sequence of months from January to December:

| Period | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |

In contrast to the *m*-values, the *A*-values <note>the average rainfall heights</note> show only one cycle, which proceeds without disruption and has its minimum in February and its maximum in October. Parallel to this are the values of $\eta$, i.e., the mean deviations regarding *A*, whose minimum likewise falls in February, while they reach their maximum one month earlier, in September. The large values of $\eta$, which consistently come very close to the *A*-values themselves, reveal the strength of the fluctuations that occur between the individual rainfall heights. The relative mean fluctuation, as indicated by the ratio $\eta : A$, is approximately constant, equal to 0.9.

According to this, the average height of rain during the year increases from February to October, only to fall again from that point until February. However, one does not obtain a correct picture of the distribution of rain across individual months in this way. This is because the frequency of precipitation also comes into consideration. If one distributes the total amount of rain occurring in a month during the 48-year period accordingly—not just across the individual days when rain actually occurred, but across all days in general—one also obtains a twofold periodicity for the amount of rain, just as for the frequency of rain, as <term>Plantamour</term> <note>Philippe Plantamour (1816–1898), a Swiss astronomer and meteorologist known for his extensive climate observations in Geneva.</note> has demonstrated. # Meteorological Collective Objects <note>The abbreviation "K.-G." stands for *Kollektiv-Gegenstände* (Collective Objects). This is a term used by the physicist and philosopher Gustav Fechner to describe groups of natural phenomena that, while individually random, follow predictable statistical laws when viewed as a whole.</note>

...tables were used as a direct basis. However, if the values of 0.0 mm—to which a logarithmic value of <term>negative infinity</term> <note>In mathematics, the logarithm of zero is undefined and approaches negative infinity, which cannot be plotted on a standard graph or used in typical calculations.</note> would correspond—are not to disappear from the table during the transition to **logarithmic intervals**, then a decision must be made regarding the interpretation of the rainy days recorded with these values. Since this measure of rainfall height is clearly intended to indicate an actual, albeit vanishingly small, amount of precipitation of less than 0.1 mm in height, it seems justified to set the value at 0.05 mm instead of 0.0. To mitigate the arbitrariness of this choice, log 0.05 = –1.3 is simultaneously chosen as the boundary between the first and second logarithmic intervals, so that consistently one half of those values falls into the first occurring interval and the other half into the next. Furthermore, the size of the logarithmic intervals was fixed at 0.2. Consequently, the *a*-values <note>In this context, *a* represents the measured height of the rainfall.</note> fluctuate between the limits of 0 and 100 mm, whereas the logarithmic *a*-values fluctuate between the limits of –1.5 and +2.1, as can be seen from the following distribution tables. Corresponding to the strong irregularities of the empirical <note>Empirical values are those actually observed in nature, as opposed to "theoretical" values calculated from a mathematical formula.</note> values, there are sometimes significant differences between the empirical and theoretical values; however, these are softened when adjacent intervals are taken together. These differences should therefore be regarded as insignificant disturbances, so that the theoretical values represent a smoothing out of the random variations inherent in the empirical data. Regarding the elements, it is noteworthy that *G* <note>The geometric mean.</note> lies below *C* <note>The median.</note> and thus—with consideration of Table II—*C* lies between *G* and *A* <note>The arithmetic mean.</note>. This further proves the exceedingly large fluctuation in rainfall amounts. Connected to this is the fact that the *u*-values regarding 𝔇ₚ, as well as the *u*-values regarding *A₁*, are negative. "...it has long been known that the lowering of mercury below the average is generally greater than its elevation above this point." <note>original French: "depuis longtemps, que l'abaissement du mercure au-dessous de la moyenne est en général plus grand que son élévation au-dessus de ce terme"</note>. According to this, a positive asymmetry regarding *A* <term>A: the parameter used in Fechner’s formulas to measure the skewness or "lopsidedness" of a data set</term> is to be expected throughout, or at least in the majority of cases. To test this and simultaneously prove the validity of the two-sided Gaussian Law <note>The "zweiseitige G. G." refers to Fechner's adaptation of the Gaussian normal distribution to account for asymmetrical data</note> for barometric deviations, I have taken the deviation values from the monthly normal state from the *Netherlands Yearbook for Meteorology*¹) reported in the section "Temperature and Barometric Deviations." For this purpose, it is sufficient to base the calculations on an arithmetic method; the range of fluctuation for the deviation values is not so large that the effort of a logarithmic treatment would be worthwhile. Therefore, the theoretical comparison values accompanying the empirical values were also derived from the arithmetic two-sided distribution law. [It is useful to compare the statements of BRAVAIS <note>Auguste Bravais (1811–1863), a French physicist known for his work in crystallography and atmospheric science</note> regarding various forms of possible probability laws, because they show that BRAVAIS, just like QUETELET <note>Adolphe Quetelet (1796–1874), the "father" of social statistics</note> himself, certainly recognized the possibility of an asymmetrical distribution law. However, he mistakenly assigned the role of the "most dense value" <term>dichtesten Wert: the mode, or the value that occurs most frequently in a data set</term> to the arithmetic mean, and thus fundamentally failed to grasp the correct understanding of the asymmetrical law. The relevant passage of BRAVAIS’s letter states (at the place cited above, p. 413): "It is known that the largest deviations of the barometer toward the top of the column are hardly more than half or 2/3 of the deviations of the barometer toward the bottom; so that one will have a probability curve of the form . . . whose two halves will not be symmetrical; only the average vertical line must always divide the total segment into two equal areas."] <note>original French: "On sait que les plus grands écarts du baromètre vers le haut de la colonne, ne sont guère que la moitié ou les 2/3 des écarts du baromètre vers le bas; de sorte que l'on aura une courbe de possibilité de la forme . . . dont les deux moitiés ne seront pas symmétriques; seulement l'ordonnée moyenne doit toujours partager le segment total en deux aires égales."</note>.

This is shown, on the one hand, by the agreement between the empirical and theoretical values and, on the other hand, by the position of the main values *A*, *C*, *D<sub>p</sub>*, *D<sub>i</sub>*, the ratio values *p*, as well as the values of *u* and *u*. However, the values of *u* and *u* consistently teach us that this asymmetry is by no means constant over the course of the year. Rather, a regular pattern reveals itself throughout the year, whereby the strong asymmetry of winter and the less pronounced asymmetry of summer are interrupted in the spring and autumn by asymmetry that either vanishes or flips into its opposite. Here, too, the agreement between theory and experience is satisfactory, even if it appears slightly less consistent than for the barometer deviations—likely due to the relatively smaller scale of reduction used. The asymmetry is positive with respect to $A$ only for the month of January; for the other three months, it is negative. That exception in January might be considered accidental, especially since the observed value for $u$ is small. However, since I also consulted December for comparison and found the same direction of asymmetry—again with a similarly weak value as in January—one may safely assume that the asymmetry remains negative with respect to $A$ for most of the year. During the winter, however, it approaches a value of zero, with a tendency to shift into positive territory. Finally, it is worth mentioning that the average fluctuation <term>η</term> for the months investigated (and likely for the entire year) remains fairly constant.

Based on these results, the validity of the two-sided Gaussian Law <note>The Normal Distribution or "Bell Curve" developed by Carl Friedrich Gauss</note> cannot be doubted. The differences between the empirical and theoretical values are, on average, smaller here than in the corresponding comparison tables for barometer and thermometer deviations. Likewise, the main values and the ratio values of *p* satisfy the theoretical requirements. At the same time, the asymmetry proves itself to be essential—partly through the consistency of its direction, and partly through its strength, which is particularly prominent in the *u*-value for January. Because these daily variations generally provide more favorable results than the barometer and thermometer deviations (both of which are affected by serial dependence <note>original: "Successionsabhängigkeit"; the statistical phenomenon where data points are influenced by those immediately preceding them, common in weather patterns</note>), it seems that the absence of serial dependence indeed favors the development of the laws of pure chance.

[Furthermore, to compare Quetelet’s <note>Adolphe Quetelet (1796–1874), a Belgian astronomer and statistician who applied probability to social and natural sciences</note> discussions on asymmetry¹) to this, the following must be shared regarding his method of investigation. Quetelet starts from the premise that, in cases of essential symmetry, the probabilities <note>original: "W." for "Wahrscheinlichkeit"</note> of positive and negative deviations from the arithmetic mean are equal. From this, he concludes that asymmetry is rooted in the inequality of the probabilities for deviations on either side of the mean. Accordingly, he illustrates the probability ratios occurring here using an urn containing an infinitely large number of black and white balls in various proportions, which must be specifically chosen in each case. In particular, he provides a tabular summary of the probabilities for the appearance of balls of one type when drawing 16 balls, given that 50, 55, 60, . . . . 90, 95 balls of that type occur for every 100 balls. He then compares these tables of theoretical probabilities with the tables of empirical values resulting from the reduced distribution tables for daily temperature variations (for Brussels), by dividing the *z* of each interval by the corresponding *m* <note>where *z* is the frequency and *m* is the total population or sample size</note>.

### Meteorological Collective Objects <note>The term "Kollektiv-Gegenstände" refers to large data sets treated as a single mathematical entity.</note>

Thus, for the month of January, which he uses as the basis for his arguments, he finds that the progression of the empirical probabilities <note>original: "W." for "Wahrscheinlichkeit"</note> closely approaches the progression of those theoretical probabilities for which the numbers of white and black balls <note>A reference to the "urn model" in probability, where ratios of colored balls represent likelihood.</note> exist in a ratio of 80 to 20. He notes that the analogy would be even stronger if the ratio of 80:20 were replaced by 81:19. From this, and with regard to the average value <term>Mittelwert: the arithmetic mean or average of a set of numbers</term> he previously reported, he concludes the following¹):

» 1) there exists a daily variation in temperature of four to five degrees, or more precisely 4.7°; this is given by the average of all observations; 2) this variation is subject to the influence of unequal causes; 3) the causes that tend to drive the daily variation to its minimum have more chances in their favor than those that tend to raise it to its maximum, and the chances are in a ratio of 81 to 19, or more simply 4 to 1; 4) the distances from the average to the two limit values are governed by this same ratio of 4 to 1«] <note>original: French quote by Adolphe Quetelet</note>.

[From this, it can be seen that Quetelet’s theory is fundamentally inadmissible insofar as the arithmetic mean is regarded as the most probable value even when asymmetry prevails. However, if this erroneous assumption still seems to find support through experience, it should further be noted that the comparison between theory and experience relies only on the appearance of the tables—that is, the position of the extreme values relative to the mean and the progression of the values lying between them. Consequently, the entire method of investigation possesses little precision and bears the mark of being incomplete. On the other hand, it must be emphasized that Quetelet’s approach leads to the two-sided Gaussian Law <note>The "Bell Curve" or normal distribution; abbreviated in the original as "G. G." for "Gaußsches Gesetz."</note> as soon as the densest value <note>The "mode," or the value that appears most frequently in a data set.</note>, as defined by the Proportional Law, takes the place of the arithmetic mean. The supplement to Chapter **XIX** (§ 136) illustrates this connection.]

## XXVIII. The Asymmetry of Error Series.

§ 180. [There is no doubt that series of errors represent Collective Objects <note>original: "K.-G." for "Kollektiv-Gegenstände," a term used in early statistics to describe a large group of individual values treated as a single mathematical unit.</note>, which allow for the same treatment as the Collective Objects discussed in the preceding chapters. It is, however, questionable whether it is fundamentally necessary on the one hand, or shown to be advantageous in practice on the other, to apply the methods of collective asymmetry to these series. The alternative is to consider whether a premise of essential symmetry should instead be established both theoretically and empirically. Having left this question open in § 8, it shall find its answer here. In doing so, separating the theoretical standpoint from the empirical one is not a pointless exercise. 

For if the laws of asymmetry are fundamentally valid, their application will always bring empirical advantages, provided the treatment is precise enough to allow the difference existing between the arithmetic mean <term>arithmetisches Mittel: the standard average of a set of numbers</term> and the most frequent value <term>dichtester Wert: also known as the "mode"; the specific value that appears most often in a data set</term> to emerge. It is, however, conceivable that the two-sided Gaussian Law <note>original: "G. G." for "Gauß'sches Gesetz," the classic bell curve or normal distribution.</note>, even if not required by theory, might still prove effective in practice, insofar as—compare § 95—it accounts for the empirically different values of $m'$ and $m$ (or rather $D$); whereas, according to the simple Gaussian Law, one must substitute $\frac{1}{2}m$ on both sides in place of the likewise empirically different values of $\mu'$ and $\mu$ (or rather $A$).]

Such an observation is intended, on the one hand, to establish the point in time at which the observed star passes through the meridian and, on the other, to determine the zenith distance <term>zenith distance: the angular distance from the point directly overhead (the zenith) to the celestial body being observed</term> at which the passage occurs. Since there are twenty-three such vertical wires, this act can be repeated accordingly, thereby fixing the corresponding point in time each time. 

The second act serves to precisely adjust the instrument as soon as the star approaches the middle of the 23 wires. Regarding its execution, the following should be noted: the setup of the instrument differed from the usual one, as the fine adjustment for the zenith distance was not performed (as is common) by means of a key, but was instead mediated by a chain drive. This chain ran around a knob located on the instrument's clamp arm and—since the clamp arm was firmly connected to the instrument—it was always located in the immediate vicinity of the eyepiece <term>eyepiece: the lens or combination of lenses through which the astronomer looks to see the magnified image</term>. Both acts can therefore be performed without any mutual interference when the instrument is in the position where the clamp is on the east side. # The Asymmetry of Error Series.

These error series show only slight fluctuations within the individual groups, indicating that the eight series in each group form a uniform system, as was already to be assumed based on their origin. The fluctuation range of the errors can be seen from the differences between the upper and lower extremes, *$E'$* and *$E_{,}$*; for the <term>thread distance</term> <note>The physical spacing between the fine wires in the eyepiece of a transit telescope used to time the passage of stars.</note> 2–12 of group $\alpha$, it amounts to only $0^{s}.95$. However, the magnitude of this value is essentially determined by the amount of the upper extreme deviation *$U'$* = $0^{s}.66$, which significantly exceeds the average expected amount and is to be regarded as abnormal.

Above all, however, the values of *$u$* and, in connection with them, those of *$U' — U_{,}$* are of interest, as they allow an answer to the question of whether the asymmetry of the error series should be considered significant or insignificant. Now, the *$u$*-values are consistently very small and occur in an unregulated sequence, sometimes with a positive and sometimes with a negative sign. The same can be said of the differences *$U' — U_{,}$*, which only in group $\alpha$ show no change between signs; here, they rise to a significant height only in the single value of $0^{s}.37$, which, according to the above remarks regarding the associated upper extreme deviation, cannot be taken into consideration. From this, the conclusion follows with certainty that no significant asymmetry is present. Confirmation of this can furthermore be found in the fact that only in 18 out of 32 cases are the signs of *$u$* and *$U' — U_{,}$* opposite to each other. Thus, the <term>inversion law of asymmetry</term> <note>A statistical principle suggesting that in a skewed distribution, the direction of the mean's shift is usually opposite to the direction of the most extreme outliers.</note>—concerning the difference between the deviation numbers and the extreme deviations relative to *$A$*—does not hold true, whereas experience shows it to be valid when significant asymmetry prevails.

§ 182. There is therefore no reason to apply the principles of collective asymmetry to these error series. However, to show that the application of the <term>two-sided Gaussian Law</term> <note>A modified version of the standard normal distribution curve used to account for data that is "lopsided" or skewed.</note> offers no advantages over the simple law regarding the agreement between theory and experience, I provide in the following comparison tables in such a form that the empirical values are compared with those calculated according to both the simple <term>Gaussian Law</term> <note>original: "G. G." (Gaußsches Gesetz); the standard "bell curve" of errors.</note> relative to *$A$* as well as the two-sided Gaussian Law relative to *$D$*—

# The Asymmetry of Error Series. 466

Since both theoretical reasoning and practical experience show that while the two-sided <term>Gaussian Law (G. G.)</term><note>original: "G. G." (Gauß'sche Gesetz), referring to the Normal Distribution or "Bell Curve."</note> is indeed applicable, it offers no real advantage over the simple Gaussian Law, we may consider it a defining characteristic of these error series that their asymmetry is essentially insignificant—merely a result of unbalanced, random occurrences. Consequently, if one were seeking a criterion for judging the quality of error series, one could even use asymmetry itself as such a standard. One might establish the principle that any error series exhibiting signs of significant asymmetry should be discarded.

# Appendix.

## The $t$-Table.

§ 183. [The $t$-table provides the values of the <term>Gaussian Law (G. G.)</term><note>original: "G. G." (Gauß'sche Gesetz), known today as the Normal Distribution or the Error Function.</note>, that is, of the integral

->$\Phi[t] = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int\limits_{0}^{t} \exp [-\tau^2] d\tau$<-

in its dependence on the argument $t = \Theta : \varepsilon \sqrt{\pi}$. Since four-decimal integral values generally suffice for the needs of <term>Collective Measurement Theory</term><note>The study of variability and distributions in large datasets, a precursor to modern statistics.</note>, the four-decimal table, which <insert>Bruno</insert> Kämpfe published in <insert>Wilhelm</insert> Wundt's *Philosophical Studies*, Volume IX, pages 147—150, is first reprinted here as $t$-Table I. However, to provide an additional decimal place for special cases, a five-decimal table is also provided as $t$-Table II in a corresponding scope.]

[Both tables are based in the same way on the seven-decimal table found in <insert>Oskar Edvard</insert> Meyer's *Lectures on Probability Theory*, pages 545—549. But because there, as is customary, the argument values $t$ are listed only to the second decimal place, the second <term>differences</term><note>A mathematical method used to estimate values between known points in a table.</note> would usually have to be used for <term>interpolation</term><note>Calculating an unknown value between two known values.</note>. To save the reader this effort, the argument was extended to the third decimal place in the four-decimal table for the interval $t = 0$ to $t = 1.51$, and in the five-decimal table for the interval $t = 0$ to $t = 2.01$, so that simple interpolation is sufficient everywhere. For this purpose, interpolation was performed in the designated intervals using the formula:

->$f(a + xi) = f(a + \frac{i}{2}) + (x - \frac{1}{2}) f'(a + \frac{i}{2}) +$<-
->$+ \frac{x(x - 1)}{1 \cdot 2} f''(a + \frac{i}{2}) + \frac{x(x - 1)(x - \frac{1}{2})}{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3} f'''(a + \frac{i}{2}) + \dots$<-

based on the seven-decimal table values and utilizing their second differences. The third differences could be disregarded.]

[The arrangement of the tables is modeled after that of logarithm tables. In particular, the asterisks found in individual horizontal rows of Table II indicate that the first decimal printed at the start of the line is to be increased by 1.]

<summary>This appendix introduces the mathematical tables used to calculate values for the Gaussian Law (Normal Distribution). It explains that the tables were expanded to three decimal places to allow for easier calculation (interpolation) by the user.</summary>
<keywords>t-table, Gaussian Law, Collective Measurement Theory, Bruno Kämpfe, Wilhelm Wundt, interpolation, probability theory, mathematical tables</keywords>

# The *t*-Table II.

## **Contributions** to Psychology and Philosophy, edited by Götz Martius. Volume I, Issue 1. Large Octavo. 1896. 4 Marks. <note>The "Mark" (M) refers to the Goldmark, the official currency of the German Empire from 1871 to 1914.</note>

With 4 figures in the text. — Kretzmann, Some notes on the brightness of complementary mixtures. — Martius, On the concept of the specific brightness of color sensation. With 2 figures in the text.

Large Octavo. 1895. 1.60 Marks. <note>Christian Huygens (1629–1695) was a Dutch mathematician and physicist who invented the pendulum clock and proposed the wave theory of light.</note>

## **Engelmann, Th. W.,** Memorial speech for Hermann von Helmholtz. Held on September 28, 1894, in the Great Hall of Utrecht University. Octavo. 1894. —.60 Marks. <note>Hermann von Helmholtz was a towering figure in 19th-century science, known for his work on the conservation of energy and the mathematics of eyesight and hearing.</note>

---

## **Galle, J. G.,** Directory of the elements of comet orbits calculated to date, along with notes and literary references; newly revised, expanded, and continued up to the year 1894. Large Octavo. 1894. 12 Marks. <note>Johann Gottfried Galle was the German astronomer who first observed Neptune in 1846.</note>

> In the compilation of this work, the thoroughness with which it has been done is a striking feature throughout, and Prof. Galle deserves the thanks of all astronomers for the completion of the volume. The information is brought up to the beginning of this year, thus making the book, besides the best, the most recent of all other lists.

->(**Nature**, from September 13, 1894.)<-

---

## **Külpe, Oswald,** Outline of Psychology presented on an experimental basis. With 10 figures in the text. Large Octavo. 1893. Paperback 9 Marks, bound 11 Marks.

> "This work is a very useful, unusually rich textbook of psychology, despite all its brevity. It provides the results of the inductive, experimental school; physiological information is limited to the absolute essentials. The author, a student of Wundt's, <note>Wilhelm Wundt is widely regarded as the father of experimental psychology.</note> demonstrates a steady mastery of the great wealth of facts in his field throughout, a strong independence in his interpretation of them, and good criticism where he has to choose between different views . . . Completeness and brevity are the advantages of the book."

->(**Literary Central Journal** 1894. No. 6.)<-

---

## **Uphues, Goswin K.,** Psychology of Cognition from an empirical standpoint. Volume One. Large Octavo. 1893. 6 Marks.

> "It must be readily admitted that the author has strived in a very careful and exact manner to do justice to his task. — Alongside the care and diligence, it must also be emphasized that the author thinks through his problems in a sharp, consistent, and independent manner. Thus, the section on the 'Origin of our worldview' in particular provides much that is interesting and stimulating."

->(**Journal for Psychology and Physiology of the Sense Organs.** Vol. X, Issue 3/4.)<-

# **Wundt, Wilhelm,** Outline of Psychology. Second Edition.
Octavo. 1897. Paperbound 6 Marks, clothbound 7 Marks. <note>Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920) is widely regarded as the "father of experimental psychology." He established the first formal laboratory for psychological research at the University of Leipzig.</note>

> "We may therefore well indulge in the justified hope that this work—and indeed not only in the specialized scientific world—may find the interest it deserves; the layperson in particular, even one who does not happen to possess much useful prior knowledge, will be able to orient themselves with relative ease in the difficult questions of philosophical research with the help of this expert and incorruptible guide."
->(DR. TH. ACHELIS in the *Täglichen Rundschau* of Nov. 30, 1896.)<-

---

### — **Principles of Physiological Psychology.** Fourth revised edition. Two volumes. With 237 woodcuts. Large octavo. 1893. <note>In Wundt's time, "Physiological Psychology" referred to what we now call experimental psychology—using the methods of physiology to study the mind.</note>

> "This overview is likely sufficient to prove that Wundt's work keeps pace with the progress of the science to whose foundation it has significantly contributed. As has long been recognized, it is unique in its kind through the combination of mastery over physiological facts, methods, and concepts with the critical caution in inference and precision in analysis peculiar only to the strict philosopher. The clarity of the presentation makes it useful even for those who, without pursuing experimental psychology as their specialty, are familiar with the elements of the anatomy and physiology of the nervous system and only wish to follow the progress of this new science."
->(*Literar. Centralblatt.* 1893. No. 26.)<-

---

### — **System of Philosophy.** Second revised edition. Large octavo. 1897. Paperbound 12 Marks, clothbound 14.50 Marks.

> "After Wundt has treated the fields of psychology, logic, and ethics in detailed specialized writings, he gives us in his *System of Philosophy* a coherent presentation of his fundamental philosophical convictions. Without doubt, we are dealing in this work with a very outstanding and significant achievement, which is greeted by us all the more joyfully as it appears at a time that brings a very strong mistrust to all attempts at philosophical system-building. When such a work originates from a man who, through his scientific past, provides from the outset a sufficient guarantee for the solidity of the empirical foundation of his structure—especially regarding the natural sciences—it will in any case be highly suitable for helping to dispel a multitude of prejudices that still stand in the way of an unbiased and somewhat benevolent reception of metaphysical investigations."
->(GEORG ERHARDT in *Zeitschrift f. Philosophie.* Vol. 102. Issue 1.)<-

---

->Printed by Breitkopf & Härtel in Leipzig.<-
